# The Spiritual Sun / by Bartholomeus Korndorffer.

Take four *Loth* <note>A historical unit of weight, roughly equivalent to half an ounce or 15 grams.</note> of mercury sublimate <note>original: "Mercurij sublimatum," or mercuric chloride, a highly toxic white crystalline powder.</note> and pour a strong nitric acid <term>Aquafort <note>original: "Aquafort" (aqua fortis), literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid.</note></term> over it so that it rises a hand’s breadth above it. Always distill off half of the water over gentle heat in an ash bath <note>A container filled with ashes used to distribute heat evenly around a glass vessel.</note>. Pour it back on, and distill it off again. Do this four times, pouring on and drawing off; the final time, use strong heat so that all the "volatile gold" <note>The alchemist likely refers to the yellow-colored distillate resulting from the reaction of mercury and acid.</note> rises over along with the water.

When it has all risen over, distill it very gently in a water bath <term>Balneo Mariæ <note>literally "Mary's Bath," a double boiler used for consistent, gentle heating.</note></term> for a short while until the watery parts <term>Phlegma <note>In alchemy, the "phlegm" is the tasteless, watery, or inactive part of a distilled liquid.</note></term> are removed; thus is the oil of the Spiritual Sun prepared.

Take four *Loth* of Armenian clay <term>Bolus Armeni <note>A red, iron-rich earth traditionally used in alchemical seals and as a flux.</note></term> and six *Loth* of common salt; grind them together finely. Take eight *Loth* of fine silver and place the powder in a crucible <note>A heat-resistant container for melting metals.</note> with the silver in the middle. Seal the crucible with lute <note>original: "perlutier," meaning to seal the vessel with a clay paste to make it airtight.</note>. The silver must lie entirely within the substance. Let it flow strongly for two hours in a wind furnace <term>Windofen <note>A furnace designed to create a natural draft through a chimney to reach higher temperatures.</note></term>. Afterward, take it out and let it melt by itself in a crucible; add a little borax <term>Borras <note>A flux used to help metals melt and to remove impurities.</note></term>. Pour it out and beat it into thin rolls. Place these in a glass vial so they do not lie upon one another. Pour the Spiritual Sun over them and seal the glass. Set it in gentle warmth, just as the sun shines, for sixteen days. Then the silver will become entirely black-brown and will be graded <term>gradieren <note>The process of increasing the purity, color, or "grade" of a metal.</note></term> through and through into gold of the best and highest degree. Afterward, pour off the "hellish water" <note>original: "hellisch Wasser," likely referring to the potent, corrosive acidic oil.</note> so that you spill nothing. Wash the silver that has become gold several times with clean water. Melt it together with an equal weight of common gold; thus you have the best and most excellent gold, highly graded in weight <term>pondus <note>Latin for weight or heaviness.</note></term>; in its coloration <term>Coloriz <note>Refers to the depth and quality of the gold's color.</note></term>, it will withstand all tests.

When you notice that the nitric acid from the Spiritual Sun has evaporated and it appears somewhat dry, always moisten it with six *Loth* of strong nitric acid and add five *Loth* of purified silver. Let it stand for sixteen days. You can do this again and again, for it does not lose its strength. Bartholomeus Korndorffer.

### A true and just process / or, the bringing of four ounces <term>Loth <note>A German unit of weight, roughly 14–16 grams.</note></term> of **Gold** <term>☉</term> into the **Mark** <note>A unit of weight for precious metals, approximately 8 ounces.</note> of **Silver** <term>☾</term> / as I myself (says Korndorffer) have seen.

Now take one ounce <term>Loth</term> of the first prepared Redness of Antimony, two ounces of the prepared Blade Dross, and one ounce of **red arsenic**. ## Following is the Process with Gold.

This is the true Philosophical fixation upon leaden <term>Viscosa <note>a "viscous" or sticky intermediate substance</note></term> which common laboratory workers call Mercury of Lead <note>original: ☿ ♄</note>; and it is to be known that Gold <note>original: ☉</note> does not allow itself to be mastered into a *Viscosa* as easily as Silver <note>original: Luna</note>.

Afterward, draw off the *Aqua regis* until dry. This Gold <term>☉ <note>Gold</note></term>, whether it has remained in a physical body <note>original: "corporaliter"</note> or has become a powder, amalgamate it with the six <term>Loths <note>A historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce.</note></term> of the two viscous substances <note>original: "Viscosis"</note>. ## Note this.

When you have six Loths of the fire-resistant viscous substance made at the beginning, you can add six Loths of raw viscous substance or leaden Mercury <term>☿ ♄</term> for every one Loth [of the fixed matter]. # Another fixation upon Moon <term>☾ <note>Silver</note></term> with the Viscous Substance
## derived from Saturn <term>♄ <note>Lead</note></term> or Mercury <term>☿ <note>Quicksilver</note></term>.

Take two <term>Loths <note>A historical unit of weight, approximately 15 grams.</note></term> of fine silver <term>☾</term>; beat it very thin, and sulfurize it with sulfur <term>stratum super stratum <note>Latin: "layer upon layer." A technique where alternating layers of metal and sulfur are placed in a crucible.</note></term>, judged by eye in a crucible. Do this three times, so that the sulfur penetrates it well; then grind it small, and add one Loth of <term>Salmiax <note>Sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride), used as a flux to help metals volatilize or "rise."</note></term> beneath it. Put it in a flask, and pour upon it four Loths of unique <term>Jafaron <note>Likely "Saffron," referring to a metallic oxide or a specific chemical oil used as a solvent.</note></term> until it sizzles a little. Distill it <term>per latus <note>Latin: "through the side," using a retort or a side-neck flask.</note></term> out of the sand bath into another flask until it reaches an oily consistency. Pour the water back upon it and draw it off as before; do this three times, so that the Silver <term>☾</term> rises over through the side. Afterward, draw the water gently from the material in the receiver until it is dry. Then coat the glass with <term>lute <note>A protective clay-based sealant.</note></term> and drive it strongly with coal fire; thus the body of the silver <term>☾</term> rises up with the sal ammoniac. Scrape it off into a glass dish and pour warm water over it so that the sal ammoniac dissolves away; then the <term>viscosa <note>The "viscous substance"—a thickened, metallic oil or resin-like state of the metal.</note></term> falls to the bottom; dry this.

->An alchemical symbol consisting of three horizontal bars crossed by two vertical bars, resembling a grid or grate.<-

Recipe: Take 8 Loths of the viscous substance made from Lead <term>♄</term>, which the vagabonds <note>A derogatory term for traveling, self-taught, or fraudulent alchemists.</note> call Mercury of Saturn <term>☿ ♄</term>, which is merely quickened and yet spiritual; it must not be fluid. Place it in an earthenware <term>sublimatorium <note>A vessel designed for sublimation, where solids are heated to become vapor and then re-solidify at the top.</note></term> upon a pound [containing] 5 Loths of <term>Spongrün <note>Verdigris or "Spanish Green," a copper acetate.</note></term> at the bottom <note>original: "in fundo"</note>, and on top of that, a finger's breadth of <term>Eysensinther <note>Iron dross or forge scales, likely used for its iron oxide content.</note></term> that has been washed clean. It will rise up as a white powder; scrape this off. Take 7 Loths of this and 1 Loth of the Silver <term>☾</term> viscous substance; grind them both together until they have become one thing.

->An alchemical symbol consisting of three horizontal bars crossed by two vertical bars.<-

Now take 4 Loths of fresh viscous Lead <term>♄</term> or Mercury <term>☿</term> that has been previously quickened, cleanly washed <note>original: "abluiert"</note>, or boiled in fresh vinegar. Make an <term>amalgama <note>A mixture of mercury with another metal.</note></term> with three <term>quintle <note>A small weight, about 3.7 grams.</note></term> of fine silver <term>☾</term>. Grind into it one Loth of the two previously ground viscous substances of the Moon [Silver]. Put it all together in a flat glass, sealed with lute at the top. Place it in the sand bath with a low fire for eight days and nights so that nothing rises from it. Afterward, for eight days and nights with a strong fire, and for a third eight days even stronger; thus it will all become fixed and fire-resistant. Of this, take 4 Loths; add to it again as before 4 Loths of fresh Mercury of Saturn <term>☿ ♄</term>. Let it fix slowly for eight days, and then strengthen it with fire for 12 days; thus the 4 Loths are fixed once more. In this way, every 20 days and nights, add four Loths of fresh Mercury of Saturn <term>☿ ♄</term>. When you have taken out the four Loths you previously fixed, you will have an eternal fixation. Do not attempt more than four Loths at once; Nature will not endure it.

## A short way to make the two Viscous Substances <term>Viscosa <note>Refers to thick, oily, or "sticky" alchemical extracts believed to hold the essential soul of a metal.</note></term> out of Moon <term>☾ <note>Silver</note></term> and Saturn <term>♄ <note>Lead</note></term>, which one otherwise must make from each individually.

Take two <term>Loths <note>A historical unit of weight, about 15 grams.</note></term> of fine silver <term>☾</term> and 4 Loths of common lead <term>♄</term>; melt these two metals together and sublimate them four times, for four hours each; layer them <term>stratificiers <note>The process of "stratification," placing materials in alternating layers.</note></term> in a crucible with pure, common sulfur. Afterward, grind the metals small and put them into a flask <term>Kolbenglaß</term>; add one and a half Loths of sal ammoniac <term>Salmiar</term> to it. Pour four Loths of <term>Jassoron <note>Likely "Saffron" (Crocus), referring to a metallic oxide or an alchemical oil used as a solvent.</note></term> upon it. Distill it "through the side" <term>per latus <note>Using a retort or side-neck flask to draw off vapors laterally.</note></term> out of the sand bath; four times take this material into the receiver <term>Fürlegglaß</term> and draw the water off gently. Afterward, coat the glass with <term>lute <note>A protective clay sealant.</note></term> and drive it strongly with a coal fire. Thus, the viscous substances <term>Viscosma</term> rise upward. Scrape them off again, as described above, and wash them <term>abluiers <note>From the Latin "abluere," to wash or rinse.</note></term> with warm water, then dry them again; thus they are ready. Amen.

# How One Should Clarify the Seven Metals.

If you intended to take up metals with all kinds of filth <note>original: "Sudelwerck," referring to impurities or base, poorly-prepared materials</note> and try to make them into a perfect metal (as you call it), such as Gold <term>☉ <note>The Sun/Gold</note></term> and Silver <term>☾ <note>The Moon/Silver</note></term>—which are actually imperfect in themselves—yet make them good and stable in all tests: you will not achieve this with all your art in this case. You have not investigated the possibilities of nature within the metals. You and your crowd always work with the impossible, whereby one deceives the other, often costing life, honor, and property, and the true secret art is suppressed and brought to shame. In short, our alchemists want to make Gold <term>☉</term> and Silver <term>☾</term> out of unclarified metals, and afterwards they find nothing but filth and dung. Since this my hidden art is so important to you, as you report—nearly losing your mind with many thoughts over it—and since you would gladly have the foundation of this truth, and are also destined for it by the influence of the Almighty's grace: So I send you not only the right foundation from which you proceeded, the Mercury of Saturn <term>☿ ℏ <note>Mercury of Lead</note></term>, but all seven metals by a short way, to precipitate and to <term>tinge <note>From "tingirn," meaning to transform or "dye" a substance into another state, usually into gold or silver.</note></term> one into the other, with which everything is to be established. If you now know the right foundation to dissolve and clarify all metallic bodies and bring them into a **running dry water**, <note>An alchemical term for a liquid that does not wet the hands, often a metaphor for a purified solvent or a specific state of mercury.</note> you will bring this to an end, which I have explained to you according to my practice.

Although some vagabonds <note>original: "Landstreicher," a disparaging term for fraudulent traveling alchemists</note> forcibly bring some metals into their running water, and with many absurd corrosive substances (which are more harmful to the metals, whereby they lose their best power), yet this is not the way which belongs to my *precipitated practice* <note>original Latin: "Practicam præcipitatem"</note> of the metals. Rather, you, as a faithful follower of this art, will undoubtedly also encounter my short way for the *restoration of metals* <note>original Latin: "restaurationem metallorum"</note> in the meantime. This foundation, of which our ancient Egyptians wrote, I did not wish to hide from you, in a secret and trusted opinion (which you should keep hidden from all the godless). I commend myself to your prayers. Given in the 37th year. <note>Likely 1537, a period during which Paracelsus was active.</note>

->ℏ.<-

The first metal, Saturn <term>ℏ <note>Lead</note></term>, precipitates itself with its clarified body with its own kind, down to a simple powder; and this powder immediately tinges a clarified leaden body also into a precipitate or powder with its fixation, established and precipitated again for 30 hours. If this **Salamandrine** <note>Referring to the salamander, a mythical creature believed to live in fire; in alchemy, this implies a substance that is fire-resistant or "fixed."</note> precipitate is soaked with the water of the clarified body, then one part tinges 30 parts Silver <term>☾</term> into Gold <term>☉</term>, and this precipitate well covers all costs—unless the Mercury of Saturn <term>☿ ℏ</term> is made at great expense.

# How One Should Clarify the Seven Metals.

->centered text<- ☉ <note>The Sun / Gold</note>

The second metal, Gold <term>☉</term>, precipitated with its corresponding clarified body; one part of this precipitate cast upon eight parts of Mercury <term>☿</term>, Saturn <term>♄ <note>Lead</note></term>, or Luna <term>☽ <note>Silver</note></term>, tinges <note>original: "thingiert," meaning to transmute or color a base substance into a noble one</note> into the best Gold <term>☉</term>.

->centered text<- ☽ <note>The Moon / Silver</note>

Luna <term>☽</term>, the third metal; this clarified body precipitated with a clarified metal, tinges one part of purged Venus <term>♀ <note>Copper</note></term> in the flow into the best Luna <term>☽</term>, as well as Mercury <term>☿</term> and Saturn <term>♄</term>.

->centered text<- ♂ <note>Mars / Iron</note>

Mars <term>♂</term>, the fourth metal, precipitated with its corresponding clarified metal; when this precipitate is finely prepared, it gives three <term>Loth <note>A traditional German unit of weight, approximately 15-16 grams or half an ounce.</note></term> of Gold <term>☉</term> into one <term>mark <note>A weight unit, usually equal to 8 ounces or 16 Loth.</note></term> of Luna <term>☽</term>.

->centered text<- ♀ <note>Venus / Copper</note>

Venus <term>♀</term>, the fifth metal; this clarified body, precipitated with another clarified metal, tinges three parts in one mark of fine Luna <term>☽</term> into Gold <term>☉</term>.

->centered text<- ♃ <note>Jupiter / Tin</note>

Jupiter <term>♃</term>, the sixth metal; this clarified corpus <note>body</note> precipitated with its corresponding sublimated metal. This precipitate tinges one part to four parts; it purges Jupiter <term>♃</term> into Luna <term>☽</term> and precipitates Mercury <term>☿</term> again <term>per se <note>by itself</note></term>.

->centered text<- ☿ <note>Mercury / Quicksilver</note>

The seventh metal, Mercury <term>☿</term>, with its four bodies and essences—elements drawn from the bodies of the metals—fixed and precipitated. One part of this precipitate cast upon two parts of molten Luna <term>☽</term> remains as Gold <term>☉</term>.

## Explanations of the Aforementioned Precipitates.

Take three Loth of Mercury of Saturn <term>☿ ♄ <note>Mercury derived from Lead</note></term> and one Loth of Mercury of Gold <term>☿ ☉</term>; to this add an <term>Orth <note>A small weight unit, typically a quarter of a Loth.</note></term> of a Guilder's worth of pure gold calx <note>original: "Goldkalch," gold reduced to a fine powder through heating or chemical action</note> for a ferment or seed. For whatever seed you see in the ashes <note>Referring to the ash-bath used to provide gentle, even heat to the vessel</note>, that you shall have. Precipitate this according to custom in a vial until it turns into a fixed precipitate; then add again as much Mercury of Saturn <term>☿ ♄</term> as the precipitate weighs. However, always take a little gold calx first and precipitate it again into a fixed precipitate. You may augment <note>Increase the quantity or potency</note> this as often as you wish. But it tinges no more than the sixth part into Gold; if, however, this precipitate is again pressed into the Mercury of Gold <term>☿ ☉</term> and precipitated, it tinges 30 parts into Gold <term>☉</term>.

# The Bishop’s Spring
## or Graduating Water/
### in which fine silver is graduated into good gold in four hours.
### A True Process.

How one should distill and prepare a truly excellent and strong Graduating Water <term>Gradierwasser <note>In alchemy, a "graduating water" was a solution used to "improve" or "graduate" a metal—specifically to turn silver into gold or to increase the purity and color of gold.</note></term> according to chemical usage, which graduates silver into the best gold without loss <note>original: "ohn raub," literally "without robbery," meaning no mass is lost in the process</note>, and creates great, unspeakable profit through which many thousands of <term>marks <note>A traditional weight unit, usually equal to 8 ounces.</note></term> of gold can be obtained. Furthermore, such gold does not lose its grade in the manner of gold during the cupellation of <term>Saturn <note>Lead. "Abtreiben deß Saturni" refers to the process of cupellation, where gold or silver is refined by melting it with lead.</note></term>, and it lacks nothing in any examinations <note>original: "Examinibus," refers to assaying tests to prove the metal's purity.</note>, but rather it is high and beyond high gold. This graduating water also has a swift operation for graduating. Now, whoever prepares this graduating water and whoever receives it, let him keep it hidden; it will not fail you, and you have a great treasure herein. Do not forget the poor; let this be dear to you, for this was the piece that brought me joy; no such truth is to be found in all other graduating waters. This graduating water is also to be used without ceasing, as follows hereafter.

Take four <term>Loth <note>A German unit of weight, approximately 15-16 grams.</note></term> of Hungarian gold, which has no additives; beat it thin, and take two Loth of <term>Cinnabar <note>Mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral used often in alchemy as a source for both mercury and sulfur.</note></term>; grind it into a fine powder and arrange it layer upon layer <note>Latin: "stratum super stratum"</note> in a cementing crucible. Keep it closed and calcine it <note>heat it to a high temperature without melting it</note> in a charcoal fire. Take it out after it has stood for half an hour; grind it on a hard stone until it is almost imperceptible. Afterward, take it and put it into a glass flask and pour a strong <term>Aqua Regia <note>Latin for "Royal Water," a mixture of acids (typically nitric and hydrochloric) capable of dissolving gold.</note></term> over it, about eight Loth. Place it in a <term>Mary’s Bath <note>Latin: "Balneum Mariae," a water bath used for gentle, even heating.</note></term> and distill it through an alembic head. Pour the liquid back onto the residue and draw it off again; do this five times, always until no more drops come over. The distillation should happen very slowly, as the gold then putrefies <note>decomposes or breaks down into its primary components</note> all the better. Afterward, take the dry residue that remains behind, which will be like a paste; pour a very sharp distilled wine vinegar over it, so that it stands quite high above it. Let it remain covered—

# Concerning the Philosopher's Stone, John of Padua

...ation of the perfect whiteness, when you should bring the one part—which is the <term>male seed</term> <note>The "male seed" typically refers to the alchemical principle of Sulfur, representing the active, solar force.</note>—to redness with a stronger fire without any additives, as has been mentioned here in many places. And maintain the fire thus sweetly, with gentle, mild warmth, so that when you feel with your hand, or touch the innermost vessel, you feel and find a comfortable, better warmth against your hand.

## The Third Degree of Fire

The third degree of fire shall be increased once more, immediately after the last <term>putrefaction</term> <note>Putrefaction is the stage where the matter turns black, symbolizing death and decay before its rebirth and purification.</note> when the <term>male and female seeds</term> <note>The union of the male (Sulfur) and female (Mercury) principles to create the "Rebis" or hermaphroditic beginning of the Stone.</note> have been mixed together; specifically, when you feel with your hand that you cannot well endure the heat against the glass or the inner part of the furnace for very long. Yet, see to it that you do not make the fire too great; otherwise, as has been said, it will <term>sublimate</term> <note>To turn directly from a solid to a vapor, which in this context risks the material escaping or the vessel exploding.</note> and you will bring the work to nothing.

->And take diligent note.<-

When you make and govern your fire well and gently, so that it does not exceed the internal warmth, then you are certain and secure in your work to accomplish it perfectly. For note: when the internal warmth of the <term>body</term> <note>The "body" refers to the physical matter or "corpus" being transformed in the vessel.</note> is awakened by and through the outermost heat of the fire, then the matter has enough fire to act perfectly within its own nature and to bring forth the fruit without doubt through the power of nature. And even if you had performed the work ten times before, you still must not govern your fire with haste. Wherever you do so, your work is spoiled.

## How to Make the Philosophical Fire

Just as I have told you the degrees of fire, I will also tell you from what our fire is made. In the beginning (to make your fire of the first degree, which is for the <term>solution</term> <note>The stage of dissolving the solid matter into a liquid state.</note> and putrefaction), take a <term>wick</term> which is called an "eternal wick," which is made of <term>feathered alum</term> <note>original: "Alumine plumolo" or "Federweiß." For in such decay, the internal natural power and warmth begins to soften the subtlety of the body, tenderly and sweetly. Thus you have the method for how the fire should be made. However, in the separation of the <term>Elements</term> <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, which the alchemist seeks to isolate and then recombine.</note>, there is another distinction, which is a distillation from the ashes to maintain the fire; and the Elements are not drawn over by the <term>Philosophical Fire</term> <note>Philosophical fire refers to a specific, constant, and regulated heat, often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen, rather than a common kitchen fire.</note>.

## How the Vessels Should Be.

For your needs, five or six glasses are enough. For it is not necessary that you have more glasses, provided they are strong, as the manual labor will teach and show you. But note: the glass should be completely round at the bottom, thick and strong, and made of <term>Venetian lumps</term> <note>original: "Venedischen Procken". Refers to high-quality Venetian glass, prized in the Renaissance for its clarity and ability to withstand heat.</note>, of a reasonable length, and led up finely and evenly so that the <term>Spirits</term> <note>The volatile vapors or gases released during heating.</note> have no obstruction in the middle and have a free path to operate.

### Must the warmth also rule around the top of the glass in which the matter is contained?

Yes. For if you govern the warmth conveniently, well, and everywhere, you will bring your work to its end all the better. Therefore, the inner part of the furnace has a reception and a reflection <note>An architectural feature of the furnace designed to bounce heat back onto the vessel.</note>, so that the warmth must remain and rule around the entire glass.

## Making the Seal of Hermes.

Bury the glass in the earth, surrounded by manure <note>Manure was frequently used as a source of steady, low-level "digestive" heat.</note>, and afterward fill it in everywhere with earth. However, the glass must protrude above the earth as far as you wish to weld it shut. After that, make a <term>circle-fire</term> <note>original: "Circulfewr". A ring of fire placed around an object to heat it evenly from all sides.</note> at a distance around it until the glass is gently warmed. Then make a fire reasonably strong so that the glass stands glowing in the middle of the hot coals, and have a pair of tongs made as hot as possible; then press the neck of the glass firmly together, and it will weld itself together into one piece. # What should he do, to whom Almighty God communicates this incomparable treasure through His blessing?

He should praise and glorify God daily in all his actions and omissions, and be grateful to Him for the high and unspeakable gifts of His Divine blessing, leading and showing an honorable and modest conduct toward everyone, to help the poor therewith. For what you do to these, you have done to God.

# If God has given you this blessed treasure, how should you further conduct yourself?

God has given you such a treasure to use with sensible and good reason, to be grateful to God, not to wastefully misuse it with any pride or pomp of eating and drinking, or other extravagant pastimes. Rather, fear God above all things and remember what a high treasure God has bestowed upon you above other men, wherein much secret wisdom is hidden, so that you see and recognize wonderful effects, how Nature governs and indicates God's gracious will. Therefore it is an inexhaustible treasure, so that you may help poor, needy people, as fellow-brothers of Christ, therewith. Thus understand, that God has placed all His gifts or goods in your hands as a <term>steward</term> <note>original: "Factor." For God, who gave you such gifts, also wants to be honored for them, for He is the Lord who created and gave everything.

# Should one then not be joyful with such a treasure, but rather fear God too much?

Almighty God forbids no joy; rather He commands joy in the Lord Jesus Christ. But to be joyful in shame and vice, and other immodest conduct, does not please God. But to be joyful with reason, observing God's commandments therein, not to offend your neighbor with bickering and quarreling, but to do everything with patience and joyful steadfas-

In the beginning, all <term>metallic bodies</term> <note>original: "Leichnam" (literally "corpses"); in alchemy, this refers to the solid, physical form of a metal.</note> were intended to be made into <term>Gold</term> <note>symbol: ☉</note> and <term>Silver</term> <note>symbol: ☾</note>. And that this does not happen is due perhaps to impure sulfur that is mixed with the quicksilver, or from the foul earth in which they come together. In the same way that a child in its mother’s womb contracts a sickness, either from impure seed, or, if the <term>matrix</term> <note>the "womb" or environment where the metal forms</note> is already quite clean, the child nevertheless becomes sick from the place where it lies in its mother’s body, which is foul and impure. It is exactly the same with the metallic bodies that come out of the earth.

<margin>Note: <term>Saturn</term> <note>symbol: ♄</note> <unclear>This is further detailed</unclear> on page 458.</margin>
Now you should know that there is a distinction between all metallic bodies; this comes from various types of sulfur, which is nothing other than the moisture of the earth. If the sulfur is black and soft, and is transformed during the maturation in its veins, then a mixture occurs through the power of a star called Saturn. This star governs Lead; for from this mixture and the influence of the star, Lead grows in the earth.

<margin><term>Jupiter</term> <note>symbol: ♃</note></margin>
If the sulfur is white and cloudy, and remains in maturation in its veins, then a mixture occurs from which Tin grows in the earth, by the power of a star called Jupiter.

<margin><term>Mars</term> <note>symbol: ♂</note></margin>
If the sulfur is black and hard, and is processed during maturation in its veins, then a mixture is formed by the influence of the planet Mars, and it becomes Iron.

<margin><term>The Sun</term> <note>symbol: ☉</note></margin>
If the sulfur is red, clear, transparent, and pure, and is transformed during the pure maturation in the veins of the earth, then a mixture occurs by the influence of the Sun, and Gold grows in the earth.

<margin><term>Venus</term> <note>symbol: ♀</note></margin>
If the sulfur is red and cloudy during the maturation through the mixture of the star Venus, then Copper grows in the earth.

<margin><term>Mercury</term> <note>symbol: ☿</note></margin>
You should also know that <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Koch"; likely a shorthand or dialect for "Quecksilber" or the process of "coction" (cooking/maturation).</note> also grows in the earth by the power of a star called Mercury.

<margin><term>The Moon</term> <note>symbol: ☽</note></margin>
But if the sulfur is white, clear, and transparent, and is transformed during the pure maturation in the veins of the earth, then a mixture arises from which Silver grows in the earth, by the power and dominion of a star called the Moon.

These are the seven planets, by whose power and dominion the metallic bodies in the earth are born and created.

Up to this point, I have spoken of how the metallic bodies in the earth come to be, and how they differ from one another in *accidental form, and not in their innate nature* <note>original: "forma accidentali, & non in innata"; this means that while they look different (accidental), their internal "metallic essence" is the same.</note>. Now I will instruct you further, so that the noble art may be proven true, in order that we may counter those who say the art is false.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of alchemical transformation. Having previously discussed how metals are generated in the earth from sulfur and mercury under planetary influences, the author now addresses critics who cite Aristotle to claim that the "Form" of a metal cannot be changed. ### Of the Key of Chemical Philosophy.
<note>original: "De Claui Philosophiæ Chemicæ"</note>

There are several who do not rightly recognize or understand the true Art <note>Alchemy</note>, and yet contradict it, not rightly knowing what its nature is, outwardly or inwardly. They throw at us <term>Aristotle's</term> <note>The Greek philosopher whose theories on the four elements and the "permanence of species" were often cited by critics to argue that one metal could not become another.</note> opinion that the **Form** <note>original: "Forma"; the essential identity or soul of a substance in Aristotelian philosophy.</note> cannot be truly transformed. But this is spoken by those who think they want to transform the **bodies** <note>original: "Corpora"; the physical metals.</note> while they are still impure, which undoubtedly cannot happen. These same people hear a word that follows, which is: that "un-malleability" <note>original: "unschmeidigkeit"; brittleness or lack of ductility.</note> destroys the form of these things, especially in the **metallic bodies**. <note>original: "Leichnamen" (literally "corpses"); the solid, physical state of metals.</note> That is true, when an

<margin>Ash</margin>
**body** is reduced to ash and well washed with sharp water <note>original: "scharpffem Wasser"; likely an acid or corrosive solvent.</note>, and ground small, and so often drenched and dried until it becomes like white

<margin>white, living lime</margin>
snow and a **living lime**: <note>original: "lebendiger Kalch" (quicklime); a chemically reactive state of a mineral.</note> Thus, from the ashing and various washings, the bodies lose their corrupt moisture and gain a foreign and purified moisture which directs and cleanses the metallic body; and from this, the purified ash is brought back to a hard, flowing water <note>likely referring to a molten state or the 'mercury of the philosophers'</note>, which may then receive white and red color. <note>White and red are the two final stages of the Great Work, representing Silver and Gold.</note>

Now it is also true that at various times things also receive **Form**. This is well demonstrated to us by **Realgar** <note>original: "Ruschgelb" (arsenic disulfide); an orange-red mineral.</note>, which appears red, and when one roasts it, it becomes black, and when one separates it according to the teachings of the Art, it becomes white—and yet it remains that which it was before.

We also see that **Vitriol** <note>original: "Atrament"; a sulfate mineral used to make ink and acids.</note> has a black color, and when one roasts it, it becomes red, and yet it is still Vitriol. Some may say that such things easily transform from one color into another, but that it is impossible for the metallic bodies. To them I answer: with an obvious matter and with many proofs, I shall nullify their speech.

Now we see openly that from **Silver**, fine **Azure** <note>original: "Lasur"; a blue pigment. The author argues that if silver can become blue, its "form" has been altered.</note> is made, and yet it is pure in its nature from all filth; and the form derived from it is more easily destroyed than the unborn form.

### Concerning the Key of Chemical Philosophy.
<note>original: "De Claui Philosophiæ Chemicæ"</note>

Now is the time for us to write further concerning the beginning of this noble Art. And first, I will teach you how to build the furnaces that are required for this Art, and how many of them there should be, or how they should be made. One thing you should know is that you must build your furnace according to the size of the Great Work you intend to perform. If you are undertaking a large work, make the furnace accordingly larger; but if you have only a little, make them small in proportion. Nevertheless, I will give you instructions for making a moderate furnace that would suit both the rich and the poor.

<margin>The first furnace.</margin> First, I will teach you how to make a masterly furnace, which you shall build in this way: You should build it by a wall, about one ell <note>An "ell" is a historical unit of length, roughly 24 to 45 inches depending on the region.</note> or a little further from the wall. There, dig a pit, which you should coat well on all sides with the **Lute of Wisdom** <term>Luto Sapientiæ</term> <note>A heat-resistant paste or cement used by alchemists to seal vessels and line furnaces.</note>. In this pit, there should be a wind-vent passing through the earth, and the air into the pit should be narrow at the opening in the pit, but a span wide on the outside by the wall where the wind and air enter; this should also be well-coated with the **Lute of Wisdom**. After this, build a wall over the pit using pure, common clay, adding a fifth part of potter's clay and a little fine sand, mixing it all together exceedingly well. With this clay, build a wall upwards over the pit, two feet <note>original: "Schuch," an archaic spelling of "Schuh" or foot.</note> high and a span thick, and make it round <note>original: "sinwel," an archaic term for circular or spherical.</note>; let it dry thoroughly. Then, have a potter make a disc from noble earth that can well withstand the fire, according to the dimensions of the furnace. This disc should have 50 or 60 holes throughout; these should be narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, so that one might poke their smallest finger through them, so that the coals, ashes, and small stones that fall into them may better pass through. Place the disc upon the furnace so that the narrow end of the holes faces upward. Afterward, build a wall over the furnace disc, nearly an ell high in thickness. Below, above the disc, make a moderate hole through which to pour coals, and at the top of the furnace, also make a hole where one puts in whatever is to be calcined <note>To "aschen" or calcine: to reduce a substance to powder or ash through prolonged heat.</note> or burned. For this same hole, you should make a lid of good potter's clay, well-tempered, so that you may cover the hole with it; the furnace, however, should remain round. And at the top, make three or four holes around the furnace, two fingers wide, to give the furnace air.

Furthermore, know that you should place a tripod upon the disc, or a stand made of good clay, so that one may set the vessels upon it in which one intends to burn or calcine. And beneath it, make a coal fire <term>Kolfewr</term>, for a coal fire burns or calcines more purely than one made of wood.

# Concerning the Key of Chemical Philosophy.
<note>original: "De Claui Philosophiæ Chemicæ"</note>

<margin>Elixir</margin>
A powder that the masters call "Elixir." Elixir is an Arabic word, and in English it means as much as a leaven or yeast <note>original: "Urhab oder Gerben." Just as leaven causes dough to rise and transform into bread, the alchemical elixir transforms "base" metals into gold.</note>. For just as bread improves and rises from good yeast, so too do the bodies <term>Corpora</term> <note>The "bodies" refer to the seven basic metals: gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, and mercury (though mercury is often classed as a spirit).</note> rise and transform into gold and silver through these five spirits <term>Spiritibus</term> <note>The "spirits" are the volatile substances: mercury, sulfur, orpiment, sal ammoniac, and sometimes others like marcasite.</note>, and most of all by mercury <term>Koch</term> <note>original: "Koch," literally "Cook." Here it is used as a technical name for quicksilver/mercury, the primary "cooker" or maturing agent of metals.</note>, for it is the origin of all bodies.

<margin>Mercury</margin>
I will instruct you about several others which do not have the power to transform the bodies on their own, but rather they help the five spirits so that they are prepared and can be more easily turned into liquid <note>original: "zu Waſſer macht," literally "made into water," referring to the process of liquefaction or dissolution.</note>. With their liquids, one mixes the ashes of the "corpses" <note>In alchemy, a "corpse" or "carcass" refers to the solid residue—the metallic oxide—left after a substance has been burned or calcined.</note> so that they gain a moisture that restores the corpses. And I will teach you one after the other how each should be prepared or made.

<margin>Mercury</margin>
Quicksilver or mercury <term>Koch</term> is nothing other than a viscous and refined water, gathered through the earth and well-tempered heat, collected within the veins of the earth until the moisture is mixed equally with dryness. And for this reason, it flees away so easily in the fire, yet it does not cling to anything, as its refined nature is well-tempered by dryness and does not allow sticking. Together with sulfur, it is a mother of all "corpses" (metals). It is found in the mountains and sometimes in ancient lakes. Its nature is warm and moist, and it is the root and origin of all bodies <note>original: "omnium Corporum"</note>; they all come from it and all mix with it—though with iron only very harshly—and without it, no other metal can be gilded.

<margin>$\triangle$ is moisture p. 451</margin>
$\triangle$ Sulfur <note>The triangle symbol usually represents the element of fire, but here the margin and text associate it with Sulfur.</note> is the earth's moisture, which is produced in its veins with well-tempered heat until it becomes hard and dry. And when it becomes dry, it is called sulfur. It is of a strong nature and of the same substance as its oil. Therefore, one cannot take its oil from it as one does with others that contain oil, except with strong and sharp waters <note>This refers to corrosive acids like sulfuric or nitric acid used to "extract" the essence of a mineral.</note> by boiling it in them. It is found in the earth, sometimes in mountains or in lakes, and it is of various kinds: one is called the "living" <term>Sulphur Vivum</term>, the other the "dead." The living sulfur is as it is brought out of the earth; the dead is that which has been melted and cast into tubes, as it is found for sale.

<margin>Orpiment</margin>
Orpiment <term>Auripigmentum</term> <note>Orpiment is a deep yellow-orange arsenic sulfide mineral once used as a pigment and in alchemy; its name literally means "gold pigment."</note> is a yellow stone grown in the veins of the earth. It is heated and boiled repeatedly from the earth's refuse and flames until it transforms into orpiment. How one should prepare and make it, however, I will teach later in its proper place.

Take one part common salt, three parts **prepared urine**, and one part **soot** that hangs from the roofs. Boil all this in a kettle until the urine boils away; and thereafter pour more urine on it, and boil it in it again. Do this for seven hours, and thereafter let it dry. And thereafter **sublime** it; that is as much as saying you purify it. Take one part common salt that has been prepared, and the other part sal ammoniac, and grind them together. Thereafter let it cool and break it open; thus you will find the sal ammoniac raised up and separated from the other salt. Take again the common prepared salt and the sal ammoniac as before, grind them, and set it on the stove as before: Do this for 3 hours, <margin>coß:</margin> then it becomes white, and in every way stable, perfect, and right.

### CALCINATION
<note>original: "CALCINATIO"</note>

Thus, **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to cause thermal decomposition or to remove volatile fractions</term> or "ashing" is nothing other—to speak plainly—than a pulverization of any thing through the power of fire, by depriving it of the moisture that it previously held and which bound it together. One powders the **bodies** <term>bodies: the solid, physical matter of a substance, as opposed to its volatile "spirits"</term> so that they become clean of their impurity. Likewise, one powders the **spirits** <term>spirits: volatile substances that easily evaporate or "flee" the fire</term> for this and many other reasons. Firstly, so that the bodies lose their impure taste <note>in early chemistry, "taste" often referred to the chemical essence or reactivity of a substance</note>; and without this, it cannot be. Thus, pulverization was discovered so that one might harden moist bodies therein. For one sees obviously that they become hard by this method, and most especially tin. But as to why one powders the spirits: that is done so that they might become stable all the sooner and transform all the better into water. For certain burnt things are stable in the fire and also turn to water sooner than unburnt ones.

### COAGULATION
<note>original: "COAGVLATIO"</note>

Thus, purification and hardening is nothing other than a deprivation of the watery or moist thing, a restoration of the moisture into a hard mass. For it is often found that mercury is hardened and purified, and that one drives the watery things it has from its moisture out of it and makes it hard. The **mercury** <note>original: "Koch," likely a variant of "Quick," referring to Quicksilver/Mercury</note> is hardened in this way, and one **kills** <term>kills: also known as "mortification," the alchemical process of changing a substance's state or stripping it of its "living" volatile qualities</term> it, by burning it thick with force. For the power of this fire takes away its moisture. And this is done in such a vessel, elongated and narrow in shape, like a canister or an iron pipe.

### FIXATION
<note>original: "FIXATIO"</note>

Thus, **fixation** <term>fixation: the process by which a volatile substance is rendered stable in fire so that it no longer evaporates</term> is nothing other than a companionable purification of fleeing things by the fire. But the reason this was discovered is so that every transformation and change of one thing into another may be complete and stable, and not revert. The imperfect bodies...

### SOLUTION AND LIQUEFACTION
<note>original: "Erlösung und Fliessiung"</note>

Thus, **solution** <note>original: "Erlösung," literally "release" or "redemption," here meaning the dissolving of a solid</note> and **liquefaction** are nothing other than the transformation of any thing that is or will be powdered into water. The reason this was discovered is so that its outer nature might become its inner nature, and also so that one might better **purify** the bodies and the spirits; and thus all its filth is purified and cleansed from it.

Take note that one may turn a thing into water in two ways. Either with heat, or with moisture, such as in a cold pit or in a cellar, as I will teach you hereafter.

### PURIFICATION
<note>original: "Leuterung"</note>

Thus, **purification** <term>purification: in this context, refers to distillation, sublimation, or filtration to remove impurities</term> is nothing other than the raising of an aqueous vapor in its vessel. The preparation is of many kinds: Some purifications are done with fire, some without fire. Those done with fire are of two types: One is upward, as through a cap <note>the "helm" or top of a still</note> or through an **alembic** <term>alembic: a classic distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term>, so that one burns something out together. 

But why each was discovered is so that a water might be purified from its dregs or tannins <note>original: "Heffen oder Gerben"</note> and that one might keep it so that it does not rot. For we see that every pure thing remains beautiful and clear. Especially also it was discovered so that one might dry the spirits and the powders, if this be needed, while having pure and clear water that afterward has no dregs or filth from which the spirits or powders might receive impurity. 

But as to why it was devised to purify downward <note>referring to *distillatio per descensum*, where the vapor is forced downward, often used for heavy oils</note>, that is because of what is pure oil in its nature, or has an expressed nature, which one cannot subdue upward in its flowering nature, as is seen with **petroleum** <note>original: "Petroleo"; referring here to naturally occurring rock oils</note>.

Thus, purification with or through the **felt** <note>filtration through cloth or felt</note> is nothing other than a preparation of hard and unfluid things into something like a soft wax. From this one may note that it was devised so that, due to thirst, nothing may enter the bodies that desires to transform until it is "born" <note>produced or brought into a new state</note> so that it becomes fluid and can enter the bodies.

Thus some believe that the preparation should be with oil and with **sharp waters** <term>sharp waters: strong acids or corrosive chemical solvents</term> <note>original: "scharpffen Wassern"</note>, yet that is nothing, for in no way does one find the truth there. For in the sulfur and orpiment, and their sense, a proof is to be made

Now I have told you what is meant by separating, ashing, watering, purifying, stabilizing, hardening, and bearing. Here I will teach you how you shall separately divide the spirits, and first of all, **mercury** <term>mercury: or quicksilver, regarded by alchemists as one of the three fundamental principles of all matter</term> <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note>.

If you now wish to separate **mercury** and turn it into a snow-white powder: take 1 part **quicklime** <term>quicklime: calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance produced by heating limestone</term> <note>original: "lebendiges Kalchs"</note>, and 1 part powder made from **eggshells**, or 1 part **verdigris** <term>verdigris: a green pigment and chemical prepared by exposing copper to vinegar vapors</term> <note>original: "Kupffergrün"</note>, and one quarter-part **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used as a flux in metallurgy and alchemy</term> <note>original: "Salarmoniac"</note>. Pour this or lay it upon a stone, and pour strong, well-purified **vinegar** upon it, and rub it very firmly together. Then take a portion of the **subject** <term>subject: refers here to the mercury being processed; the text uses the term "Koch" which likely refers to the base material or "the cooked" substance</term> <note>original: "Koch"</note> and add a little of it, and rub it firmly until the **subject** can no longer be seen. Then add a little more of it, and rub it firmly as before, until you have rubbed in all the **subject**. Then make small piles out of it and lay them in a clean vessel, and place it in a warm oven and let them dry. And take care that it does not become too hot, so that the **subject** does not vanish from the heat. And when it is well dried, rub it again with **vinegar** as before, and dry it as before. And this is a sign when it has been rubbed enough: take a little of it and rub it firmly against a silver penny with your fingers; if it sticks to the penny, it has not had enough. <note>Mercury forms an amalgam with silver; if the silver turns white or "sticky," it means the mercury is still in its raw, metallic state and not yet "fixed" or "killed."</note> Thus one shall rub it again with **vinegar** and dry it for as long as it takes until it no longer sticks to the penny when one rubs it thereon.

When you now see that it has had enough, rub it out exceedingly well and small, and make it as dry as you can. Put it into the vessel in which one separates the spirits, and cover it with its lid. And when you lay the prescribed powder into the vessel, level the powder across the top, and close the glass, and seal it well with **lute** <term>lute: a clay or cement paste used to seal alchemical vessels airtight</term> <note>original: "Luto"</note> so that it has no air. And place it in the furnace and give it at first a gentle fire for nearly half a day, until its moisture entirely smokes out through the hole that goes through the cap.

You shall note it thus: take a knife blade or other piece of sheet metal and lay it over the hole. If it becomes black or damp, it has not had enough. But when it no longer sweats, then seal the hole above well with **lute**, and increase the fire more and more. And at the last, make a strong fire.

But when you wish to separate **Orpiment** <term>Orpiment: a deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral formerly used as a pigment and in alchemy</term> <note>original: "Operment"</note> / then you shall grind the Orpiment exceedingly well / and boil it thoroughly in vinegar and urine for two days / just as you did the sulfur / and skim it well. **Realgar** <term>Realgar: an arsenic sulfide mineral, often called "soot-yellow" in older German texts; it is closely related to orpiment</term> <note>original: "Rußgelb"</note> is of the same nature / as Orpiment : But it is not necessary / that one boils it / but grind it right well / and dry it for 3 hours or 4 with strong vinegar / at last grind it thus dry / and add as much hammer scale to it / and mix it well together / and separate it in all things as I have taught you concerning the sulfur / for seven hours or more / so it becomes a snow-white powder / keep that / until I teach you how to make it stable.

**Sal ammoniac** <term>Sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a volatile salt used to "cleanse" or "spiritualize" metals</term> <note>original: "Salarmoniac"</note> you shall make stable thus : Grind it quite small and well / with just as much prepared salt without any moisture / and lay that in the separation-vessel / and separate it with a gentle fire for a good quarter of a day / Thereafter with a strong fire through the day until the morning / Then open it up / and whatever is separated, keep that / And do to it in all things / as I taught you with the mercury / and separate it with the **Hessian [additive]** <note>original: "Hessen"; likely referring to the refractory clay or materials used in Hessian crucibles, or a specific additive from that region used for purification</note> thus for 2 or 3 hours.

Now I have told you / how you shall make the spirits into snow-white powder and separate them : Now I will teach you / how the fire should be / with which you shall separate them. Now know / that it should be a **charcoal furnace** <note>original: "Kolferor," likely a dialect variant of "Kohlenfeuer" (coal-fire) or a specific alchemical furnace type</note> / for two reasons : The first reason is / that it is less work to stoke coals / than wood : The other reason is / that the fire from wood smokes more / than from coals. And therefore one cannot easily burn with it / because the vessels may flow and crack / which then often happens. For they are sometimes made of poor clay / or are not well-fired. And when one of the vessels cracks / then white smoke immediately comes out of the vent / which one sees very quickly on a charcoal furnace. When you see that / then take it immediately from the fire / or you lose your work / and coals / and whatever you lay upon it.

Know also / the topmost separation-vessel / which is called the **upper lid** <note>original: "Oberlyd"</note> / should be well-glazed / and the bottom vessel does not require it. And sometimes it is accustomed to harden in the lower vessel / so that one cannot retrieve it / and it will not separate. Therefore you shall not despair of your work / but take it out / and grind it better / and add more of the Hessian [additive] to it / and separate it with a diligent fire / so it will be well-separated.

to the sinner. For when Saint Anthony, through revelation, had seen the multitude of snares <note>This refers to the "Temptations of St. Anthony," where he saw the world covered in traps laid by the devil.</note>, he cried out to God, saying: Lord, who can be saved? When it is full, let it stand and settle for 3 days, and decant it carefully into another vessel so that the dregs do not follow. Let it stand and settle again, and pour it off as before. Do this as often as necessary until it becomes entirely clear. Then boil it over a gentle fire until it has boiled down thick, and refine it quite purely, and strain it through a felt or through a hat <note>a common method of filtration using a felted wool hat</note>, which is better. Keep it in a glass vessel until you need it.

### PRACTICE.

In the name of God, take red sulfur and <term>orpiment</term> <note>arsenic trisulfide, used for its yellow color; original: "Rauschgelb"</note> that have been separated and fixed <note>referring to substances that have been purified and rendered non-volatile by fire</note>, of each an equal weight. Add to them half as much "water of silver" <note>likely a solution of silver in acid, such as silver nitrate</note> as there is of one of the others. Put these together into a glass with a narrow neck and <term>lute</term> <note>to seal a vessel with an airtight clay or paste; original: "verlutier"</note> it well so that no air may escape. You must do this with fire or with a glowing iron until it melts and fuses together. Then set it in the ashes <note>a sand bath, which provided a gentle, even heat</note> and give it a soft fire, and melt it once it coagulates and becomes hard. Thus it will become a fixed color <note>a tincture or pigment</note> which penetrates and mixes with the <term>body</term> <note>the base metal being transformed; original: "Leichnamb," literally "corpse"</note>, joining and uniting with it, and it remains eternally. Of this powder, place one part by weight upon 100 parts of well-prepared <term>copper</term> <note>original: "♀"</note> or <term>iron</term> <note>original: "♂"</note>; without doubt, it will become white, pure, and good in every test, color, and work, and it remains eternally without end.

If you wish, however, to make another powder that is also certainly good: Take <term>salt</term> <note>original: "Koch," likely referring to common salt or sal-gemme</note>, separated and fixed, one part; sulfur, separated and fixed, also one part; and powdered silver, also one part. Rub these exceedingly well together upon a stone and saturate them with <term>sal ammoniac water</term> <note>ammonium chloride solution</note> three or four times—rubbing, saturating, and drying. Then lay this upon a stone in a damp place and let it turn to water <note>the process of deliquescence, where a substance absorbs moisture from the air until it dissolves</note>, as I have taught you. Keep that which becomes water; the rest you should rub further and saturate more with sal ammoniac water, and lay it again upon the stone in a damp place until it all becomes water. Draw this water through the <term>clarifying-cap</term> <note>a filtration or distillation apparatus; original: "Leuterhut"</note> as I have taught you before. Place the water in a water bath <note>original: "setz das Wasser in Wasser," a bain-marie</note> and not in the ashes, for otherwise it will become too hard for you to purify, and you will lose your labor. And when you have clarified it thus, put it in a glass and seal it as I have just taught you, and melt it with a gentle fire. Then it will become a white and hard matter, as transparent as crystal, which melts in the fire like wax and penetrates the metallic bodies and remains with them. Place one part of this powder upon a hundred parts of any calcined and purified body; it will endure and remain always white and good.

However, I advise you not to use it upon impure <term>copper</term> <note>original: "♀"</note> or bodies, for after the third or fourth test, it will vanish and come to nothing.

If you wish to make a water that separates <term>gold</term> <note>original: $\odot$</note> from <term>silver</term> <note>original: $\leftmoon$</note>, regardless of what kind of gilded material it may be:

Afterward, take urine and strain it through a cloth into a glass, and warm it so that it becomes lukewarm, and then put the alum into it, and let it stand in a cellar for a day and a night; then pour off the urine, and you will find the alum as white and clear as crystal.

# A L C H E M Y
## A Thorough Report /
### concerning what the true Art

->contains and is capable of /<-
->In the Universal and Particular Way,<-
<note>original: "In Via Vniuerfali & Particulari"</note>
->Drawn together<-
->from all the Philosophers.<-

<margin>Calcination of the Imperfect Metals. <note>original: "tio Imperfectorum"</note></margin>
First and foremost, you must know how the four <term>imperfect metals</term> <note>metals that were believed to be "unripe" or chemically unstable compared to gold and silver; original: "Imperfecta Metalla"</note> are <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to powder through heat or chemical action; original: "calciniert"</note>. Namely: <term>Saturn</term> <note>lead; original: "Saturnus"</note> and <term>Jupiter</term> <note>tin; original: "Iupiter"</note> are calcined in one way through salt, and from Saturn comes <term>minium</term> <note>red lead; original: "Menig"</note> and <term>ceruse</term> <note>white lead; original: "Cerussa"</note>. <term>Venus</term> <note>copper; original: "Venus"</note>, however, is calcined through sulfur, and becomes <term>burnt copper</term> <note>copper oxide; original: "Aes vstum"</note>. <term>Mars</term> <note>iron; the OCR "Meeß" is likely a transcription error for "Mars" or "Marß"</note> is calcined through vinegar, and becomes <term>Saffron of Mars</term> <note>iron oxide; original: "Crocus Martis"</note>. However, the calcination of <term>Sol</term> <note>the Sun, representing gold; original: "Solis"</note> and <term>Luna</term> <note>the Moon, representing silver; original: "Lunæ"</note> you will find in the <term>Greater Work</term> <note>the quest for the Philosophers' Stone; original: "Opere Maiori"</note>.

### First follows the Particular Work.

<margin>Which calxes are to be taken. <note>original: "Qui Calces sumendi"</note></margin>
If you now wish to make a <term>Particular</term> <note>a limited alchemical process aimed at a specific result rather than the universal stone; original: "Particular"</note> from the imperfect metals and work toward the "red" <note>the final stage of transmutation</note>, then you must take the <term>calxes</term> <note>metal powders; original: "Calces"</note> of Copper, Iron, or also Lead, which are red in themselves, that is, <term>minium</term> <note>original: "Minia"</note>. But for the "white," take the calxes of Tin or Lead, that is, <term>ceruse</term> <note>original: "Cerussam"</note>.

### What is the Mercury of the Philosophers?
<note>original: "Mercurius Philosophorum quid?"</note>

Next, you must know what the <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>not common quicksilver, but a theoretical "first matter" or essential solvent; original: "Mercurius Philosophorum"</note> is, through which all metals, <term>perfect and imperfect</term> <note>gold/silver and base metals respectively</note>, are dissolved and reduced into <term>First Matter</term> <note>the primordial substance from which all things are made; original: "Primam Materiam"</note>. Regarding how it is prepared, you will find good instruction in the Second Part, "On the Greater Work," "On the Matter of the Stone," in the first chapter. For the <term>Matter of the Stone</term> <note>the raw materials for the Philosophers' Stone; original: "Materia Lapidis"</note> is the same in <term>Universal</term> and <term>Particular</term> works. The Particular works are the same as the Universal, except that the Universal must be worked more subtly and with more effort and time than the Particular. This is because their entire <term>composition</term> <note>original: "Compositum"</note> is nothing but pure gold and silver, and its <term>power</term> <note>original: "Virtute"</note> extends much further—and almost infinitely—as a medicine for human and metallic bodies than the Particular works.

# Now Follows the Second Part
->Concerning the Universal Way, or the Great Work of the Philosophers’ Stone.<-
<note>original: "De Via Vniuersali, siue Opere Maiori Philosophici Lapidis."</note>

This treatise is divided into three parts. First, it tells what the <term>Matter of the Stone</term> <note>original: "Materia Lapidis"; the physical substance used as the starting point</note> is and how it should be prepared. Second, what the <term>Form of the Stone</term> <note>original: "Forma Lapidis"; the essential character or "soul" of the substance</note> is. Third, after the Matter and Form are prepared, how one should put them together according to their proportion and cook them properly, so that the <term>Philosophers’ Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note> may be finished from them.

## CHAPTER ONE,
## Concerning the Matter of the Stone.

Initially, it is necessary to know that this gold, which one intends to use for this purpose, must be prepared through <term>antimony</term> or <term>Aqua Regis</term> <note>literally "Royal Water," a powerful mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold</note>, and thereafter <term>cemented</term> <note>A refining process where metal is heated with powdered additives to remove impurities</note> two or three times, and made as fine as possible. Then take a thick glass, shaped like a <term>urinal</term> <note>A common alchemical flask with a wide body and a neck, named for its resemblance to medical vessels</note>, not very tall. Into it, put twelve times as much weight as the gold plates of <term>Magnesia</term> <note>In this context, an alchemical mineral or flux, not the modern chemical element magnesium</note>, crushed into pieces the size of a hazelnut, or as it pleases you, provided that it can fit into the glass. Thereafter, place the gold plates upon the urinal and fit a <term>helm with a nose</term> <note>An "alembic" or still-head with a protruding spout for distillation</note> that fits correctly onto it. Seal it with <term>lute</term> <note>A specialized alchemical paste or cement used to make joints airtight</note> up over the beak to protect it from the heat so that it does not crack. Have a fine earthenware "hat" made of two pieces to go over it, so that you can surround the little furnace...

For the moisture that is in the sealant is a **spirit**, and one spirit draws another.

When it again will go no further, do in all things as you did the first time. When it has cooled, moisten the joints again, and take the ring of lute that you smeared around it before, remove it, moisten it again, and replace the ring around it. You may carry this on so that you do not need to break anything open until you have distilled 30, 40, or nearly 50 times. In a day and night, if you are not lazy, you may distill 6, 7, or 8 times.

### In the Way Universal & Particular.

...burns and causes the **urinal** <note>a glass flask with a round body and long neck</note> to break and the **magnesia** <note>in alchemy, this term rarely refers to modern magnesium; it usually denotes a crude mineral ore or the "raw matter" of the Stone</note> to be spilled. After that, take another urinal made of thick glass, like the first one was, and put the magnesia from the first urinal into it—or fresh magnesia, if the cost does not trouble you (since it is all the same)—and seal it again as before, and distill it, and drive it until it will no longer drip. **GOD** grant how it is sealed anew; provided that the **helm** <note>the top part of the still</note> sweats a little, but no more drops wish to fall. <margin>urinal of thick glass</margin>
When it will no longer proceed at all (as mentioned), then take the **recipient** <note>the collection vessel</note> with the distilled matter and break it off at the top, and place a **blind helm** <note>a helm without a spout, used to circulate vapors back down</note> upon it, sealing it with egg whites and **quicklime** <note>living lime, a common ingredient for airtight seals</note>, so that no vapor may escape. Take out those same black dregs, grind them fine, and pour your water—which you previously distilled from it in the water bath—back into the former recipient over the ground dregs; seal it quickly again with the blind helm as before, and let it stand in putrefaction for twelve days and nights.

Then distill it again, as before, in all things. Do this with distilling, grinding, etc., until the fifth or sixth time: namely, let it putrefy for ten days the third time, eight days the fourth time, and six days the fifth time. And note: when you wish to distill the oil, always pour the remaining oil among the black dregs or matter (which is like melted wax and remains in the glass after the water) and distill them down together again: with this, sharpen your oil and **Air** <note>original Latin: Aërem</note>. Also pay attention that if you obtain ten **loth** <note>a unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce</note> of water after all these separations, you should not have more than one loth of oil; for that is the right proportion.

# Report on Alchemy

->Rectification of the Water and the Oil.<-

Now that you have separated these things in this way six times, rectify both the Water and the Oil as follows: Take your water in a clean new glass vessel and place a helm <note>the cap or "head" of a still used for distillation</note> upon it, and set it in **Mary’s Bath** <note>original: *Balneum Mariæ*; a water bath used to provide gentle, even heat</note>. Distill the water with gentle warmth, so that one drop falls out between every 20 and 30 beats <note>likely referring to the pulse or a slow count</note>. Place that again in a fresh glass, as before, and do this four times, so that it reaches **a crystalline clarity** <note>original: *ad Cristallinam Serenitatem*</note>, and then it is prepared correctly. Do the same for the oil. However, you must distill the oil in the ashes <note>an ash-bath, which allows for higher temperatures than a water bath</note>. And pay close attention in all your work that it does not leak its scent <note>this warns against the evaporation of the volatile "spirit" of the substance</note>, for that would result in a great loss to you. The water you have made, call **Lunaria** <note>Moon-water</note>, and the oil, call **Water of Life** <note>original: *Aquam Vitæ*</note>.

Keep both in good glass vessels, well-secured with the **Lute of Wisdom** <note>original: *Luto Sapientiæ*; an airtight alchemical sealant made of clay, lime, and other binders</note>, so that nothing leaks out. These two, oil and water—**that is, Air and Water**—or **Lunaria** and **Water of Life**, smell foul. And this is the entire preparation of the **Matter of the Stone** <note>original: *Materiæ Lapidis*</note>.

## CHAPTER TWO,
### Concerning the Form of the Stone.

The Form of the Stone is nothing other than Gold with Magnesia for the red <note>the "Red Work" or Rubedo, the final stage for making gold</note>, and Silver with Magnesia for the white <note>the "White Work" or Albedo, for making silver</note>. Nor should anything else be added to the Stone that is meant to remain with it, for it must be worked from these things from the beginning until the end; otherwise, all effort and labor would be lost.

For the Form of the Stone <note>likely "Lapidis"</note>, take the gold that you previously covered over the "judgment" <note>this may refer to gold purified by cupellation or a specific test</note>, or another that is similar and of very good quality, and beat it thin. However much gold you take, always take for every 1 *Loth* <note>a German unit of weight, roughly 14.5 grams</note> of gold, one and a half *Loth* of Mercury (☿) or **raw Quick-silver** <note>original: *Argenti Viui Crudi*</note>. Amalgamate them and pour it out into cold water; it will then be somewhat harder than the mixture used for gilding. Weigh it, and take a fourth part of its weight in white salt. Rub the salt into the amalgam so that it becomes a pure black mass. Put it in a crucible and set it to the fire; let the mercury evaporate gradually so that nothing of it remains. Then take it out of the crucible and put it into a glazed vessel. Pour boiling pure water on it, stir it, let it settle again, and carefully strain the water away. Do this three or four times, so the salt is also removed and the gold is refined. Calcinate the "lime" <note>the resulting fine powder</note> and dry it in the sun.

->**On the Universal and Particular Way**<-

After this drying, take according to the proportion: for every 1 **Loth** <note>a historical unit of weight, approximately 1/2 ounce or 15 grams</note> of this **Gold Calx** <note>gold reduced to a fine powder through chemical means</note>, take 4 **Loth** of **Lunaria** <note>literally "Moon-water," a prepared alchemical solvent</note> made from the **Magnesia** <note>a term for a foundational alchemical mineral, not modern magnesium</note>. Or, what is most certain: if there is a large amount of the gold powder, ensure the Lunaria rises four finger-widths above it. Then pour as much fresh Lunaria as before back into the previous flask containing the gold powder. Secure it and let it stand again as before. Pour it off as you did before into the already collected water, and secure it again. Do this until you have performed the process 7 times. Whatever of the powder is not dissolved by the seventh time, keep that separately.

Afterward, take the cucurbit containing all the **liquefactions** <note>original: *Liquefactiones*; the dissolved liquid extracts</note>, set a helm upon it, place a receiver in front, and draw the water over in the water bath with gentle heat until it looks like **melted wax** at the bottom. Then stop, and pour fresh Lunaria over it again. Secure it with the blind helm and set it in the water bath to **putrefy** <note>original: *putreficieren*; a process of warm digestion meant to break down the substance</note> for 6 weeks. Whatever is then dissolved, pour the clear water into a fresh glass, set a blind helm upon it, and keep it in a warm and moist place, as before. Over the glass from which you poured this, set a helm and draw down the moisture with the gentlest heat in the water bath, and dry it gently. Add fresh Lunaria to it again (as before) so that it rises four finger-widths above it, and let it stand in putrefaction for six days and nights. Pour off the clear liquid that has dissolved and dry the **dregs** <note>original: *Fęces*</note> again as before. Continue this pouring on, pouring off, and drying until the material entirely turns to water. Keep this second liquefaction constantly in the warm water bath, well-secured with a blind helm, just as you did with the first.

When it has all turned to water, set it again for six days and nights in the water bath under a blind helm to putrefy; then take it and separate the elements.

Pour the water back onto the dregs, and let it putrefy again for 6 days and nights. Then draw the water off again with low heat...

...down in a **water bath** <note>original: *Balneo*; a gentle heating method using water to maintain a constant, low temperature</note> and the oil in **ashes** <note>original: *Cinere*; a method of dry heating where the vessel is placed in hot ashes</note>. Do this 25 times, so that the greater part of the water is converted into **air** <note>original: *Aërem*; here meaning a gaseous or highly volatile state</note> or oil. And repeat this until the **dregs** <note>original: *Fæces*</note> or **earth** <note>original: *Terra*</note>, when dried, no longer smoke upon a glowing metal plate and are like an intangible powder.

As much as you collect of this oil or air, put it into a **luted** <note>original: *verlutiert*; sealed with alchemical paste or clay to make it airtight</note> little glass and **rectify** <note>to purify a substance through repeated distillation</note> it once or thrice, just as you did with the oil earlier in the **preparation of the matter** <note>original: *præparation Materiæ*</note>, and keep it well secured.

Then weigh the intangible powder and take half its weight of the aforementioned oil. Put it in a glass, place a **blind helm** <note>a still-head without a spout, used to keep vapors inside the vessel for "digestion" rather than letting them escape</note> upon it, and set it in a water bath to **putrefy** <note>original: *putreficieren*; a stage of alchemical breakdown where the matter is allowed to rot or decompose in gentle heat</note> for six days and nights. Thus the matter will be moist. Put a helm <note>a standard distillation head with a spout</note> upon it and dry it with gentle heat. Pour the oil back in—half as much as there is powder—putrefy it and dry it again as before. And every time you dry the **earth** <note>original: *Terram*</note>, you must always weigh it so that you do not fail in the proportion of the oil. Do this until it drinks in much oil, namely four times as heavy as it was in the first drying or at the beginning. Then test it to see if it has enough: take a little of this dried powder and throw it on a glowing metal plate. If it vanishes entirely in smoke, then it has enough; if not, repeat it with the oil until you have the complete sign.

After this powder is thus well dried, put it in a **sublimation vessel** <note>original: *Sublin-torium*; a vessel designed to heat a solid until it vaporizes and deposits as a purified solid higher up</note>, put its cap on, give it a gentle fire at first, then increase it until the matter **sublimates** upward. Then take what has attached itself to the cap and the sides of the **sublimator** <note>original: *Sublimatorij*</note>; keep it cleanly together, for it is the perfect **Mineral Stone** <note>original: *Lapis Mineralis*</note>.

The black **dregs** <note>original: *Fæces*</note>, however, which remain at the bottom after the third sublimation, are no good; one need not regard them. But what hangs in the cap and on the sides of the glass, take that and put it in a clean little glass; add a little **Water of Life** <note>original: *Aquæ Vitæ*; high-proof distilled alcohol or a potent alchemical solvent</note>—though the **Ointment of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Vnguentum Philosophorum*; a specific refined alchemical preparation</note> is better. Seal it with its blind helm, set it for 8 days in a water bath to putrefy; thus it will become a pure oil. Keep that, for the **Form of the Stone** <note>original: *Forma Lapidis*</note> is then also prepared. And what was mentioned before regarding gold shall also be understood for silver if one wishes to work toward the **white** <note>the *albedo* or "whiteness" stage of the Great Work, which results in the ability to transmute metals into silver</note>.
