->Salt of Tartar<- <note>original: *Sal 🜖ri.*</note>

Place Tartar <note>original: *Weinstein*; the potassium bitartrate crusts found in wine barrels.</note> upon a stone and place glowing coals on top of it until the Tartar <note>original: *🜖m*</note> turns white. Then remove the coals and place them on the other side so it turns white there as well. Then grind it, dissolve it in a warm fire, and distill it—filtering it through a cloth or straining it cleanly. Afterward, boil it back into salt. First, let it flow <note>This refers to deliquescence, where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to become a liquid.</note> on a "flowing stone" in a cellar, then boil it hard again, grind it, dissolve it, and boil it once more. Thus you have good Salt of Tartar. If you let this salt flow on the stone, you have good Oil of Tartar <note>original: *Oleum 🜖ri.*</note>.

Afterward, pour five ounces <note>original: *Unß*</note> of Oil of Tartar into two ounces of Quintessence. Put them together in a flask and place it in a cellar. Then "little stones" <note>original: *Lapilli*; crystals.</note> will form. Place these in a flask, seal it well, and let them become warm in the flask. They will become an oil in which you can dissolve Gold <note>original: *☉*</note> or Silver <note>original: *☽*</note>. This is called the Quintessence of Tartar <note>original: *Q. Ess. è 🜖ro*</note>.

Once you have filtered it, distill it afterward using an alembic, in which it is not thinned out, then in warm or thin ashes. Finally, distill it in a sand bath until the moisture is completely gone. Then let it cool by itself. Pour the distilled water back onto the dry dregs <note>original: *Fæces*</note> and distill it off again. Pour it back on until nothing more will distill. Repeat this as often and as long as necessary until a clear stone forms in the glass.

Take one part of this crushed stone and cast it upon ten parts of purified Copper <note>original: *purgati ♀ris*</note>. Let it stand for the duration of three *Pater Nosters* <note>The time it takes to recite the "Our Father" prayer three times—a common alchemical way to measure time without a clock.</note>. It will then acquire the permanence of fine Silver. Add a third part of good Silver <note>original: *☽*</note> to it, and you will have your proof by Lead <note>original: *per ♄m*; refers to cupellation, a test where metals are melted with lead to check their purity.</note> in all respects.

## The Work upon the Mercury of Silver

### The Joining of the Two Waters

Likewise, take the water in which the mercury <note>original: *☿*</note> was dissolved, and pour it into the golden water in which the gold was dissolved, mixing them together. Thus it <term>digests</term> <note>original: *digeriert*; a process of slow, gentle heating to mature a substance.</note> itself with the mercury and becomes one nature and property.

## Also, how to separate or divide the four elements from one another.

Also, take the glass and place an <term>alembic</term> <note>A cap or lid used in distillation to collect and direct vapors into a receiving vessel.</note> upon it, and place it in a hot <term>water bath</term> <note>original: *B. M.* or *Balneum Mariae*; a vessel of hot water used to heat substances gently and evenly.</note>. Distill the first element from the <term>matter</term> <note>original: *Materia*; the physical substance being worked upon.</note> for three days and nights. This is the <term>Element of Water</term> <note>original: *Element Aqua*</note>, and it is a beautiful, pure, clear water, measuring one and a half <term>drinks</term> <note>original: *Trünckel*; a liquid measure roughly equivalent to a cup or glassful.</note>. Thus, half a small drink remains in the glass, which is entirely golden-red. Keep this Element of Water separate in a glass, well-sealed with wax.

Afterward, take the glass in which the half-drink of golden liquid remains and <term>seal it tightly</term> <note>original: *verlutiere*; to seal a vessel with "lute," a paste made of clay or other materials to prevent the escape of vapors.</note>. Thus an oil will distill over; this is called the <term>Element of Air</term> <note>original: *Element Auræ*</note>. This is the second element, the Air. Keep this element also separate in a <term>flask</term> <note>original: *Kolben*</note> well-sealed with wax.

Now you have two elements separated from each other. At the bottom of the glass from which the Element of Air was separated, you will find a dry mass or matter, which is called a <term>Body</term> <note>original: *Corpus*</note> or an Earth. This is the third element. Grind this same Body into powder upon a marble stone; it will become a black powder. Keep the powder separate in a flask, well-sealed, until you have need of it.

### Note here how one should purge and purify the two elements of their impurities.

Take the first element, Water, and place it in a water bath for eight days. Likewise, take the second element, Air, in its flask, and place it in a water bath for eight days, ensuring that the flasks are well-sealed at the top with wax.

Afterward, take each one separately and place it on a furnace in ash, and distill each element separately with a good fire. You shall <term>dissolve</term> <note>original: *ſolvieren*</note>, distill, and <term>purify</term> <note>original: *pureficieren*</note> these two elements seven times in this manner, always each one separately. Then they are purified and well-prepared for the <term>tincture</term> <note>A potent alchemical substance used to transform or "color" base materials into a higher state.</note>.

## Note now how one should ferment the blessed noble stone, so that it may transform all bodies into good gold.

Take four **Loth** <note>A traditional German unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 14-15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of mercury that has been well-purified with salt and vinegar three times. Then take 2 Loth of thin, beaten gold and make an **amalgam** <note>original: *Amalgama*; a mixture of mercury and another metal, often used as a starting point for further chemical work.</note> of it, just as goldsmiths do when they wish to gild. Afterward, wash that same amalgam with salt and vinegar three times, then let it become dry. When that is done, take the amalgam and lay it upon a marble stone, and add to it one Loth of the red sulfur—the blessed stone—and grind them together very well.

Then take the matter thus ground together and put it into a **small flask** <note>original: *Kölbel*</note>, and pour over it four Loth by weight of the **Element of Water** <note>The clear liquid distilled in the previous stage of the process.</note>. Place the flask in ash upon a **furnace** <note>original: *Capellen*</note> and distill the water back over from the matter with a gentle fire.

Afterward, take the flask out with the matter, and if anything has sublimated, add it back to the matter remaining at the bottom. Grind it small again upon a stone as before, put it back into a flask, give it another four Loth of water from the Element of Water, place it back in the ash, and distill it again as before. Perform this work **seven times**; thus the matter will become entirely **fixed** <note>original: *fix*; meaning the substance has become stable and will no longer vaporize or change when exposed to heat.</note> and constant in any fire.

# Observe here now how one should soak and incorporate the fixed materials, as mentioned above, with their oil—that is, with the other element, the element of air.

Take the material and grind it small on a stone, as before. Place it once again into a glass and pour three **Loth** <note>A traditional German unit of weight, roughly 14–15 grams or half an ounce.</note> by weight of the element of air over it. Place this on a **cupel in ash** <note>original: *Capellen in ein Aschen*; a method of heating a vessel by surrounding it with hot ashes to ensure even temperature.</note> and give it a good fire. Thus the material will also melt at the top of the glass like wax, and many beautiful colors will rise and fall in **circulation** <term>Circulatu: the alchemical process where a substance is heated so it evaporates and condenses repeatedly in a closed vessel, mimicking the natural cycles of the heavens</term>. Let it soften together in this way for three days and nights. Afterward, take the material out and grind it small as before. Add three more **Loth** of the oil, or the element of air, and place it back on the cupel in the ash. Give it a strong fire for three days and nights, as before. In this way, many kinds of colors will again rise and fall in circulation, and it will flow up and down within the glass. Thus is proven the saying of all philosophers: "Our stone rises into heaven and descends again from heaven to the earth." <note>This is a famous quote from the *Emerald Tablet*, an ancient foundational text of alchemy, describing the movement of the "Life Force" between the spiritual and physical realms.</note>

Continue this rising and falling until the material completely **coagulates** <note>thickens or solidifies from a liquid state</note> again into a beautiful red powder, like scarlet. Thus the **tincture** <term>Tinctur: a potent alchemical substance used to "dye" or transform the properties of base metals into gold</term> is now prepared, and one part now transmutates a thousand parts into well-proven gold. And I, Doctor Niclauß Melz, have worked this with my own hand and tested it before an honorable Council in the Royal City of Kronen <note>Likely Kronstadt or a similar city with "Crown" in its name</note>, for which I have a seal and letter addressed to the Holy Father, the Pope.

## Note how the projection and multiplication should occur upon the mercury or tin for which the medicine is prepared.

Take one hundred **Loth** of quicksilver or tin that has been well purified with salt and vinegar three times. Then place the **mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*</note> in a crucible and set it on a fire until it begins to smoke. Then take one **Loth** of the aforementioned medicine and throw it into the crucible onto the mercury, and blow upon it well <note>using a bellows to increase the heat</note> for a good hour. Thus the quicksilver will transform into a beautiful red powder, just as the first was. Thus has the **multiplication** <term>Mehrung: the process of increasing the quantity of the alchemical "medicine" or "stone" without losing its potency</term> now occurred; from one **Loth**, you have one hundred **Loth** of medicine.

Afterward, take one **Loth** from those hundred **Loth** and throw it upon a thousand **Loth** of quicksilver or tin, as mentioned above, and blow upon it very well for a whole hour. Thus you have good, precious, proven gold, better in all tests than natural gold.

### Also: Saltpeter Water cannot be made in any other way,
### so that it might dissolve or solve a "body," than by this
### way alone. Therefore, let this be commanded to you

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'I' with floral motifs.</image-desc>
**Also:** Take half a pound of **saltpeter** <note>Also known as nitre, a key ingredient in making acids and gunpowder.</note>, let it melt in a new pot, and keep it slowly in a **circular fire** <term>Circul Feuer: a fire that surrounds the vessel to provide even, consistent heat</term> for two hours. And when the saltpeter begins to crust over the top in the pot like ash, then pour it out into a basin that stands in a vessel of cold water. And when the saltpeter has properly cooled and begins to attract moisture, crush it fine in a mortar and put it immediately into a **bladder** <note>Likely a pig's bladder, used here as a semi-permeable membrane for a primitive form of osmosis or filtration.</note>. Hang the tightly tied bladder in ordinary warm water, and place that water in a clean vessel; this is done so that you may notice how many **Loth** <note>A traditional unit of weight, approximately 14.5 grams.</note> of the half-pound of <term>🜔</term> <gloss>Saltpeter</gloss> have turned into water. If some saltpeter passes through the bladder into the surrounding water, you must let it **crystallize** <note>original: *schiessen lassen*; to let crystals "shoot" or form out of a saturated solution.</note> therein, and afterward weigh how much of it there is. Keep that until the end. Afterward, take the water that remained in the bladder, filter it twice in succession, and then put that water immediately into a **receiver** <term>Recipienten: a glass vessel used to collect the products of distillation</term>.

And then take fresh materials: one and a half pounds of saltpeter, finely ground, and one pound of **brick dust**. Mix these two powders well together and put them into a **flask** <note>original: *Kolben*; a long-necked glass vessel used for distillation.</note> that is well **luted** <term>verlutiert: sealed with a paste made of clay or lime to make the joints airtight</term>. Place it over a lively fire and attach the receiver containing the first water. Drive the **spirits** <note>The acidic vapors or fumes.</note> through the bricks over into the water—first with a gentle fire, and afterward like **Aqua Fortis** <term>Aquafort: "Strong Water," or nitric acid, capable of dissolving most metals</term>, for as long as a day and a night, until no more red spirits come over and the **distillate** <note>original: *Olemicum*; likely referring to the oily appearance of the concentrated acid vapors.</note> turns white. Then stop; it is enough.

**Also:** afterward, take that same water in which the spirits are contained and put it into another luted glass. Distill it over again gently into the receiver. Some saltpeter that has melted will remain in the flask; take it out and weigh it along with the saltpeter that first passed through the bladder. Thus you will realize how much of the half-pound of dissolved saltpeter has turned into "warm water." And see to it that it does not evaporate, for it is very strong. Afterward, take that same water and apply it again, driving more spirits from saltpeter through the bricks into it, two or three times, always using new bricks. After this, the water is ready and will dissolve <term>☽</term> <gloss>Silver</gloss>; it even strengthens the yield significantly. It also **precipitates** <term>præcipitiert: causes a substance to settle out of a solution as a solid</term> <term>♄</term> <gloss>Lead</gloss> completely, turning it either red or white.

# If you wish to fix all things, do it with glass.

**Also:** Make an alkali salt <note>original: *Salalcali*</note> from quicklime <note>original: *Calce viua*</note> and willow ashes; then take the white, transparent pebbles <note>original: *Kißlingstein*; likely quartz or flint</note> that have been calcined <term>Calcined: heated to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter, leaving a crumbly powder</term>, crush them fine, and mix the alkali salt into them. Let them melt together with a strong fire, and a substance remains shaped like glass; this serves highly in the workings of nature.

**Also:** To this glass you may add calx of lead <note>original: *Calcem Saturni*; Saturn is the alchemical name for lead</note> to 24 parts, or of copper <note>original: *ad Veneris*; Venus is the alchemical name for copper</note>, which is burnt copper <note>original: *Aes ustum*</note> or antimony, or all these materials in equal parts <note>original: *e. a.*, likely *equales partes*</note> according to your will. Thus the glass takes the color from them and the power of the metals. And if one lets silver <note>original: *Lunam*</note> melt with it for 24 hours, see then what it has accomplished and what degrees [of purity or color] appear there; they remain through the lead or the cement <term>Cement: a dry refining mixture used to purify precious metals at high heat</term>.

# Concerning the white ore.

Furthermore, take two pounds of saltpeter, one pound of alum, and one pound of arsenic. From these make an aqua fortis <term>Aqua fortis: "Strong water," a name for nitric acid used to dissolve metals</term>. Place the white ore into it, and it will dissolve in a day and a night. Take that calx <note>the resulting precipitate or powder</note> out and let it dry. Afterward, mix it with borax <note>original: *Purraß*</note> and melt it, and then refine it upon the cupel <term>Testen: a porous clay bowl used to separate precious metals from impurities like lead</term>. Thus you will find in one pound of ore the value of one guilder of gold <note>original symbol: ☉</note> and half a *loth* <note>a unit of weight, roughly 7.5 grams</note> of silver <note>original symbol: ☽</note>.

->Oil of Sulfur.<-

Take alum and sulfur; distill it by descent <term>per Descensum: a method of distillation where the heat is applied from above, forcing the liquid to flow downward into a receiver</term>, just as you do with vitriol; thus it will be crystallized.

->Oil of Vitriol.<-

Take two pots, as you know how, and in the upper one make many holes. Place the vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfate</note> inside and seal it well. Bury the lower pot in the earth, and around the upper one make a fire of coals. Strengthen the fire until the pot glows and becomes white-hot. Then stop and let it cool. You will find in the lower pot an oil, green as grass, which is called the Milk of Mercury <note>original: *Lac Mercurij*</note>.

->Fixation of Cinnabar.<-

Furthermore, to boil the cinnabar <note>original: *Zinober*; mercury sulfide</note>, make a lye. Take one part willow ashes and one part quicklime <note>original: *Calcis viui*</note>, and pour urine upon it, and let it boil. Filter these powders through a felt until it comes out clear. Then take the lye in a glazed vessel and put the cinnabar into it,

# Beautiful Particular Works.

->Regarding Gold.<-

->The Conversion of Silver into Gold.<-

Also / Take Hungarian vitriol <term>Vitriol: a sulfate of a metal, often iron or copper</term> / put it into an earthen retort / and place it in the side of the intense furnace <note>original: *Hellofen*</note> / and attach a receiver containing water to it / and drive off the oil strongly for 8 hours / until no more oil or spirit will come forth. Dissolve it further in warm spring water / and filter it and sublimate it / Do this five times / so it becomes white. Put it into a glass / and pour the oil onto it / and let it stand in the heat / so that the oil and salt dissolve into one oil / Then place a helm <term>Helm: the top part of a still or alembic</term> upon it / and attach a receiver / and put into it four *loth* of dissolved Scorpion <note>original: *Scorpion* — in alchemy, this often refers to a preparation of antimony or a specific volatile salt</note> / it will become white.

After that take fresh spring water / and dissolve the white Scorpion in it / so a golden water comes from it / Draw this through a filter / and put more of the white Scorpion into the golden water / and coagulate it / so a white stone comes from it / Dissolve this further in hot spring water / and draw it through a filter / and put more of the white Scorpion into it / and dissolve it / and sublimate it. Do thus with dissolving / sublimating and filtering five times : Take fresh warm spring water every time / Then it is ready to tincture <term>Tincture: a substance that can change the nature or color of other materials, usually metals</term>.

# Red Melting Glass.

<margin>MB</margin>
Take one *mark* <term>Mark: a unit of weight, usually around 230 grams</term> of burnt copper <note>original: "Aëris usti"</note> / wash it / dry it / and grind it small / soak it with a good vinegar / in which one *loth* of mercury sublimate <note>original: "Sublimatum"</note> has been dissolved. ### Calcination of Common Salt.

### Composition of the Fixing Powder.

Further / Take of black and yellow glass, equal parts <note>original: "ana"</note> of one *loth* / one *loth* of Saffron of Mars <note>original: "Croci ♂," referring to iron oxide</note> / three *loth* of the brown powder made from salt and talc / all ground small / each one individually / and mix them together / thus it is ready to fix <note>To "fix" a metal in alchemy is to render it non-volatile so it can withstand the heat of a furnace without evaporating</note> the silver <note>original: ☽ (Luna)</note>.

Take four *loth* of thinly beaten silver sheet / 8 *loth* of powder / make layer upon layer <note>original: "stratum super stratum"</note> in a crucible / well-luted <note>sealed with a heat-resistant clay or "lute"</note> / place it in a reverberatory furnace with a gentle fire / for 24 hours / so that it does not melt. Then place it while still hot from the reverberatory furnace into a wind furnace / so that it flows steadily for twelve hours / see that the crucible does not open / on account of the spirits <note>volatile gases produced during heating</note>. Let this be done twice, then all the silver is fixed <note>original: "Hoc bis fiat, tunc tota Luna figitur"</note>, and it has ten or twelve degrees <note>Refers to the purity or "grade" of the silver</note>.

Also, you can graduate <note>refine to a higher purity</note> it even higher in this way. Take one *loth* of the fixed silver / one *loth* of new iron <note>original: ♂ (Mars)</note> / that has not come into contact with any lead <note>original: ♄ (Saturn)</note> / place both in a crucible / seal it in a wind furnace / and first put half a *loth* of the black glass upon it / do not let that evaporate / and let it flow thus with a steady fire for 24 hours / and do not make the fire too large / it flows easily. Then break it out onto a refining dish <term>Treibscherben: a shallow vessel used in cupellation to separate precious metals from base metals</term> / with twice as much lead by weight / refine it until it runs clear. Then place it with its own lead upon a cupel <note>original: "Test"</note> / refine it until the "flash" <note>original: "Blicken," the moment the silver becomes pure and reflects light like a mirror</note> / thus you have your silver at 14 degrees. Then pour it / so it becomes beautiful / and add natural gold to it / of 24 degrees / Thus you have fixed gold.

Then take three *loth* of the prepared gold / two *loth* of fixing powder / hammer the gold into thin sheets / and make layer upon layer with the powder in a crucible / and treat it as was written before. Should it be brittle / then cement it in a Royal Cement <term>ziment Regali: a process using salts and acids to purify gold to its highest standard</term>. Or throw borax / and mercury precipitate <note>original: ☿ præcipitat</note> upon it / then it will also become malleable.

### Cement for Potable Gold.

Let it be cemented with Royal Cement <note>original: "Cemento regali," a corrosive mixture used to purify gold</note>. Also take melted salt / and vitriol / in equal parts <note>original: "ana"</note>, verdigris / brick dust / cemented with it for ten or 12 hours / one part gold <note>original: ☉</note> / four parts mercury <note>original: ☿</note> / let an amalgam be made. Afterward amalgamate it again / burned out with sulfur / as before. (I think the same should be repeated three times <note>original: "Puto ter idem repetendum"</note>.)

### Precipitate of Gold and Mercury.

Take one *loth* <term>Loth: a traditional German unit of weight, roughly 15-16 grams</term> of gold / four *loth* of mercury / perform calcination, as you know <note>original: "vt scis"</note>, in a glass with a long neck / until it no longer rises. Amalgamate half of this again / with 4 *loth* of mercury. Put the other half of it into a circulatory vessel <term>Circulatory vessel: A "pelican" or sealed vessel where vapors condense and flow back down</term>, do as you know / until it no longer rises. Then take it out / grind it / put it into a vial / let it rise again / so long / until it remains at the bottom / red. Then grind it again / etc. / and it will be prepared. It is effective against the plague, various poisons, and against the poison of mercury <note>original: "Valet contra pestem, venena diuersa, contra Mercurij venenum"</note>. Abraham took two pigeons, to which he gave sublimated mercury in their food, like a pill: but when they began to move their wings / and stagger / and emit a yellow fluid from their nostrils, then he gave one of them this Precipitate, and to the other nothing: this one died, the other was delivered from death.

### How Gold may ascend through the Alembic: and this is the Tincture of the Sun.

Take Alsatian wine, distill it by the true and correct method, so that you have the Quintessence <term>Quintessence: The "fifth essence," a highly purified and potent extract</term> from it. But what remains behind in the first distillation, boil that down in a copper kettle to an electuary <term>Electuary: A paste or thick liquid (Latwerge) made by mixing medicine with honey or syrup</term>. Upon this pour boiling hot water <note>original: 🜄</note> (namely, that water which remained after the Quintessence was drawn off, according to the way of Raymond Lully or Theophrastus Paracelsus), and so it dissolves. Let it settle, and you will find the Tartar of Wine <term>Tartar of Wine: Potassium bitartrate, the sediment found in wine casks</term>. But if it is still black, calcine <term>Calcine: To heat a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or oxidize it</term> it until it becomes white. Thereafter, dissolve a little of the Tartar in its Essence, let it putrefy for one day, and distill it over. If the Tartar does not yet wish to rise [distill], let it putrefy for several days and distill again, for so long until it comes over. Thus, continue to dissolve the Tartar until everything passes over into the Essence.

From all flowers and herbs you can extract the true <term>Specific Property: The unique medicinal virtue or "signature" of a plant (specificam Proprietatem)</term> with this. Put this white Tartar into the Quintessence of Wine, and add the Gold <note>symbol: ☉</note> [purified by] Antimony <note>symbol: ♁</note> to it, and so it rises over. The red Spirit [passes] through the Alembic, which is its Essence or color, and it is entirely volatile. Use that as you know how.

Concerning this [Quintessence of Gold], which is made through the water of Salt, not with Wine. Count Ludwig of Oettingen <note>original: Ludouicus ab Ottinga</note> had a bailiff who for three days had neither reason nor speech, and was just about to lie down in his passing <note>original: "Hinzügen," referring to the final throes of death</note>. Of this (I say) Quintessence of Gold, he gave him three drops in rosemary water <note>original: aqua Rorisimarini</note>; and within one hour he returned to himself, and spoke, and was revived, and remained alive for a long time afterward. But his Quintessence of Gold was made with oil of Salt, which Abraham gave to his wife, who was gravely ill, and she recovered, so that she said she had not been so healthy for a long time.

He makes the oil of Salt thus: common Salt is melted three times; a fourth time it is poured into water, which he allows to stand in the cellar until it flows, and thereafter...

->OIL OF SALT.<-

Soak common salt in distilled vinegar, four times: then dry it / and take four times as much salt again, rub it / etc.

->ANOTHER METHOD.<-

Take common salt (perhaps melted three times) and moisten it / with distilled vinegar / four times / After that, dry it / And take four times as much other salt / rub it then in a good jar / Then distill it / at first gently / and following that as the art demonstrates / etc.

### Another good work / for coagulating.

Let Tartar <term>Tartarum: A potassium salt found in wine casks, used as a flux or reagent</term> melt / into it introduce quicklime <term>Calx viva: Burnt lime, a caustic substance used to increase the potency of alkalis</term>, as much as it can take / then dissolve <note>original: tunc solue</note> it in warm water / pour it through a lye-bag / so that it passes through clear / Then coagulate <note>original: coagula; to thicken or solidify a liquid</note>. Let it melt again / but introduce quicklime into it / as much as it will take / and do as above. This should be done three times. Dissolve this salt on a stone / or glass plate / and coagulate it. Do this three times. Take this water / and quench raw Mercury <note>original: Mercurium crudum</note> in it; it will become like powder / let that join together / it will become a body <note>a solid mass</note>, And the remaining mercury, which is still "living" <note>liquid</note> / quench it again / as before. In this way you may coagulate / as much as you wish. You may put the salt back onto the stone / and use it as before.

->ANOTHER METHOD.<-

Let Tartar melt / soak brick-pieces <note>original: Ziegelbröcklein; used to provide surface area or absorb materials during heating</note> into it / as much as it can take. Also let Silver <note>original: ☽ (Luna)</note> melt / also introduce brick-pieces into it / afterwards put it in a jar / and distill it / so that water and spirit <note>the volatile vapor</note> come forth, Into this put Mercury / and let it stand for a day / so Mercury will become hard like Lead <note>original: ♄ (Saturnus)</note>.

# Beautiful Work from Doctor Schenck.

Take one pound / one and a half pounds of crude tartar <term>Tartarum Crudum: A salty crust found in wine barrels, used here as a flux to help metals melt</term>, whether it be red or white; let it flow <note>melt</note> together clearly, and pour a regulus <term>König: Literally 'King,' the metallic 'button' that settles at the bottom of a crucible</term>. Let the dross <term>Blachmal: The dark, impure byproduct or 'matte' produced during the smelting of metals, especially antimony</term> flow again, and pour another regulus. Perform this pouring and flowing until it yields no more regulus, and everything is dross of the antimony and tartar.

Extract the redness or the Fifth Essence <term>Quintam Essentiam: The most purified and potent medicinal or chemical core of a substance</term> from this dross with a good lye <term>Laugen: A strong alkaline solution</term>. Pour the lye over it and place it in a gentle warmth—in a room on the stove where one heats—for three days and nights. Then pour the lye off cleanly into a glass and seal it against dust, and pour fresh lye over the dregs <note>original: Fæces</note> again, and proceed in all ways as before. Do this until you have extracted all the redness or Fifth Essence of these materials or antimony. 

Then take all the colored lyes together in a wide glass vessel and pour cold water into it; the redness will fall to the bottom. Then strain the lye—

Then put the lye back into the vessel, dip a brush into a sharp wine vinegar, and sprinkle it into the lye; thus the redness falls to the bottom. Then strain the lye off from the redness and boil the lye down by half; then sprinkle more vinegar into it with the brush, and more redness will fall to the bottom. Let the vinegar and the lye evaporate completely, and you will find the tartar <term>Tartarum: A potassium salt (cream of tartar) often used as a flux or solvent in alchemy</term> again, and you will see wonders.

## The Preparation of Sulfur.

Take as much yellow cast sulfur <note>original: *Sulphuris*</note> as you wish, put it into a glazed pot, and pour the aforementioned lye into it so that it covers it slightly. Let it boil gently day and night, and skim it with an iron skimmer. As the lye boils away, pour in more fresh lye made from lime <term>Kalck: Quicklime or calcium oxide, used to create highly caustic alkaline solutions</term>, as before. When it has boiled for a day and a night, remove it from the fire and let the sulfur settle. The lye will be colored by the fattiness <note>original: Feistigkeit; referring to the oily, flammable essence or "soul" of the mineral</note> of the sulfur. Pour the yellow-colored lye into another vessel, and wash the sulfur <note>original: *Sulphur*</note> that lies at the bottom cleanly with warm water.

Continue this until the water comes away clear. Then pour fresh lye made from lime onto this washed residue <note>original: *Kalch*, here meaning the solid matter</note>, that is, sulfur <note>original: *id est, Sulphur*</note>, and boil it again day and night, skimming and refilling it. Then wash it as before. This work must be done three times in succession; in this way, the sulfur retains all its moisture <note>In alchemy, 'moisture' refers to the internal principle that gives a substance its properties</note>. Dry it over a small fire, and the sulfur will become entirely gray-colored to some extent.

Then take iron scales <term>Hammerschlag: The black flakes of iron oxide that fall from red-hot iron when it is hammered in a forge</term>, grind them fine, and wash them until they are beautifully clear. Dry them in a very gentle warmth, like sunshine. Then take two parts of the prepared sulfur and one part of the iron scales. Rub them well together, moisten them slightly with vinegar, and then let them dry in a sublimation vessel <term>Sublimatorio: An apparatus used to heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then re-solidifies in the cooler upper part of the vessel</term> with a gentle fire until the moisture evaporates. Then give it the fire as is proper for sublimation. When it has sublimated, take the sulfur and rub it again with well-washed iron scales, moisten it with vinegar, and sublimate it again as done before. Perform this sublimation three times; then the sulfur will become red, will no longer burn, and will no longer stink. Keep it until its time <note>A common phrase meaning to save the material for the next stage of a larger alchemical process</note>.

# Preparation and Fixation of Saltpeter / for the purpose of making the Red Sulfur fixed.
<note>"Fixed" refers to a substance that has been rendered stable under heat, so it no longer evaporates or burns.</note>

Have a suitable jar made for you, and in it melt two pounds of antimony <note>original: *Antimonium*</note>. And when it has melted, gradually add saltpeter <note>original: *Salniter*</note> to it, one assay-spoonful at a time. Do this until you have added all the saltpeter; then let it flow quite gently. Then pour the entire matter into a large mold <note>original: *Buckel*</note> or vessel; the saltpeter will remain in the upper part, and the antimony will be underneath, and it will become a regulus <term>König: Literally "king," the heavy metallic part of an ore that settles at the bottom of a crucible.</term>. Melt the regulus again with saltpeter, as before, and you will have fixed saltpeter. There should be as much saltpeter as there is regulus. This saltpeter does not burn. Grind it, and set it out to dissolve <note>original: *solvieren*; likely referring to deliquescence, where a salt absorbs moisture from the air to become a liquid oil.</note>, and it will become a yellow oil. With this oil, one fixes the sulfur <note>original: *Sulphur*</note> that has been prepared as mentioned above.

Afterward, take one part of the redness of antimony and two parts of the prepared sulfur; grind them together very finely, put them into a glass, and imbibe <note>soak or saturate</note> them with the saltpeter oil, stirring well with a wooden stick so that the material becomes quite moist. Afterward, let the moisture evaporate <note>original: *verriechen*</note> over a gentle heat. And when it is quite dry, grind it again, and imbibe it more with the saltpeter oil. Perform this imbibing, drying, and grinding five times, and you will see whether the sulfur is fixed or not. Test it like this: Take a small sheet of silver, make it red-hot, and place the sulfur upon it. If it still smokes, then imbibe it, dry it, and grind it again—and repeat this with the saltpeter oil until the sulfur flows upon the silver sheet without any smoke. With this fixed sulfur, fix the silver in the following manner.

Take finely filed silver and make small sheets from it; take one mark <term>Marck: A traditional European unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 230 grams.</term> of these, and make layer upon layer <note>original: *stratum super stratum*</note> with the sulfur and silver. There should be three loth <term>Loth: A unit of weight, about 1/16th of a pound or 14-15 grams.</term> of sulfur to one mark of silver, well-sealed with lute <note>original: *verlutiert*; sealed with a clay paste to make it airtight</note> in a crucible, and placed in a reverberatory furnace <note>original: *Reverber Ofen*; a furnace that reflects heat onto the material</note>; let it reverberate well for eight hours. Afterward, place it in a wind furnace and let it flow well together. Then refine it on a cupel <term>Capellen: A shallow, porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</term> or a testing-shard, as you know how to do. Perform this cementing and refining four times. I have done it three times, and in the mark of silver, I found beautiful, stable, and high-grade gold worth 9 gulden.

# A true procedure with talc, to fix the Mercury, and likewise to make the spirits in the nitric acid fixed so that they coagulate together with the Mercury.
<note>"Fixing" a substance means making it resistant to heat so it does not evaporate.</note>

Take one part talc <term>Talck: In alchemy, this often refers to mica or translucent minerals rather than modern cosmetic talc; it was highly prized for its supposed ability to resist fire.</term>—which can be found in the apothecary—the "Star of the Moon" <note>original: *Stellam Lunæ*; likely a specific crystalline form of silver or a mineral</note>, and one part saltpeter. Grind them together, put them into a good crucible or small pot, seal it very well with lute <note>original: *verlutiers*; a clay paste used to make vessels airtight</note>, and place it in a fire, under a salt pan, or a brick kiln. Let it burn well for three days and nights. Or, place it in a wind-furnace <note>a furnace with a strong natural draft</note> and only take care that the seal does not break and the matter does not evaporate <note>original: *außrieche*; literally "smell out"</note>. And when it has stood for the three days, take it out; it should be of a green color, then it is correct.

Then take a parting-water <term>Scheidwasser: Nitric acid, used to "part" or separate silver from gold.</term> made of saltpeter, vitriol, and alum. Once the water is made, take as much of the water as you wish and throw a little of the above-mentioned material into it—it must be ground small—and it will dissolve quickly. Then throw a little more in, and continue doing this until it will no longer dissolve. Then the spirits dissolve and coagulate the water like a jelly. Then for every three *Loth* <note>a weight unit, approximately 15 grams</note> of the water, take one *Loth* of Mercury <note>original: ☿</note>; add the Mercury to it and draw off the water <note>distill it</note>. Do this four or five times, and a beautiful precipitate <note>original: *Præcipitat*</note> will remain. Then you can equalize the Silver <note>original: *Lunam*</note> and the Sulfur so that they flow <note>melt</note> together by the light of a candle. With that same equalized material, imbibe <note>soak</note> the Mercury into the lead and then cupel it <note>original: *abtreib*; a process of refining precious metals by burning off base metals</note>. Thus, from one *Loth* of Mercury precipitate, you will keep one *Quintlein* <note>about 3.75 grams</note> of Silver <note>original: *Luna*</note> that is almost golden.

For this, I have taken one part saltpeter, one part talc, and one and a half parts tartar <note>original: *Tartarum*</note>.

### How one should equalize the Silver <note>original: ☽</note> and Sulfur in the manner mentioned above.

Take one *Marck* <note>a weight of approximately 250 grams</note> of Sulfur and one *Marck* of verdigris <note>original: *Spangrün*</note>. Grind them together, put them in a glass, place a still-head <note>original: *Helm*</note> upon it, attach a receiver, and make a liquid <note>original: *Agnum*; possibly a corruption of *Aqua*</note> like a nitric acid. Pour this water onto the Mercury precipitate all at once. And when you wish to draw off the water or "phlegm" <note>the watery, inactive part of a distillate</note> at the end—or as you draw it off—it will become a stone that melts over a candle flame. With this, reduce the aforementioned Silver.

### Coagulation of Mercury with Talc.

Take the talc which is called "Star of the Earth" <note>original: *Stella Terræ*; likely a reference to a specific variety of mica or a sparkling mineral</note>, roast it, and wash it three times in Oil of Tartar <term>Oleo Tartari: A concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, used by alchemists as a powerful alkaline solvent.</term>. Then take one part of this talc and half a part of litharge <term>Glett (Glätte): Lead oxide, often used as a flux in smelting to help metals flow.</term>, ground fine. Mix them together, place the mixture in a crucible, and set it before a bellows. Let it melt thoroughly so that it quickly reaches a liquid state. And when it has flowed, pour it into a casting mold <note>original: *Gießbuckel*</note> and tap upon it; the lead will then settle at the bottom into a "king" <term>König: A regulated button of pure metal found at the bottom of a crucible after the impurities have been separated.</term>, and the talc will lie on top, having turned into dross <note>original: *Schlacken*</note>. Grind this dross. If you add lead to it, you will find the same result a second time.

Afterward, take Mercury <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> that has been prepared upon lead, and dissolve it in a common nitric acid <term>Aquafort: *Aqua fortis*, a powerful acid used to dissolve silver and other metals.</term> that is strong. Once the mercury is dissolved, add an equal amount of the prepared lime <note>referring to the calcined talc/dross mentioned previously</note>; in this way, the mercury unites with the talc. Then draw the water off using an alembic <term>Alembicum: A distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</term> and take the matter out of the glass, grinding it to a powder.

Next, take two crucibles, let them become hot and glow, and in one crucible melt 4 *loth* <term>Loth: A pre-metric German unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 14.5 grams or half an ounce.</term> of lead. When the lead is flowing well, pour 1 *loth* of the powder from the glass into the other hot crucible, and quickly pour the molten lead over it. Stir it all together with a piece of wood and let it flow together for one hour. Then pour it into a casting mold to form a king. Break this king in half, and cupel <term>treibe ab: The process of refining precious metals by heating them in a shallow cup (cupel) to oxidize and remove base metals like lead.</term> the other half. Thus, one *loth* of mercury yields a *quintlein* <term>Quintlein: A small unit of weight, approximately 3.6 grams.</term> of silver that is nearly golden.

### To bring four *Loth* of Gold into one Mark of Silver.

Likewise: Take one pound of quicksilver <note>original: *☿ viuum* or *mercurius vivus*</note> and 14 *loth* of sulfur; mix them well together over a glow, and a gray powder will form. From this powder, create a cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note>. Grind this cinnabar into a fine powder and boil it for an entire day in wine vinegar in which you have dissolved saltpeter. Dissolve and distill it through a filter <note>original: *per Filtrum*</note>; afterward, dry it and grind it fine. Then boil it for a whole day in linseed oil.

Afterward, make a strong alkaline lye from two parts lime and one part beechwood ashes; pour this three times over fresh lime and ashes, and distill it through a filter. Boil the cinnabar in this lye for one day as well. Then take saltpeter, alum that has been calcined, burnt salt, and tartar; boil these down in the alkaline lye, and you will have a liquid salt. Now, take one part of the cinnabar in a crucible and one part of the salt, and let them melt very well together, so the cinnabar remains "fixed" <note>meaning it has become resistant to evaporation by fire</note> at the bottom. Repeat this melting three times, and the cinnabar is ready.

Then take one *loth* of silver filings and three *loth* of litharge, and pour vinegar upon it...

### To make cinnabar fixed.

Take wood ash and calcined tartar <note>potassium bitartrate that has been heated to high temperatures</note>; from these make a lye, and pour it through three times. Take three measures of the lye and four lots of cinnabar, grind it small, and put it into the lye. Let the lye boil down completely. Afterward, refine the cinnabar upon the cupel <note>original: *auff dem Test*; a shallow, porous dish used in assaying</note>; then you will have good silver.

### To fix copper.

Take one pound of arsenic, one pound of alum, one pound of saltpeter, one pound of talc, one pound of tartar, and then Oil of Tartar <term>Oleum Tartari: A concentrated potassium carbonate solution.</term>. Digest these together and let them sit for six weeks so that the mixture coagulates. Put one part of this upon one part copper <note>referred to as "Venus"</note> and let it flow; thus a fourth part remains in the lead and becomes good silver.

### To bring gold into silver.

Take eight lots of antimony <note>original: *Spießglaß*</note>, six lots of steel filings, and one lot of copper <note>Venus</note>. Let them melt in a crucible, pour it into a casting mold, and grind the resulting metal button <term>König: Literally a "king"; a regulated button of purified metal found at the bottom of a crucible.</term> into powder. Put it back into the crucible and add to it three more lots of steel filings and one lot of copper. Let it melt again and pour it into a casting mold. Grind the button to powder again and let it melt once more with three lots of steel filings and no copper. Then grind the button and calcine it in a reverberatory furnace <note>original: *reverberier*; to heat with a flame reflected onto the material</note> day and night; then the powder is ready. Imbibe the powder with Oil of Alkali three times, and then it is ready.
Take five lots of this powder for one mark <note>A *Marck* is a unit of weight, roughly 230 grams.</note> of silver, adding it one and a half lots at a time until you have driven all five lots into it. Then refine it and separate it; thus you will have one lot of gold.

### To bring gold into silver.

## The Practice upon Silver in this Work.

Take one part of fine mill-sand <note>fine silica sand</note>—cut it from where there is no lime—one and a half parts glass, and one and a half parts of heavy smithy-sand <note>iron scales or slag from a forge</note> that is as heavy as lead and shaped like a marcasite <term>Marcasit: A mineral (iron pyrite) or a metallic bismuth/antimony formation.</term>. You may see color in the cut, which is conductive and heavy. Combine them all together, mix, and grind them; thus the additive is prepared. Take one and a half lot of this for every one lot of silver; let them melt together in a strong fire. Afterward, let it cool; take that same silver for [making] gold.

## To bring Gold into Silver.

Take two parts of salt <note>original: *Salch*, likely a dialect variant of *Salz* or referring to a specific flux salt</note> and one part of antimony <note>original: *Spießglaß*</note>; grind it all small, mix it together, seal it with luting, and place it in a pot. First, build a circular fire <note>a fire that surrounds the crucible</note> beneath it; afterward, push the coals closer so that the pot glows. Then, while it is still hot, place it in a kettle of water and let it boil for two good surges. Afterward, pour it through a lye-bag <note>a cloth filter</note>. Take that same filtered lye and strike it again with distilled spirits <note>original: *gebrandtem Wein*, literally "burnt wine"</note> using just a few droplets. This residue, when soaked into the melt, turns gold into silver <note>likely referring to a process of whitening gold or creating a specific alloy</note>. Let the water stand in a gentle heat.

## Albertus Magnus,
->writes thus in the first book of the *Naturalia* <note>original: *Naturalium*; refers to Albertus Magnus's major work on natural philosophy</note>, in the third chapter.<-

In every transformation of the elements, a certain suffering <note>original: *Leiden*; in alchemical philosophy, this refers to a "passion" or a passive state a substance enters before its nature is changed</note> occurs first, so that the powers or virtues of the changed element take on or adopt a form within it from the transformation of the substance. And once they have been mixed into some element, that element will have a material—by which it is an element—possessing the virtue and power of the other element.

And this is the highest ingenuity of the masters of nature. For Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary mythical founder of alchemy</note> teaches, in the Book of Secrets, regarding the most hidden things, with veiled words or through parables. Thus our Stone proceeds with great cunning; it ascends from the earth into heaven, and again down to the earth. 
> Its nurse is the earth, and the wind has carried it in its belly. <note>This is a famous excerpt from the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational text of Western alchemy.</note>

When he took it upon himself to teach the art of <term>Alchemy</term>, he said: It ascends into heaven, where it takes on the property of fire through its cooking and <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note>. For the alchemists call <term>calcination</term>—which happens through <term>precipitation</term> and cooking—the making of a <term>material</term> into a powder. This <term>material</term> then descends again from heaven to the earth, as it takes on the virtue and power of the earth through burial <note>Often refers to placing the alchemical vessel in the ground or in warm horse dung to maintain a steady, gentle heat.</note>. When that has occurred, that which was previously killed through the <term>calcination</term> is made living and awakened again through the burial.

But where he says, "The wind has carried it in its belly": here he indicates the governance or purification of the material, <gloss>so that</gloss> it attains the virtues or powers of the air. And for that reason he says, "The wind carries the material in its belly."

## Of the Nature and Property of Azoth.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' featuring a floral or landscape scene.</image-desc>
The child **Azoth** <term>Azot; the "universal medicine" or essential transformative agent, often identified with Mercury</term> is of the lineage of Alum, and is red-colored, yellow, or green on the outside or in the manifest, and on the inside or in the hidden, it is a red-colored silt—the very fattest part of the ore or of the earth. But it is an obstacle, acting harshly on the tongue and making the mouth pucker <note>original: *rumpffen*</note> just like white alum. Therefore it is called by the Sages "Red Alum" or "**Red Roman Oil**" <note>original: *Oleum rubeum Romanum*</note>. It is also called Ⓐ <note>alchemical symbol for Salt or Vitriol</note> and "**Holy Earth**" <note>original: *Tera Sanctum*</note> of the Sages, which is then very necessary for the **Tincture** <term>the concentrated power used to color or transform metals</term> and the coloring of **Sol** <note>original: *Solis*; the Sun or Gold</note>, and to subdue or retain the metals. Concerning this, **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century alchemist</note> writes to his son thus: This is the origin of our work in this art, and in the coloring or Tincture of Sol it is greatly exalted, coloring through itself, and increasing with the addition of the Tincture—and it is a light of all lights.

But it is of itself of hard penetration, unless it is added to the oil which is the head of all oils, which colors perfectly and penetrates whatever it bodily colors with it. And there is no other thing that has all salts within it; and it is the bitter salt of which the Sages say much. There is also no other thing that can so perfectly color the "Stone of Vapors"—"a stone, and not a stone"—as this brief Azoth. And it is a Tincture that increases the redness, without which alone the **Elixir** <term>the transformative substance, often the liquid form of the Philosopher's Stone</term> of growing things is colored.

One reads in the **Assembly of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages</note> that if anything true is found in the art of **Alchemy** <note>original: *Alchemiæ*</note>, it is nothing else than adding the moist to the dry. All the natural masters say this. By "the dry," one understands the perfect, pure **body** <note>the solid, material substance</note> when it has been turned into ash or reduced to a state of ash; and by "the moist," one understands the **spirit** <note>the volatile or liquid principle</note> when it has been cleansed of all impurity.

And truly, this composition consists entirely of **dissolution** <term>Solutio; the process of turning a solid into a liquid state</term> and **coagulation** <term>Coagulatio; the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid</term>. Dissolution, according to the opinion of the natural masters, is bringing the body to the nature of the spirit. Coagulation is bringing the spirit to the nature of the body. And thus the body becomes spiritual, and the spirit becomes corporeal. In this way, the words and sayings of the masters are fulfilled, who say: "The fixed shall become volatile, and the volatile shall become fixed." And thus you may obtain the entire mastery by the grace of God.

And God knows that this dissolution may never happen without the **transmutation of the elements**. Therefore, one reads in the *Turba Philosophorum*: "Turn your elements, and you will find the thing you seek." Truly, the turning of the elements is nothing other than transforming one element into the nature of another.

The natural masters say: That in every "enclosed weather" <note>likely referring to the atmosphere or a sealed vessel mimicking celestial conditions</note> in the heavens, four elements are present in essence, though they are not visible. And they say: That no thing may arise or be born without the four elements. Yet, in various ways of "elementing" <note>the process of balancing or arranging the elements</note>, the mixed things dominate in various forms. As in the Stone of the natural masters, who say: Our Stone is composed of a body and a spirit. One clearly sees in the spirit of our Stone that Water and Air have the upper hand over the other elements: yet **Fire** <note>symbol: $\triangle$</note> surpasses the Air. ### Of the Philosopher’s Stone

The artists of **Alchemy** <term>Alchemia; the ancient art of transformation, aimed at perfecting both metals and the human spirit</term> say that the essential forms of metals cannot be truly transformed as they are: But it follows thereafter / Unless / a reduction into their first nature occurs.

For the material of all metals, as said before, is found in **Mercury** <term>Quecksilber; quicksilver, viewed by alchemists as the "mother" or the primal fluid matter of all metallic bodies</term>. At first, it is a water, but such water is very closely aligned with nature—indeed, almost natural—and by its hand, Nature itself is assisted by this art. Because of the difficulty of this work, many have been made fools by this art, having spent their youth and their wealth upon it. There are as many error-filled books as there are follies. So many manual labors are performed by these incapable or ignorant workers. Even the strongest man despairs of the art, so that he does not attain the highest deed, or the fruit of the end.

But when I observed all things, and how the kings <note>The author likely refers to "Sovereigns of the Art," the elite masters who claimed to have achieved the Great Work, or perhaps actual royal patrons.</note> performed clever and subtle work yet could seldom reach perfection, I thought this art was nothing. But when I came to myself again and paid attention to the books, **The Secret of Secrets of Aristotle** <note>original: *De Secretis Secretorum Aristotelis*; a famous medieval treatise on statecraft and occult sciences once attributed to Aristotle</note> and **Avicenna** <note>original: *Auicennę*; Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational to European alchemy</note>, that is, to the books of hidden and secret things: I found them empty or hollow of natural causes, despite how highly they guard their secrets and recount them in hiding. I avoided those books that argue against the art, and I discovered their errors and changes / just as I also paid attention to the beginnings or origins of natural things. Through this, I found that the work can indeed happen, or is possible. For I have seen mercury penetrate and other metals grow.

Therefore, I ask that no one presume to begin the work based on the things that shall be said here, unless he be very cautious, experienced, and skilled in natural origins, and very well-informed in minerals, **distillation**, **coagulation**, **dissolution** <term>Dissolution; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid, often seen as the first step in the "Great Work"</term> or dissolving, and most of all in the management of the **fire**. Also, he should not be a man who wishes to hurry, but rather one who works leisurely, with reason, and with purity. Therefore, it is a growing metallic or practical Stone, from which is extracted the power or virtue of the white **Azoth** <term>Azot; the "universal solvent" or the essential transformative agent, often symbolized as the beginning and end of the work</term>, of the red clear radiance, so that they add nothing further to it: And it is extracted through separation, purification, and the joining together of the **four elements**.

## A Complete and True Practice; But Search It Out Rightly, Philosophically and Not Fantastically.

After our stone is placed in our vessel and feels the heat of the sun, it immediately dissolves into water and rises entirely upward into the head of the vessel. And it rises upward through its wind, that is, through the smoke. When the natural masters saw this rising, so that the matter rose upward, they spoke and held a counsel as to what they should call this, and they decided that this should be called their **Sublimation** <term>Sublimation: in alchemy, the process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and condenses in the upper part of a vessel</term>. After that, when they saw the matter descending, or sinking to the bottom of the vessel and turning into water, they devised in their hearts that they should call the other by way of **Distillation**, and **Descension** <note>the act of moving downward</note> or **Solution** <note>dissolving</note> and **Dissolution**. And when they saw such rising and falling turning into water, they said that this was the perfect Distillation, which then is the third way; and the falling, which then is the fourth.

Likewise, when they saw that the matter became thick and turned into an earth, and this thickening stood at first on top of the water; and as they let it thus slowly thicken, they saw the earth sink and stay at the bottom of the glass under the water. Which earth was blackish-yellow and filthy or stinking; they devised it in their minds that they should call this effect the **Destruction** <note>original: *Zerstörung*; often called putrefaction, where the matter "dies" and turns black before its rebirth</note>, which then is the fifth way.

Also, when they saw even more of this filthy earth staying under the water, changing color through long cooking in our sun and leaving its evil stench, they called this effect **Albation** <note>original Latin: *Albationem*; the process of whitening or washing the matter to reach the silver stage</note> or washing.

Therefore **Morienes** <note>Morienus, a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemical secrets to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: You should know that the entire mastery is nothing other than a drawing out of the water from the earth and a pouring of this water onto the earth until the earth **putrefies** <note>decomposes</note> or decays. And this earth decays with this water and is purified; which, when it is purified, the whole mastery is completed with help. Therefore the natural master says: Whiten the **Laton** <term>Laton: a term for the impure metallic "body" (often likened to brass) that must be purified into silver or gold</term>, and put away the books; which then is the sixth way.

As then the natural master has said: The earth is moistened with the natural water and showered or washed, and is dried through moderate cooking of our sun, and the entire matter is turned into earth. Here **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note>, a father of all natural masters, says: Its power is complete if it be turned into earth. And that is the seventh way.

# Of the Philosophical Stone.

I, who have written these things, have seen all these things until now. I pray to God that He may grant me grace to also see the end one day.

->God will give. <note>original: "DEVS dabit"</note> Note well, my Son. <note>original: "Nota bene, mi Fili"</note><-

Son, now I will lead you into the **Garden of Delight** and all voluptuousness, and into its **Bath**, in which its power is generated or multiplied without end. And that is our salvation and the **Secret of all Secrets**.

# OIL OF ANTIMONY:
## The Fixation, its Quintessence.
### Caspar Oberlein.

Take one pound of ♁ <note>Antimony</note>, one pound of **Salt of Tartar** <term>Salt of Tartar: Potassium carbonate, often used as a flux</term>, rub it all small together, and put it into a crucible; let it flow in a wind-furnace for half an hour. Then pour it onto a stone and rub it very small again. Put the same into a glass and pour good, rectified **Aqua vitæ** <term>Aqua vitæ: "Water of Life," a term for concentrated distilled alcohol</term> or brandy upon it; place it in gentle heat for eight days, and it will become golden yellow. Then pour that off into a clean glass, well-stoppered, and then pour fresh Aqua vitæ upon it. Place it in the heat for eight days, or as long as it takes until it colors itself again as before, and it will then also become yellow. Pour that then with the other yellow ▽ <note>Water/Liquid</note>, and then pour fresh Aqua vitæ upon it again. Continue this pouring on and drawing off as long and as often until it extracts no more yellowness. Then distill the yellow Aqua vitæ off via a **Water Bath** <note>original: "per Baln." (per balneum)</note>, so that a thick **Oil** remains. And the Aqua vitæ is always good to draw out more in this work. When you have drawn off the yellow Aqua vitæ down to the **Oil** <note>original: "Oleum"</note>, and when one coagulates that same Oil again into a powder or mass, that same thing may then truly be the **Quintessence**, as I am certainly assured.

Afterward, take twice as much **brick-dust** as there is of the Oil, and mix it well together, and put it into a small flask, and lay it on its side in the furnace with a receiver before it; and distill it like a water, at first with gentle fire and at last very strong; thus the Oil will pass over or rise up entirely red, and then it is prepared.

Afterward, take three parts of **living** ☿ <note>Mercury</note> and one part of ☉ <note>Gold</note>, amalgamate them together, and then pour the Oil upon it, so that it stands a thumb's breadth above it. And then place it in ashes for four or five days in gentle heat; thus the **Amalgam** will become entirely black, and hard-coagulated, and **fixed** <term>Fixed: a substance that is no longer volatile and can withstand the heat of the fire without evaporating</term>. Then pour the Oil off and keep it, for it is always good as long as it lasts. Then pour fresh Aqua vitæ upon the coagulated mass of ☉ <note>Gold</note> and ☿ <note>Mercury</note>, and wash the Oil of ☉ <note>Gold</note> clean from it; it dissolves into the Aqua vitæ. Then distill the Aqua vitæ down through an **Alembic** in a Water Bath until the Oil remains. Put that Oil then with the first Oil; it is then always as good as the first. Reduce the coagulated mass with **Borax** <note>original: "Purras"</note>; thus there remains three parts of Gold at twenty-four degrees <note>referring to 24-karat purity</note>.

<header>Of the Oil of Antimony. <note>original Latin: "De Oleo Antimonij"</note></header>

### How to extract the Quintessence from Antimony ore.

Take Antimony ore, pound it or rub it into a fine powder until it becomes very subtle. After that, take the very best distilled wine vinegar you can find and pour it into a glass flask <note>specifically a "Kolbenglaß" or retort</note>, and pour the powder into it so that the vinegar stands about two fingers' width above it. Stir it well together, then let it stand in gentle heat for 8 days, or until the vinegar turns red. Pour off that red-colored liquid and keep it clean. Pour more vinegar onto the powder as before, and let it stand as before. Take the redness from it again, along with the vinegar, as before. Continue this pouring off and extraction until the vinegar no longer turns red.

Afterward, put the colored material into a flask and distill it very gently through an alembic <note>a "per Alembicum" distillation apparatus used for purifying liquids</note>. First, a white phlegm <term>Phlegm: in alchemy, this refers to the tasteless, watery byproduct of distillation</term> or water will come over. Then, it will come over in red drops. At that point, take away the receiver and put another one in its place. Then collect the redness separately; that is the true Quintessence of Antimony. Use it then as you know how. It has a sweet taste like honey.

Also, the vinegar along with the extracted Antimony must first stand for 40 days in dung for putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: the process of allowing a substance to rot or ferment in a warm environment, often simulated by burying the flask in a warm dung heap</term>, and decay in the glass, well-sealed; only then should it be worked as indicated above. The Oil of Antimony is as excellent a medicine for wounds as any to be found on earth. The *Pleyl* <note>likely "Bleiglanz" or galena, a lead ore often associated with antimony</note> is almost equal to it; you will find that in another booklet.

### To extract the Sulfur from Antimony.

Take two ounces <note>original: "Loth"</note> of Saltpeter, one pound of Vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfate</note>, and eight ounces of Alum. From these, a water is distilled as is customary, and the spirits are driven out strongly. Pour this *Aqua Fortis* <term>Aqua Fortis: "Strong Water," or nitric acid, used to dissolve metals</term> onto pounded ♁ <note>Antimony</note> in a "Benedict flask" so that it covers it slightly. Let it stand for one day, and the Antimony will draw the *Aqua Fortis* entirely into itself. Then pour more *Aqua Fortis* over it so that it is well covered, by about two or three fingers' width. Afterward, distill the *Aqua Fortis* back off through the alembic with very gentle heat and slowly. Thus the ♁ <note>Antimony</note> rises over with the *Aqua Fortis* through the alembic, and the Sulfur remains lying at the bottom, white and coarse. It becomes so hard that it cannot be removed, and the glass must be broken. And if the Sulfur still has moisture in it, it must be dried on a lime kiln. Afterward, use the Sulfur as you know how. Also, one might try the distilled water for something; it may without doubt be useful for something.

### A work of Antimony by "part for part." <note>original Latin: "pars cum parte," a method of alloying or refining</note>

Take Tartar <note>potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking</note>, Saltpeter, and common salt in equal parts <note>original: "ana"</note>; rub it all fine together, put it in a new, unglazed pot, and luten <note>seal with clay</note> a piece of brick on top of it. Place it in a charcoal fire and let it calcine <term>Calcine: to roast or heat a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile matter or reduce it to powder</term> well, for about a good hour, in good heat. Then when it has cooled, you will find the Tartar calcined white. Then pound that material into a fine powder and dissolve it in hot water. Throw away the dregs <note>original: "Feces"</note>, then filter the dissolved liquid and boil it down into salt.

Afterward, take one pound of Antimony, rub it fine, and mix half a pound of the salt described above into it. Mix it well together, then let it melt thoroughly in a crucible. Afterward, pour it into a casting basin; keep that King <term>King: also called a "Regulus," the button of pure metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible after melting</term>. Pound the slag fine, but add half as much salt to it, mixing it well together, and let it melt as before. Pour it to the King as before; keep the Kings together. Continue this work as long as it produces a King.

Afterward, pound all the Kings together into a fine powder. Take fine, small-grained ☾ <note>Silver</note> equal in weight to the powder of ♁ <note>Antimony</note>. Mix it well together and let it melt together. Pour it into a casting basin, and the ☾ <note>Silver</note> will settle as a King. Take that King out and let the Antimony "smoke away" <note>evaporate through heat</note> from it; then the ☾ <note>Silver</note> will be heavier than before. Afterward, take another pound of fresh Antimony and work it into a King as before. Work all those Kings again with this ☾ <note>Silver</note>, as above <note>original: "ut supra"</note>. And do the same a third time with a pound of fresh ♁ <note>Antimony</note>, as before.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for working with Antimony, specifically detailing the "cementing" and "grading" of metals. It follows the previous page's discussion on extracting the quintessence and transitions into metallurgical applications.</meta>

<page-num>581</page-num>
<header>Of the Oil of Antimony. <note>original Latin: "De Oleo Antimonij"</note></header>

When the Silver <note>original symbol: ☽ (Luna)</note> has smoked off for the third time on the shard in the flux, then take that same Silver and place it on another shard. Add three times as much Lead as there is Silver, and drive the Antimony <term>Antimony: a semi-metal used in alchemy to "purify" gold and silver, as it reacts with impurities</term> entirely away from it. Afterward, drive it on the cupel <note>a "Test" or cupel is a shallow, porous dish used in assaying</note> until the "Blick" <term>Blick: the sudden "flash" or brightening seen when a precious metal becomes pure during cupellation</term>. After that, take as much Gold <note>original symbol: ☉ (Sol)</note> by weight as there is Silver; let them flow together well in a crucible. Then pour it into an ingot <note>original: "Zain"</note> and laminate it <note>hammer it into thin sheets</note>, and cut small plates from it. Wet them in urine and stratify them <term>Stratify: to layer substances, usually for "cementation" where a metal is purified by being heated while packed in a reactive powder</term> with verdigris <note>a green pigment/acetate formed on copper</note>, not in thick layers <note>original Latin: "stratum super stratum"</note>, and seal it up with luting clay. Cement it in sand for two days and nights. Then let all the materials flow together well with Alkali Salt in a crucible; in this way, the Silver has been graded <note>refined or "exalted" in quality</note> with the Gold to 24 degrees <note>referring to the highest purity, similar to 24-karat</note>.

The slag that remains, let it flow again, so that the remaining Silver settles into a **King** <term>King: also called a "regulus," this is the button of pure metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</term>; in this way, you recover all the Silver again.

### A profitable way to bring Gold into a Silver through Antimony, namely one Loth <note>about 1/2 ounce</note> of Gold into one Mark <note>about 8 ounces</note> of Silver at 24 degrees.

You should first purge the Silver <note>original symbol: ☽ (Luna)</note> in this way. Take three pounds of rock salt, crush it small, and then rub one pound of unslaked lime into it. Then take a melting crucible, coat the inside with chalk, and then lay in it one Mark of fine Silver, or however much you wish. According to its amount, and for every Mark of Silver, add eight *Loth* of the powder, as described above <note>original Latin: "ut supra"</note>. Seal it with a shard, place it in a wind-furnace <term>Wind-furnace: a blast furnace that uses a strong draft of air to reach the high temperatures needed for melting metals</term>, and let the fire start gently for about an hour. Afterward, give it a strong fire for three hours so that it flows well, until the salt is entirely consumed. After the four hours, lift it out; when it has cooled, you will find the Silver without any loss. Perform this work 4 times, then drive the Silver off in Lead; thus it is purged.

Furthermore, there are many better purifications than this for Silver. Afterward, take eight *Loth* of Antimony <note>original symbol: ♁</note> that has been purged, one and a half *Loth* of Copper <note>original symbol: ♀</note> filings, one *Loth* of Lead, and one and a half *Quint* <note>a small weight, roughly 1/4 of a Loth</note> of iron filings. Let it all flow together for one hour. Then take it out. When it cools, you will find a beautiful **King**. Then grind one *Loth* of the King and one *Loth* of Silver. Put it in a mortar, or throw a glowing coal into it; stir it well together and let it burn out. Afterward, grind it all small into a powder. With this powder, make layers <note>original Latin: "stratum super stratum"</note> in a cementing shard, the thickness of a knife's back, and use the aforementioned Silver that has been purged. Cover it with a shard on top, and cement it thus for eight hours; the plates will become quite brittle. Afterward, take all the material together as it was in the cement, put it in a crucible, cover it with Venetian glass, and place a shard over it. Let it flow in a wind-furnace for at least one hour. Drive the King for a while on the cupel so that the Antimony smokes away. Then drive it on the cupel to the "Blick." Separate that, and the "lime" <note>calx/powder</note> of the Gold will fall to the bottom; use it as is proper, and the Silver is then at twenty-four degrees.

### To prepare the Antimony for the aforementioned work.

Take one pound of Antimony <note>original symbol: ♁</note>, put it in a crucible, and then pour it into a vessel that has been smeared with a rind <note>animal fat or grease</note>; in this way, its "wildness" <note>volatility or unruly chemical nature</note> is taken from it. Afterward, take the cast Antimony, put it back in a crucible, and add two *Loth* of saltpeter, two *Loth* of **Caput Mortuum** <term>Caput Mortuum: Latin for "dead head," the useless residue left after a chemical distillation—in this case, from making aqua fortis (nitric acid)</term>, two *Loth* of red tartar, and 2 *Loth* of sulfur. Crush everything together and put the powder onto the flowing Antimony. Let it flow well for about a quarter of an hour. Pour it together into a vessel smeared with rind, as before. Thus the Antimony is prepared and black, ready to be used for this work. It also serves goldsmiths for casting Gold <note>original symbol: ☉</note>, for it does not "rob" <note>consume or diminish the metal</note as much as raw antimony. Michael Blaman also makes his prepared Antimony in this way, except he takes two *Loth* of Lead and one *Loth* of Copper <note>original symbol: ♀</note> and no tartar. With that, he grades low-quality Gold and casts through it. I saw this myself in Kutná Hora <note>original: "Küttenberg," a famous silver mining town in Bohemia</note>.
