### To extract the Quintessence from Antimony, or the Ore.

Take Antimony, as much as you wish, grind it to the smallest size, put it into a glass, and pour very sharp lye upon it, which is made from unslaked lime and willow ash <note>original: "Weidaschen"</note>. Boil the Antimony in it, so the lye becomes red, like blood. Then pour off the lye into a glass, and add another batch of lye, and boil as before until it turns red. Pour it off again, as before. Do this as long as necessary until the lye no longer turns red. Put all the red lye together into a glass, seal it well, and place it in horse manure <term>Horse manure: used by early chemists to provide a gentle, constant heat for fermentation or "digestion"</term> for forty days. Then distill it with a gentle fire; first, pure water comes out. Then red drops come out like blood; collect these separately. With this, you may sublimate Mercury red, and also grade and fixate <term>Fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand heat without evaporating</term> with it. Also, a tincture may be made from it, as I myself know.

### To make the Tartar red for the Antimony.

<margin>Preparation of vinegar for extracting the redness of Mercury. <note>original Latin: "aceti præparatio pro Mercurij rubedine extrahenda"</note></margin>
Likewise, take two quarters of very sharp, distilled vinegar <note>original: "Acetum acerrimum, distillatum"</note>, and one pound of calcined tartar <note>original: "Tartarum calcinatum"</note>. Put the vinegar into a glass flask, and a receiver <term>Receiver: a vessel (Fürlag) used to catch the condensed vapors during distillation</term> before it. Into that [the receiver], put half a pound of calcined tartar, and distill the vinegar over. Then take the receiver away, and pour the vinegar into a flask, and set it in sand. Distill it through an Alembic <term>Alembic: a type of still-head used for distilling liquids</term> into another receiver with the tartar <note>original Latin: "cum Tartaro"</note>. Perform this exchange seven times. Afterward, put all the tartar together into a flask and distill the vinegar from it. At last, give it a good fire, as if you were making Aqua Fortis <term>Aqua Fortis: literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid</term>; thus the vinegar is prepared.

### Oil of Antimony.

Likewise, take one pound of vinegar and one pound of Antimony, ground very small. Pour the vinegar onto the Antimony in a glass and let it stand in gentle warmth for three days. Thus the vinegar becomes red. Pour this off very carefully so that nothing cloudy goes with it, and pour another batch of vinegar onto it. Let it stand for seven days until the vinegar turns red. Do this until no more redness comes from it. Then distill the vinegar from it through an Alembic, and you will find the Oil of Antimony at the bottom <note>original Latin: "in Fundo"</note>.

### To make Oil of Antimony, and a fixation therewith, to bring four Loth of Gold into one Mark of Silver. <note>A "Loth" was a unit of weight roughly equal to 15 grams; a "Mark" was roughly 230 grams.</note>

Likewise, take black calcined tartar <note>original: "Weinstein"</note>, half a pound, and eight Loth [of Antimony]. Rub it all together, then let it flow in a crucible; cover it with a lid. When it has flowed well, pour it into a sharp vinegar, which should be warm. Let it stand until it becomes clear. Then pour off the vinegar, and you will find the Antimony <note>original: "Spießglaß"</note> lying red on the bottom, like clotted blood; make this into a pure dry powder.

Afterward, take Oil of Tartar <note>original: "Oleum Tartari"</note>, as much as you wish, and dissolve Sal Ammoniac <term>Sal Ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used to help dissolve metals and minerals</term> in it, as much as can be dissolved. Soak the red Antimony with it, and dry it again. Then grind it, and soak <term>Imbibition: the process of repeatedly soaking a dry powder with liquid and drying it to "feed" the substance</term> it again, as before, and let it become dry. Do this four times. Afterward, place it in a damp cellar, and a red oil will form from it. This is then called Oil of Antimony. And whatever has not dissolved, let it become dry, and grind it small, and soak it again three or four times, as before. Then place it in the cellar, and it will dissolve entirely.

Likewise, make the **second Oil** thus: Take four Loth <term>Loth: a historical unit of weight, roughly 15-16 grams or half an ounce</term> of Vitriol <term>Vitriol: a sulfate mineral often used for its acidic properties</term>, dissolve it in urine, and boil it in an unglazed pot <note>original: "unverglasten Hafen"</note> until it is reduced by more than half. Add to it four Loth of Alum <note>symbol: 🜔</note>, three Loth of Saltpeter <note>original: "Saliter"</note>, and four Loth of Antimony <note>symbol: ♁</note>, all finely ground. Boil it all until it is dry, turn it into a powder, and place it in a cellar to dissolve <note>The moisture in a damp cellar would cause the salts to deliquesce into a liquid</note>; thus you have the second oil.

Likewise, afterward take these two oils in equal weight or volume. Rub filed Copper <note>symbol: ♀</note> well with them on a hard grinding stone so that it becomes entirely small and subtle. Then put it into a flask <note>original: "Kolbenglaß"</note> and set it to digest for seven days. Pour the oil over it so that it rises just a little above it. And when it has distilled over, pour the distilled water back onto it. Do this seven times. Afterward, put it in a luted <term>Luting: sealing a vessel with clay or paste to make it airtight</term> crucible and let it cement in a low fire for 16 hours; afterward, let it melt in a wind furnace for four hours. Then refine it <note>original: "treibs ab", referring to cupellation</note> in lead and separate it; thus you will find in one Loth of Silver a Quintlin <note>A small weight, 1/4 of a Loth</note> of Gold at 24 degrees <note>referring to high-purity, 24-karat gold</note>.

->**To make Silver from Antimony.**<-

Take <note>original Latin: "Recipe"</note> one pound of Antimony, four Loth of Lead <note>symbol: ♄</note>, and one Loth of Copper <note>symbol: ♀</note>. Let it all melt together in a crucible. Pour it into an ingot mold <note>original: "Gießbuckel"</note>. You should refine this "King" <term>Regulus (King): the metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</term> a little on a cupel <note>original: "Treibscherben"</note>, and afterward on the refining test; then you will have the Silver <note>symbol: ☾</note>.

->**To refine Antimony for Gold.**<-

Take two Loth of Sulfur and two Loth of Saltpeter. Grind these two well together. Then place Antimony <note>original: "Spießglaß"</note> in a crucible and let it melt well. Then throw a little of the powder (as described above) into it; cover it with a flask. Then throw a little more into it. Then pour the Antimony into an ingot mold, and it will have a "King" <note>regulus</note>; use it as is proper.

->**To refine Antimony for Silver.**<-

Take one pound of Antimony and two pounds of burnt Tartar <term>Tartar: potassium bitartrate, often obtained from wine barrels and used as a flux</term>. Put these pieces together in a mortar; afterward, put them in a crucible, seal it at the top, and let it melt well. Refine the "King" as is proper.

->**To test the Antimony, to see if it is good for extracting the redness.**<-

Take the Antimony and stroke it upon yellow paper that has been smoothed with a tooth <note>Using a tooth for burnishing paper was a common way to create a perfectly smooth surface for testing mineral streaks</note>. If it leaves a red streak, it is good; but if it leaves a black streak, it is not good. So take the Antimony <note>symbol: ♁</note> with the red streaks, grind it small, and mix it with good lime <note>original: "Kalch"</note>. Let there be much more lime than Antimony. Add some clean water to it, let it boil well, then let it settle until clear, and strain it into a glass; then it will be beautifully pure. Then pour distilled wine vinegar into it, and it will turn as if you had poured blood into it. Let it settle, then carefully draw off or drain the liquid. Thus you have a beautiful red powder, which is the **Quintessence of Antimony**.

Take eight Loth of Antimony <note>symbol: ♁</note>, two Loth of filed Iron <note>symbol: ♂</note>, two Loth of filed Copper <note>symbol: ♀</note>, one Loth of raw Tartar, one Loth of Lead <note>symbol: ♄</note>, half a Loth of Tin <note>symbol: ♃</note>, and half a Loth of Glass. These pieces should all

...let them all flow together. When it has flowed for half an hour, let it cool so that it settles into a **Regulus** <term>Regulus: the heavy, metallic portion of an ore that sinks to the bottom of a crucible; in German alchemy, this was called the "König" or King</term>; then strike off the Regulus. Take one Loth <term>Loth: a unit of weight, approximately 15–16 grams</term> of the ground Regulus and add it to two Loth of **Silver** <note>symbol: Luna</note>. Let it flow for two hours, then refine it in **Lead** <note>original: "abgetrieben im Pley," referring to cupellation, a refining process where lead is oxidized to separate it from precious metals</note>. This Silver receives all degrees of improvement in the addition, as follows:

### Gradation. <note>Gradation: a process intended to increase the purity, color, or weight of a precious metal</note>

Take Verdigris <note>original Latin: "viridi Aeris"</note>, **Oil of Salt** <note>symbol: 🜖</note>, **Oil of Antimony** <note>symbol: ♁</note>, and **Oil or Powder of Mercury** <note>symbol: ☿</note>, of each an equal part <note>original Latin: "ana"</note>. If you can obtain **Oil of Iron** <note>original: "Oleum Martis"</note>, take one part of that as well. Put it all together, and when it is coagulated, dissolve it again in a cellar <note>The humidity of a cellar causes certain salts to absorb moisture and turn into liquid</note> or in a "Graduation Water" <note>original: "Aqua, das zum gradieren gemacht ist"</note>. And the more often you do this, the further it tinges <note>The "tinge" refers to the alchemical power to transform the color and nature of a base metal into gold</note>. If a third or fourth part of this powder is thrown into the molten metal, it brings forth **Gold** <note>symbol: ☉</note>.

### To extract the Redness of Antimony, which is used for gradation and fixation. <term>Fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated</term>

Take as much **Tartar** <term>Tartar: "Weinstein," the potassium bitartrate crusts found in wine barrels</term> as you wish in a pot, luted <term>Luted: sealed with an airtight clay or paste</term> at the top; place it in a furnace and let it burn until it no longer smokes; then it is sufficiently turned to black. Pour warm water over it repeatedly until it is no longer "sharp" <note>The sharpness indicates the presence of alkaline salts; the water extracts these to make a lye</note>. Then boil this same lye in a cauldron or glazed pot until it becomes a salt; keep that. Take as much **Antimony** as you wish in a crucible, let it flow gently, and throw the above-described salt into it, finely crushed, for as long and as much as it takes until the **Antimony** <note>symbol: ♁</note> becomes red. Use this for cementing or grading.

Hammer this Antimony into pieces and pour a good **vinegar** over it; the vinegar will pull the redness entirely out until no more red remains. This is also used for grading. But if you strain off the vinegar, as before, that is the most noble way: when fixed Silver, beaten into thin sheets, is stratified <note>placed in alternating layers</note> beneath it, sealed in a glass or pot with a bit of dough, and held in the fire for a day and a night—first with a gentle heat, then a stronger fire. This **Antimony** <note>symbol: ♁</note> prepared in this way is good for **Cinnabar** <term>Cinnabar: a bright red mineral, mercury sulfide, often used as a source of mercury or as a pigment</term> in which you wish to fix Silver.

### A small Tincture.

Take **Oil of Mercury** <note>symbol: ☿</note>; dissolve in it **Sal Ammoniac** <note>original symbol: *</note> that has been made red through **Iron** <note>symbol: ♂</note>. Then take **Oil of Vitriol**, and dissolve **Alum** <note>symbol: 🜔</note> in it. Then take both Oils together and let a fourth part evaporate. Afterward, dissolve **Corrosive Sublimate** <note>original Latin: "Mercurium sublimatum"</note> in the oil, for it will dissolve like water. Afterward, take one part of **calcined Gold** <note>symbol: ☉ calcinatum; gold reduced to a fine powder through heat</note>, and moisten it with three parts of the oil, as above <note>original Latin: "ut suprà"</note>. Then place it in warm dung <note>A common alchemical method for providing steady, gentle heat over weeks or months</note>; from this, a very red water will form. Coagulate this with a strong fire, and place it back in the dung. When it has become water again, coagulate it once more. Do this ten times, and it will become a golden water or oil. Then take one part of this oil or water, throw it upon a hundred parts of **raw Mercury** <note>original Latin: "Mercurij crudi"</note>, and it will become good Gold.

# Regarding the Fifth and Final Part
## Preface to the Reader.

Nature, favorable and dear reader, gives us a fine parable, example, and lesson through the bees <note>The author uses the archaic German word "Immen" for bees, a common symbol in early modern literature for industriousness and discernment.</note>, who suck the honey out of all sorts of herbs and flowers—both the poisonous and the non-poisonous—and leave the poison behind. In the same way, we should pick out, draw, and separate the honey alone—that is, the good and useful—from everything we have before us or deal with, and set aside the evil and the worthless. To this, the holy Apostle Paul also points and teaches us through the supernatural light kindled in him in the third heaven, where he says: *Test all things and hold fast only to that which is good.* <note>original Latin: "Omnia probate & solum bonum tenete." (1 Thessalonians 5:21)</note> For we have become subject to good and evil through the Fall of Adam and Eve in original sin, and fire and water are laid before us, with free will given to us to reach for whichever we desire.

For this reason, Nature mixes everything good and evil together for us; she hides nothing by separating or setting it apart. However, she has simultaneously incorporated into us—just as she gave the bees and spiders the power and virtue to draw to themselves, the one the poison and the other the good honey, by an attractive and nourishing power <note>original Latin: "attractiva nutritiva virtute"</note>—perfect understanding, knowledge, and discernment <term>discernment|the ability to judge well or distinguish between things</term> to recognize good and evil, poured into our souls from God's merciful gifts. Thus, we can offer no excuse that we did not know how to distinguish between the good and the evil.

Nature has commanded such innate knowledge and discretion <note>The original term "Discretion" here refers to the power of distinguishing or separating.</note> to us not only in things that fall under reason or the senses <note>original Latin: "rebus quæ sub rationem sive sensus cadunt"</note>, which pertain to reason alone, but she has also left and taught us a certain art in material things, namely Alchemy. Through this art—just as the stomach separates the nourishment from the waste <note>original Latin: "Nutrimentum" and "Excrementum"</note>, or as the vintner <note>original: "Trotner," referring to one who treads or presses grapes.</note> separates the juice and the husks from grapes through the

<summary>This preface introduces the final volume of the alchemical collection by arguing that humans have a divinely given duty to separate the "good" from the "evil" in both spiritual and physical matters, framing alchemy as the tool for this separation in the material world.</summary>
<keywords>Nature, alchemy, Apostle Paul, free will, discernment, separation of substances, bees and spiders, Adam and Eve, philosophy of science</keywords>

--- Page 646 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of the fifth volume, moving from the innate ability to distinguish good from evil to the historical reasons why alchemy became a "secret" science. It connects the previous page's discussion of human discernment to the practical application of separating materials.</meta>

...to proceed / in all material things / being able to distinguish and separate the good and the evil from one another.

This art of Alchemy, however—after the tyrannical Emperor Diocletian <note>Emperor Diocletian (reigned 284–305 AD) reportedly ordered the burning of Egyptian books on alchemy around 297 AD to prevent the production of gold from funding rebellions.</note> had all chemical books burned—was thereafter never again explicitly described. Instead, those who practiced the Philosophical Art sought out the strangest and most unusual names, words, and figures. With these, they hid the secrets of nature <note>original Latin: "Arcana Naturæ"</note> behind strange, wonderful images and under the veil and cover of obscurity. This is apparent in poetic fables and poems, especially in the *History of Fortunatus* <note>A popular European folk tale about a man who receives a bottomless purse and a wishing hat; here, the author views it as an alchemical allegory.</note> and Ovid's *Metamorphoses* <note>A Roman narrative poem describing the history of the world through transformations; alchemists often viewed these myths as metaphors for chemical change.</note>, which is a pure hieroglyphic description <note>In this period, "hieroglyphic" referred to symbolic or allegorical representation rather than specifically Egyptian writing.</note> of the changing of forms. In these, the learned and the commentators <term>Expositores|Scholars who interpret or explain the hidden meanings of difficult texts</term> clearly understand what sweet juice lies hidden beneath the outer bark of the fables. Because of this, however, this art has not only gradually fallen into oblivion through the "injury of time" <note>original Latin: "temporis iniuria"</note>, but has also become more an object of suspicion than esteem among the good-hearted. Among the envious, it has grown more into a thing of mockery than wonder, and thus Nature has fallen into darkness.

Now, to offer assistance to oppressed Nature and to bring her art—which has for a long time now lain hidden and despised "under the bench," not without significant loss and damage to the common good (as can be seen from the preface to the first part of this work)—back into the sunshine and the light of day, I have undertaken a work that is difficult for me personally, given the many hostile eyes watching. This work involves bringing the writings of the ancient philosophers and spagyrists <term>Spagirorum|Alchemists who followed the Paracelsian tradition of "spagyria," the art of separating and then recombining substances to create potent medicines</term>, as well as various treatises <note>original German: "Tractaͤtlin," or "little treatises."</note> collected from all sorts of authors, into the light through public printing. I will, however, gladly bear such a burden with patience and pay little heed to the ignorance and ill-will of enemies, so long as I am comforted by this: that I am doing a favor to the wise and impartial, and that my spirit and intention [is for the] common...

He announces his intention to restore this "oppressed" art to the public by printing a collection of ancient philosophical and spagyric treatises.</summary>

# Preface to the Reader.

...be recognized as promoting the common good and the art of secret philosophy and medicine.

So I now require of the favorable reader’s spirit / not the nature and character of spiders / but of bees (who do not despise any little flower / no matter how small / how poor / how misshapen or poisonous it may be / but take it for themselves / and extract only the good and the honey / leaving the poison for the spiders) who know how to separate and set apart the righteous and good from the evil / the useful from the harmful / the true from the false / and for their own benefit / to pick it out like the nut from the shell / and to cast away the rest which is of no use / for in the same way / as the Art itself is an art of separating and dividing *pari & impari* <note>original Latin: "the equal and the unequal," referring here to the balanced and unbalanced elements of a substance</note> / the evil and the good / the honey from the poison / the wheat from the chaff : So must also in the description of this Art by various authors and conflicting teachings / a separation of the true from the false / and that which was added solely to obscure as useless / be maintained and established / the reason is / that the philosophers mixed everything / truth and lies / proven and unproven / among each other / not only disorderly / and unintelligibly / but wrote the *Contrarium* <note>original Latin: "the contrary"</note> and the reverse / and often on a single page two types of conflicting opinions on one thing / so that one cannot find a way out or conclude / whether they began or ceased to write halfway or entirely / wrongly or rightly. They also did not strive for any external ornament / order / or loveliness of speech in their *Phrasium* <note>original Latin: "phrases"</note> / sayings and words / or any *Rhetoricæ* <note>original Latin: "rhetoric"</note> / but often without *Ration* <note>original Latin: "reason"</note> / like laughable folly / with unadorned / impolite speeches against the *præcepta Grammatices* <note>original Latin: "precepts of grammar"</note> and *vitiose* <note>original Latin: "faultily" or "corruptly"</note> / (I would say Bachantish <note>original German: "Bachantisch." For *example* <note>original: "Exempel"</note>, we see how Nature brings forth the plants and dear fruits of the earth, and when she has brought them forth, Nature then stops, and Art comes, a helper of Nature, bringing the miller and baker; the miller grinds the grain into flour, from which the baker afterwards makes the dear and holy bread. *Likewise* <note>original Latin: "Item"</note>, as is also to be seen in the mines: there Nature brings forth the ore, but Art takes that same ore and makes from it Gold, Silver, and all kinds of metals which it contains, which Nature would bring forth so slowly if Art did not come to her aid through man. Furthermore, Nature gives birth to wood from the earth, but Art, through fire, makes ash from the wood, and from the ash, a glass—and such *examples* <note>original: "Exempel"</note> there is no need to recount at length. Now, if in the grain, ore, and wood, or ash, this first *Matter* <note>original Latin: "Matery"</note> of the bread, the metals, and the glass were not hidden, then Art would be in no way able to make and bring out what reveals itself, if the...

Since the artist is thus a co-worker and helper of Nature, and is and should be its <term>imitator</term> <note>original Latin: "Imitator"</note>, he must first well recognize the nature of each and every thing, so that he does not override it, but knows how to follow it in all its <term>limits</term> <note>original Latin: "Limitibus"; the natural boundaries or laws of a substance</note>. Herein it is required that he be a good, well-practiced, and experienced <term>philosopher</term> <note>original Latin: "Philosophus"; in this context, a student of natural science and divine laws</note> of a subtle understanding, so that he may well understand, weigh, and recognize the <term>causes</term> <note>original Latin: "causas"</note> of all things; he should have experienced so much in <term>philosophy</term> that he has brought all its <term>subjects</term> <note>original Latin: "subiecta"; the materials or matters being studied</note> into sufficient knowledge, knows their <term>seeds</term> <note>original Latin: "Semina"</note>, beginning, and element from which they arose, how they are generated, and what they may suffer or undergo in Nature. He should know the power of heat and fire, understand the birthing warmth, and know how all these perform their <term>effects</term> <note>original Latin: "Effectus"</note> in the air, water, and earth. The changes of the seasons should be known to him, as well as how the upper things <note>the celestial bodies/heavens</note> influence and flow into the lower things, and the like.

Therefore, let him <term>conjoin</term> <note>original Latin: "coniungiere"; to join or unite</note> and unite <term>philosophy</term> with <term>alchemy</term>, which is the practice of <term>philosophy</term>; for whoever wishes to come to practice without philosophy is just as if he wanted to fly and had no feathers, or walks without any understanding, like the donkey to its fodder, who does not know why he stretches out his mouth.

Now, if the true <term>philosopher</term> will thus arrange, establish, and consider his <term>practical operations</term> <note>original Latin: "Operationes Practica"</note> and <term>way of working</term> <note>original Latin: "Modum operandi"</note> according to true <term>physics</term> <note>original Latin: "Physica"; the study of the physical/natural world</note>, then the use of these writings and books will be more furthering and helpful to him than can be told in brief; he will also find the benefit in practice and experimentation—like one who receives a rich reward for his labor through the tasting of a lovely dish or food in the mouth. He should also first—which I shall in no way forget to exhort him—call upon and pray to God the Lord, who gives richly to everyone, for grace and understanding, that He might wish to kindle the fire of His Divine grace in the work.

# Preface to the Reader.

that which Nature promises, and wishes to seek and find it in the work itself, he should spare no expense to equip himself with all kinds of <term>mechanical instruments</term> <note>original Latin: "Mechanicis Instrumentis"; here meaning the specialized tools of the laboratory</note> that serve the craft. In these, he should also be fairly well-instructed in all manner of manual labor. He must have a well-equipped <term>laboratory</term> <note>original Latin: "Laboratorium"</note> with all kinds of furnaces, glassware, and other supplies, so that if something is needed in haste, it is immediately at hand, and one is not hindered, led astray, or delayed in the middle of the work for lack of tools. Therefore, if he wishes to undertake or begin anything, he must first be well-advised as to everything that belongs to it and what is necessary. He must also have previously learned all the manual techniques of <term>distilling</term>, <term>sublimating</term>, <term>calcining</term>, <term>reverberating</term>, <term>putrefying</term>, <term>casting</term>, and <term>refining</term> <note>original: "distillieren / supplimieren / calcinieren / reuerberieren / putrificieren / giessen / abtreiben"; these are the fundamental chemical processes of the era</note>, etc.

Now, if he has all this, and can, knows, and understands what belongs thereto, then the most important thing is that he does not shy away from any expense, effort, or labor; rather, let him be diligent, industrious, watchful, zealous, and of tireless constancy in his work. He must try things in various ways and repeat them often if they do not immediately succeed according to his wishes. For upon this point of constancy and perseverance in the work, everything depends. The secrets of nature are not opened to the lazy, sleepy, and negligent; for in this matter, one should well consider the saying of the philosopher <term>Epicharmus</term> <note>original Latin: "Epicarmi Philosophi"; a Greek poet and philosopher known for his moral maxims</note>, where he says: "The gods offer their gifts for sale, not for money, but for labor and service."

If the kind reader uses these writings in the manner described, he will not regret the effort and the expense incurred (if he desires to be a true and perfect <term>physician</term> <note>original Latin: "Medicus"</note>). Not only will he recover the value of what he has invested <term>with interest</term> <note>original Latin: "cum foenore"</note> through the noble medicines, but he will also see other things that will delight and please him many times over. It will so enlighten his understanding that he will not be able to wonder enough at the knowledge of nature. He will recognize God more and better, praising, honoring, and glorifying Him in His creatures, helping his neighbor with medicine, and thereby earning for himself both temporal and eternal reward. Thus, he will usefully spend his time in the fear and honor of God and will know how to be sufficiently grateful to God.

May the kind reader, therefore, take this fifth and last part—as well as the first mentioned writings of **Theophrastus Paracelsus** and other philosophers—under his care, and in time, with patience, expect something better, more intelligible, and more detailed. And with this, be commended to Divine protection. Done on the 30th of August, in the year 1604.

## On the Revelation of the Philosophical Materials and Things /
### From which the Mastery is accomplished / in the operation of the Noble and Blessed Stone of the Philosophers.

## Chapter One.

Seven children <note>Often referring to the "Children of the Art," or the seven planetary metals (Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, Lead).</note> and lovers of wisdom, you should diligently mark and observe in this noble art of Nature. The roots and the very best herbs of the philosophers <note>In alchemical "Deckname" (cover-names), "herbs" and "roots" rarely refer to literal plants, but rather to the minerals or metallic "seeds" from which the Stone grows.</note> are in part green mixed with white, in part citrine-colored <note>original: "Citrinfarb"; a lemon-yellow color signaling a specific stage of maturation in the alchemical process.</note> mixed with red and white colors; there are also some of blue colors. The smell and taste of them all is so noble and sweet that nothing sweeter may be found in this world, and the juice that is drawn from them is of such varied colors that it becomes red in the sunshine and white in the moonlight. And these herbs are common, and a heavenly gift, which are found at all times; the ancient philosophers have shrouded and hidden their power and virtue, and wished to write nothing of them nor reveal them, but rather spared no diligence to preserve and hide them most carefully. I, however, have named them to you quite perfectly by their right name, and swear by the Creator of Heaven and Earth that the art is accomplished from these and no other things in this world.

# Concerning Revelation

<margin>7</margin> Of these herbs, take a good portion, but take as much of one as of the others; mix them together and crush them quite small and put them into the Philosophical Vessel <note>A specialized alchemical glass container, such as a retort or cucurbit, designed to withstand heat.</note>, and draw out from them the four Elements: first the Water, second the <term>Ally</term> <note>original: "Ally"; likely a derivation of the Arabic "al-qali," referring here to the volatile alkaline spirit or oily substance produced during distillation.</note>, thirdly the Fire. In this way, the Element of Earth will remain in the bottom or base of the vessel. Crush or grind this Earth to the smallest possible size, and pour its recently extracted Water back upon it, and distill or draw the Water away from it again as was done before. This distillation or Sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collecting the purified result as it cools.</note> shall occur seven times, etc.

Namely, these seven times are to wake the dead or make them rise—that is, to kill them seven times through the ascent and to make them living seven times through the descent. For when Father Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy and the "father" of this Art.</note>, the inventor of this Art, was asked what the beginning and the first work of this Art might be, he answered and spoke: "You shall raise the dead seven times or exalt them or make them ascend, and let the living descend again; then you will have that which you seek and desire." For then the power of each is entirely inseparable, transformed one into the other, and a firm and lasting bond is made between the Bridegroom and the Bride—namely, between the Water and the Meal <note>original: "Mels"; likely referring to the dry, powdered substance or "flour" of the metal, though in some contexts it may signify "Mel" (Latin for honey).</note>. And in this degree, this Water of Life attains seven <term>Quintel Essentias</term> <note>original: "Quintel Essentias"; a Germanized plural of the Latin "Quinta Essentia," or the Fifth Essence—the purest, most potent celestial part of a substance.</note>; that is, a sevenfold fifth essence. For in the mentioned seven Sublimations or Distillations, it drinks in all the natures, essences, and life of the aforementioned herbs. Thereafter, you shall sublimate—that is, distill—this venerable water, which is called a Well of Life, two or three times by itself upon its Earth or dregs, and you shall cast away all impurity and foulness that it leaves behind in each sublimation. After this, you shall once again drive it very gently and slowly with a moderate fire, until the Watery Substance is pulled over entirely; keep this same substance alone and separately in a clean, well-stopped glass, for it has much magnificent power and virtue. When now the Watery Substance, as heard, is entirely out, and the Ally begins to rise, then you shall put forward another glass or receiver to receive the Ally, and strengthen the fire a little, and a little more, until nothing more of the Ally ascends. This Ally of the Philosophers you shall keep very well-sealed in a glass, for this is the Matter and our secret, to which the philosophers have given countless many names. Namely, it is called <term>Azach</term> <note>A common alchemical cover-name (Deckname) for Mercury or the universal spirit.</note>: according to the Indian language, it is or is called Gold; according to the Hungarian language, Azach is as much as to say Silver; but according to the Alexandrian and Macedonian, as much as Iron; and according to the Greek, Mercury or living silver <note>original: "Argentum viuum"</note>; according to the Hebrew, Tin; and according to the Tartar...

### The Fifth Chapter.

<margin>The Seal of Hermes</margin>
My Dear Son / much depends on the sealing or closing of the glasses / therefore you shall diligently pay attention and take heed of the following teaching / for / I will teach you here the sealing which our father **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> invented / and used / and it proceeds thus: Take first the **Philosophical** <note>original: "Philosophisch"</note> water mentioned before, which is divided with its most noble Earth / which is well mixed with its fresh Blood <note>Allegorical terms for the reagents: "Blood" often refers to the red mercury or a vitalizing agent, while "Earth" is the solid base.</note> / and put that together into a suitable one of the previously indicated glasses / but you should first diligently weigh the glass with its **Seal** <note>original: "Sigel"</note> or stopper / to / note the weight / before the matter goes into it / and weigh the matter also / and note it diligently / so that you may prepare yourself accordingly with that which follows / and then close its mouth thus: You should first have / a round glass disc or small sphere that closes upon or into the mouth of the glass / then you should have very finely crushed glass and coat the disc or sphere / and the mouth with it / just as goldsmiths are accustomed to use it for soldering / then you must likewise spread **Borax** <note>original: "Borras"; a mineral used as a flux to help glass and metals melt together at lower temperatures.</note> over it / but / the glass with the matter should first be placed in a vessel with ashes / then the mouth should be stopped with the glass [disc] / after that, lay charcoal / around and over the top / and let the coals catch fire nicely and slowly / after that, increase the fire and blow upon it gradually / until the neck and mouth become quite glowing red / then sprinkle **Borax** into the mouth / so it will / flow and melt shut and solder at the top. After this, let the fire burn out by itself / and go out / and when the glass has thus become cold of its own accord / then take the glass with the matter and place it in the furnace / as was taught before. You should also know that this sealing also happens with the tongs / namely / thus / when the neck of the glass is quite glowing red / then you should have a pair of tongs / which have been made a little hot / and press the neck shut with them / then it will also be entirely as if / it were melted shut / and then let it cool by itself with the covered coals / the form and shape of the vessel with the ashes / and it will be so.

# How the Philosophers' Furnace should be made / in which our Stone is cooked.

## The Sixth Chapter.

Son, you shall have made for yourself / a barrel or vessel of the very best potter's clay <note>original: "Haffner Erden"; a heat-resistant clay used for kilns and crucibles.</note> / which may well endure the fire / in which you shall place the stone or our water / securely enclosed. It should be so wide and spacious / that the glass standing within / has two or three fingers’ breadth of space on all sides / between the glass and the width of the vessel / and that same space should be filled with sifted ashes. Its form and shape shall be thus: / upon this same vessel a lid of potter’s clay shall also be made / so that it does not touch the glass / in which our matter is contained. ## The Twelfth Chapter.

Therefore you shall know, my dear son, that the blackness in the cooking of the **Stone** appears in forty days or in forty-two days, and it also lasts until the 40th or 42nd day—at times longer or shorter, depending on whether there is much or little of the matter. Through this, it changes itself into four kinds of colors, as mentioned above, until it comes to perfect whiteness. Furthermore, when you have the perfect White Elixir, it does not change or transform until it comes to the perfect Red, in which the final and all-powerful strength of the **Stone** resides.

However, the ancient philosophers held many different opinions regarding the multiplication and fermentation of their **Stone**, whether for the **White** <note>the stage for producing silver</note> or the **Red** <note>the stage for producing gold</note>, and have written various opinions on it. Yet, in the preparation and purification of the Stone, there is but one single way and one single labor, whether for the White or the Red.

## How the Medicine is finally fermented, so that it may perfectly tincture.

### The 18th Chapter.

If you wish to **tincture** <note>original: "tingieren"; to transform the nature and color of a base metal into a noble one</note>, then take of the **body** <note>original: "Leichnam," literally "corpse"; refers to the solid material base of the metal</note>, either Red or White, whichever you desire. Make that same body entirely subtle—<term>that</term> <note>original: "dz," an abbreviation for "das"</note> is, you shall turn it into a subtle powder or **calx** <note>a fine powder produced by heating a metal or mineral</note>. Place it into a glass vessel that is well-sealed with **lute** <note>a clay-like paste used to make vessels airtight</note> or into a strong crucible, and place it in the fire. Let the <term>Ally</term> <note>a term for the liquid essence or "oil" of the elixir</note> of the Elixir fall bit by bit into the powder of the body, so that they unite with one another and become the most subtle powder of all. But take care that you do not add too much of the Elixir <term>Ally</term>. This ferment is then a true Elixir, with which you may tincture and transform all metals. You can also turn **mercury** <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note> into fine silver, once the Medicine has been prepared for silver or gold. It becomes stable and is, moreover, much better than natural mineral silver or gold.

## Of the Power and Effect of the Blessed Stone.

### The 19th Chapter.

This honorable, highly praised, and **blessed Philosophical Stone** restores and delivers the bodies of men from all manner of sicknesses or diseases, whatever they may be. Secondly, it brings all imperfect, impure bodies of metals to their perfection; it cleanses them and heals them of their **leprosy** <note>original: "Außsatz"; a common alchemical metaphor for the impurities and corrosion found in base metals like lead or iron</note>. Thirdly, it transforms common stones into precious gemstones. Fourthly, it makes glass malleable, so that it may be worked and hammered like silver and gold.

# TREASURY OF PHILO-
# SOPHY, BY EUFERARIUS.

<margin><unclear>Ludovicus Ferrarius</unclear></margin>
<margin>The philosophers have presented the art in two ways: one true, one false.</margin>
May He be willing to reveal His bounty to us—He to whom all things belong, the Heavens, Earth, and Sea, and who could create everything out of nothing and join the unequal into harmony, and who ordained according to His goodness that the sick might be helped with medicines. Regarding this, the ancient sages—who presented this perfect understanding in their books in two ways: one true, and one false. The righteous ones <note>meaning the true alchemists</note> set down their work with veiled words, so that they might be perfectly understood by no one except their own children <note>in this context, "children" refers to their students or initiated followers</note>. They kept it hidden for this reason: so that the godless might not use this Art and become even more prepared to commit evil deeds, for which sins they would have to give an account. Therefore, take care, most beloved, that you do not reveal this Art to any unworthy person, but rather, according to philosophical custom, keep it secret; for if you prove it through the Work and find it to be righteous, the joy and love within you to preserve it will increase.

The false way, however, is described with clear words; I will now bypass the recounting of that erroneous path and its circumstances. But, most beloved, listen and pay attention to the truth, and so God will enlighten your understanding.

<margin>The true art.</margin>
<margin>Things are the 4 Elements, page 612.</margin>
Know then, that our Art is an Art of the 4 Elements, and in its essence, it is transformed within itself—a point upon which all philosophers agree. You should also know that in the aforementioned "thing" <note>referring to the primary matter of the Stone</note> under the Heavens are the 4 Elements, not according to their outward appearance, but according to their inner virtue; for this reason, the philosophers have not taught or worked this Art under the mere cover of the Art of the elements. However, when some did not understand the literal sense of this operation, they tried to attempt all of this in blood, urine, and eggs, as well as in many other similar approaches; and I likewise attempted them, and was horrified by it. And therefore, as I had fallen into complete doubt regarding this Art, I set such work aside and accomplished nothing, due to the weakness of my understanding.

Afterward, however, I came back to myself and began to reflect with **Avicenna** <note>a famous Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose writings on medicine and philosophy were foundational to Western alchemy</note>: if this "single thing" is indeed a single thing, how can it be? Or if it is not, how is it not? Thus, I found that the matter of all metals—

# Treasure of Philosophy.

<margin>//</margin>The mother is moist and cold, which nourishes the newborn. Therefore, the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"; representing Gold</note> by itself and the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; representing Silver</note> by itself are most impossible to cast together. But when they are united, in the manner that the hardening into **Gold** occurs, they are easily cast. Therefore Maria <note>referring to Maria Prophetissima, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says: take the precipitated **Body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note> or clear pearls that take on no putrefaction, and rub it with *Elsapenes* <note>original: "Elsapenes"; likely a corruption of an Arabic alchemical term for a specific solvent or salt</note>, which contains within itself the **Tincture of Spirits**, and move it toward the fire; and it will soon melt completely if you project upon it his wife, the **Moon**. Therefore, if only one of these two were in our **Stone** <note>original: "Lapide"</note>, this medicine would not flow easily or provide a **Tincture**; and even if it did provide one, it would not tint any further than its own mass; the rest would pass away, just as **Mercury** <note>original: "mercurius"</note> passes away in smoke. For there would be no staying of the tincture for them; but that is our final secret: to have a medicine that flows before the disappearance of the **Mercury**. The union of these two is necessary in this our **Work**.

Hence **Geber** <note>an 8th-century alchemist known for his "sum of perfection"</note> says: in a perfect work, **Gold** is better than other metals, for it is the **Tincture of Redness** that transforms all bodies; it is the leaven <note>original: "Heffel"; literally "yeast"</note> that brings the whole dough to its proper quality. It is also the **Soul** that unites the **Spirit** with the **Body**. For just as the human body is immobile without the soul, so too the impure body—whose soul is earthly—is powerless. For the leaven of the well-prepared body transforms the entire body into its own nature. And there is no **Ferment** <note>original: "Fermentum"</note> except only the **Sun** and **Moon**, assigned to the <margin>//</margin>planets; for just as the Sun and Moon rule over other planets, so these two bodies rule over the other bodies of the metals, which are transformed into the capability of these two mentioned natures. And for this reason it is called **Ferment**, <margin>//</margin>since indeed size adds no improvement to it; as **Raymond** <note>referring to Raymond Llull</note> says: "you cannot improve this unless it is made subtle through art and operation." Therefore **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: "Bring forth from the Sun’s radiance its shadow." Consequently, the preparation and refining of such a ferment is necessary, as in a well; for as far as the creation is concerned, it certainly washes, but not as far as the effect is concerned, unless it is first fed with a little milk, then not more, and finally with much; and thus it happens entirely with this our **Stone**.

Take therefore one quarter—that is, one part of the **Ferment**—and three parts of the **perfect Body**; let it dissolve again into the ferment, into its likeness through the **Water of Mercury**; cook it together with the gentlest fire and coagulate the **Ferment**, so that it becomes like an imperfect body, in a closed vessel: <note>original: "Geschirr"; referring to the philosopher's egg or sealed flask</note>

> a King of Arabia has said: the water is not made hard <note>solidified or congealed</note> except by the like of its sulfur, which is within it.

Afterward, we make that which is above equal to that which is below—that is, that the body becomes a spirit, and the spirit becomes a body, just as it is at the beginning of our work, as in the sublimation <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the purified deposit as it cools</term>. <margin>Sublimation:</margin>
> Therefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founding figure of alchemy</note> says: that which is above through sublimation is below through descent; that which is below through compaction is just like that which is above through ascent, to accomplish the wonder-work of a single thing.

Water and earth have their nature; the air and fire below rise above themselves. Water and Earth <note>original: "Aqua und Terra"</note> receive and nourish Air and Fire <note>original: "Aerem und Ignis"</note>, joining and driving them together. These four elements come into agreement in our Stone <note>original: "Lapide"</note>, etc.

> Of this Senior <note>Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabic alchemist often cited in European texts</note> says: the fourth element in our Stone should be purified; for within it is fixed water <note>original: "aqua fixa" — a liquid that resists evaporation by heat</note>, a light air, a still earth, a fire that surrounds everything, and discord is not one with it; and these four natures are born in it, from it, and through it.

Thus it is known from the above-mentioned that our Stone is of four elements. So the Philosophers have said that our Stone has Body, Spirit, and Soul, and these three are said to be of one nature, of one thing, with one water, from one root. And they say rightly that our entire work happens with our water, and from it and out of it all things are necessary; for it dissolves the bodies <note>original: "soluiert die corpora"</note>, not according to common dissolution as the inexperienced claim—that they are turned into cloud-water <note>original: "aquam nubis"</note>—but with true philosophical dissolution, so that they are transformed into the water from which they came.

> Therefore Socrates <note>In alchemical literature, "Socrates" is often a pseudonym for an anonymous authority or refers to the "Socrates of the alchemists"</note> says: the secret in every thing and life is Water; this dissolves the body into spirit and makes the dead living; that is, the sharpest Vinegar <note>original: "Acetum"</note>, which clings to everything, surpasses everything, and scours away.

Therefore, cook our Stone <note>original: "Lapidem"</note> with the sharpest vinegar until it becomes hard, yet quite quickly, so that the vinegar does not turn into smoke and come to nothing.

> According to which King Marches <note>likely referring to King Morienus, a legendary hermit-alchemist</note> says: our Water dissolves our bodies, congeals and blackens them, washes off every body, takes away all blackness, and tinctures all blackness and makes it white; tinctures everything white and makes it red; also makes alive all the dead, leading them into eternal life.

Therefore, this Water is highly praised and highly esteemed.

Therefore, it makes a marriage between the Husband and <margin>Amalgam: also moisture</margin> Wife; for every Spirit consists of the subtlety of the Air, for everything that has a living growth draws its Spirit from the Air. But Fire <note>original: "Ignis"</note> makes the dead Water alive; the Air makes a marriage and protects such composed things from the consumption of the fire. Therefore, the Philosophers have said: turn the Water into Air so that a Life may be made, yet a Life with a Life; for it is Life and Spirit which it receives.

<margin>Philosophical Sublimation</margin> Therefore, our Water <note>original: "Aqua"</note> does not sublimate the Bodies <note>original: "Corpora"</note> according to common sublimation, which the unlearned practice, sublimating them upward into the heights; they call them calcinated bodies <note>original: "calcinata corpora"</note>, mixing them and making them rise with the sublimated Spirits. They say then that the bodies and Spirits—Sulfur <note>original: "sulphur"</note> and Mercury <note>original: "mercurius"</note>—added with a recipe <note>original symbol: "℞"</note>, and performing a sublimation through a strong fire so that the Bodies rise with the Spirits, they say then that the Bodies and Spirits are sublimated and purified of their superfluity. But they are deceived, for they find them afterward more unclean than they were before. Of this, Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note> speaks in the book *On Minerals* <note>original: "libro de mineralib."</note>: since two foreign humors from the substance of the Sulfur have been purified by the work and the artful property of Nature, they could not be better purified or cleaned by Art. For Nature's masterpiece is more certain <margin>Philosophical Sublimation</margin> and higher than Art. Therefore, our Sublimation is not an ascent, but the sublimation of the Philosophers is from a small, low...

Therefore, between the <term>solution</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note> of the <term>body</term> <note>original: "Corpus"</note> and the <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process of a liquid becoming solid or semi-solid.</note> of the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "Spiritus"</note>, there is no difference in time, nor does anything happen within it at different intervals, etc. Thus, one is made without the other, just as during the joining of water and earth there is no unequal distribution of time. # TREATISE
## In which the entire Secret of Alchemy / of the Philosopher’s Stone is contained.

<margin>
Treatise of
Johann Isaac Hollandus,
Work 52
</margin>

My child, you should know that from **Saturn** <note>In alchemy, Saturn is the code name for lead.</note> the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note> comes and is made; and once it is made, it performs a great **projection** <note>term: "projection" — the final stage of alchemy where a small amount of the Stone is "cast" upon a base substance to transform it</note> into the human body, against all infirmities that may afflict a person, whether inward or outward, whatever they may be, and also into the metals. In the whole **vegetable work** <note>A term implying that the alchemical process mimics the organic growth and life cycles of plants.</note>, there is no greater secret than that which lies in <margin>veg:</margin> Saturn: for we do not find in gold the perfection that we find in Saturn. Truly, Saturn is good gold in its interior; in this <margin>gold is good internally</margin> all the philosophers are in agreement. Since it is now good gold in its interior, and lacks nothing else except that one removes from it what is excessive and superfluous—its impurity—therefore one should make it pure, and then turn its interior outward, that is, its redness; then it is good gold. For gold cannot be worked as easily as one works Saturn; because Saturn allows itself to be easily **dissolved** and **coagulated** <note>The processes of liquefying a solid and then making it solid again.</note>, and it also very easily allows its **mercury** <note>In this context, the "mercury" of a metal refers to its essential, volatile spirit or "soul."</note> to be drawn out. The mercury that is drawn from Saturn, when one cleanses and **sublimes** <note>term: "sublimation" — heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again, used here as a purification method</note> it as one is accustomed to sublime, I tell you truly that this mercury is as good as that which is drawn from gold, for all works. For since Saturn is good gold internally—as it is in truth—its mercury must also be as good as the mercury of gold; for if you were to draw from [the mercury of gold], you would certainly need a whole year to "open" the gold before the mercury comes from the gold. But you draw the mercury out of Saturn in 14 days, and both are equally good. If you want to make a work from gold alone, you must work for a full 2 years until you complete it; but if you make a work from Saturn, you complete it in 32 or 30 weeks at the longest, and when both are finished, they are both equally good.

All the wonderful parables which the philosophers made dark...

<margin>Calcined Saturn (Lead)</margin>
roughly two or three fingers high above it, on an iron hook made for this purpose. The jar should be properly and well-sealed so that the **spirits** <note>Volatile vapors</note> do not escape. Then, take good distilled wine vinegar again and grind the Saturn with the distilled vinegar on a stone, as fine as you possibly can. Stir it 3 or 4 times every day. Close it with a glass or stone lid and place it in **Mary's Bath** <note>original: "Balneum Mariæ" — a water bath used for gentle, consistent heating.</note>, or else in a warm place. Stir it three or 4 times every day with a small wood stick or spoon, and 
<margin>Warmth.</margin>
always close it up well again. The bath should not be hotter than what a hand can endure, but only lukewarm. Let it stand for fourteen days.

<margin>Dissolved Saturn.</margin>

# Secret of the Philosopher’s Stone

<margin>residue <note>original: "feces"</note>.</margin>
Once fully dissolved, proceed as you have been taught: discard the residue <note>The solid waste or impurities left after dissolution.</note>, and coagulate the dissolved substance, then dissolve it again. Because its coldness is on the outside—as in **Luna** <note>The alchemical name for Silver (☽).</note>—and its warmth is within, it is meltable like wax and sweet as sugar candy.

<margin>Saturn is clear as snow. Sweet. White: sweet.</margin>

Why is it sweet as sugar candy? <note>This refers to Lead Acetate, historically called "Sugar of Lead" for its sweet taste. It has immediately become material and like nature because it is so pure and clean. It gives off a little of its innermost power, such as its watery nature, but the warmth is so covered by the cold that it cannot yet put forth its full power.

Regarding the coldness that is on the outside—the spirit of taste is the most subtle thing in all the world. This is taught at length in the **Herbal** <note>original: "Kräuter-buch" — a book detailing the medicinal properties of plants.</note>: how the air permeates all herbs and flowers from the outside, for the spirit of the air resides in the innermost part of all things in the world. For God has created nothing that does not have its particular taste or "air." Taste and air are a spirit; taste comes out of the air like smoke comes from a fire. But how does it happen that a thing containing its own air tastes bitter? This comes from the residue that is rotten and stinking within the elements; this is **Choler** <note>original: "Colera" — one of the four humors, associated with heat, dryness, and bitterness.</note> or heat. For whatever is unnaturally hot always has a bitter taste. Air and taste are both one spirit, and as the spirit presses upward through the air like a hot thing, the air encloses the taste within itself and protects the subtle taste so that it is not burned by the hot Choler, as is taught at length in the *Herbal*.

# Now follows the preparation of the second principle <note>original: *Principij*</note>, namely the Sulfur of the Sun <note>original: *Sulphuris Solis*</note> or of the Philosophers, which the philosophers often and frequently call the Soul <note>original: *Animam*</note>.

<margin>Sun <note>original: *Sol.*</note> 5</margin>
If you wish to prepare your Soul <note>original: *Anima*</note> and the Philosophical Sulfur or Tincture <term>Tincture: In alchemy, a medicine or spirit capable of transmuting or healing</term> anew, you must continue and proceed as mentioned from the beginning until the separation of the Soul. However, because in the preparation of the Earth <note>original: *Terra*</note> the second principle is not yet completed, it is not necessary to begin anew; rather, take only your Soul which you have previously set aside, and take the purified, often-distilled, and spiritualized water. Pour them together into a clean flask <note>original: *Kolben*</note>, set a blind alembic head <term>Blind helm: A distillation cap without a spout, used to force vapors to condense and fall back into the vessel for "circulation"</term> upon it, seal it with the aforementioned luting <note>original: *luto supradicto*</note>, and place it in warm sand or ash—which, however, should not be too hot. Let it elevate, circulate, and putrefy for three days, and then separate it as described. Place that same Soul into a clean glass, well-sealed as first mentioned, and keep it until the Composition <note>The final joining of the three principles</note>.

However, I have taken new and earthy "inflated matter" <note>original: *materiam inflatam*</note> and placed it into a coated flask, well-sealed, and distilled it gently out of the sand. I poured it over several times and afterwards drove it over with a strong fire and separated it; thus the Soul was much more beautiful, redder, more transparent, and possessed many more colors than the other which came out of the putrefaction. I have also used a good portion of it, as can be seen in the description of the composition.

<margin>Luting</margin>
Note one more thing: when you attach the receiver or recipient vessel, you should also seal it with our luting; otherwise, you will labor in vain and will not bring the **Red Lion** into his stall, nor will you see the **Green Lion**. <note>The "Red Lion" often symbolizes the concentrated sulfur or the mercury of gold, while the "Green Lion" represents the raw mineral or the acidic solvent used at the start of the work.</note> You must also be prepared with another good luting made from egg whites, brick dust, glue, and wool, in case our luting becomes weak or tired in the great heat, so that you may come to its aid with this one. Take great care that you do not anger the **Red Lion**, lest he inflict an insurmountable harm upon you—as happened to me—and strike you poorly. All of this is to be prevented if you let our luting dry thoroughly before you light the fire. Thereafter you will know how to conduct yourself; let this be a warning to you. Thus you have also prepared the second principle, namely the Sulfur of the Philosophers.

# Regarding the Philosophical Stone.

In the same way, by varying the heat—just as you did with the others—until you have separated the Soul <note>original: *Anima*</note> from it; however, you must not drive the Spirits <note>original: *Spiritus*</note> so strongly from the Earth <note>original: *Erden*</note> as you did before in the other work, so that the Water may retain its strength and spirituality in its preparation. It would also not be harmful, since it is the preparation of Mercury <note>original: *præparatio Mercurij*</note>, if one were to distill and pour it back over repeatedly until the Soul remains entirely fixed <term>Fixed: In alchemy, a substance that is stable under heat and does not evaporate or change</term> behind, and only the Water and Air pass over together. I have not tried it myself, but I know well that it happens and becomes entirely fixed through multiple repetitions. Then the work of this third Principle <note>original: *Principij*</note> follows further, namely that of Mercury <note>original: *Mercurij*</note>: Take a well-coated flask <note>original: *Kolben*</note>, put your Earth <note>original: *Terra*</note> into it, and pour in the Water from which you separated your Soul; seal it very well with lute <term>Lute: A clay or paste used to seal laboratory vessels airtight</term>, and place it in sand. Distill it gently at first, and at the last very strongly—as strongly as you can—so that all the Spirits enter into it until no more pass over. Afterwards, let it cool and put it back into a coated flask, and distill and drive it as before; do this six or seven times, but watch carefully that the Spirit does not fly away. When this has been done, it would be necessary that you have a large amount of the prepared Earth in which the Spirit still remained, and drive that same Earth four times with its Spirit. And when this has happened, let it cool and put it back into a whole coated flask, and distill and drive it as before; do this five or six times—the more, the better—but watch carefully that the Spirit does not escape. When that has also been done, it would be necessary (according to Morienus <note>original: *secundum Morienem*; Morienus was a legendary 7th-century alchemist</note>) that the Mercury, for its Alteration <term>Alteration: A stage of transformation where the properties of the matter are changed</term>, be distilled four times with the prepared Earth in which its Spirit still remains, and the Spirit be driven into it. After all this, let it cool.

# On Philosophical Vitriol.

<margin>7 times</margin>
<margin>Water <note>The symbol ∇ represents the element of Water.</note></margin>
The more often you rectify it <note>Rectification is the process of repeated distillation to increase purity and potency.</note>, the better it is. It should be rectified seven times in this manner, or as many times as necessary until it no longer rises; this makes it much better and more virtuous for the **residues** <term>Feces: The solid matter or dregs remaining in the vessel after distillation.</term>, which will be discussed later.
Now, if you wish to use this water as medicine for the human body, place it in a small glass with a long neck, two or three hand-breadths long, upon a stove with a gentle fire. In this way, it will be perfected; and the longer it stands, the more perfect it becomes. It does not even need to be tightly sealed at the top; one only needs to ensure that no impurities fall into it.

### How the Water Should be Used.

Furthermore, take a half-beaker of wine and let one drop of the **secret water** <term>aqua secreta: A purified alchemical solvent or essence.</term> fall into it. Mix it well into the wine with a knife, for it is heavy and tends to sink to the bottom. Then taste it; if it is far too sharp, pour more wine into it; if it is too sweet, add water until it has the proper flavor that pleases you and is well-mixed, as has been said.

This substance cures the **residues** <term>Feces: In a medical context, this refers to waste products or blockages within the body.</term>, and is good in times of Plague if one washes the painful areas with it. It cures the gout <note>original: Podagram</note>, and this is the true **potable gold** <term>aurum potabile: A legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold dissolved in a drinkable form, thought to grant eternal youth.</term>, in which the **secrets of nature** <note>original: secreta naturæ</note> are hidden. You will find this through practice; this is the true **human blood** <note>original: sanguis Humanus; likely a metaphor for its life-giving properties.</note>, the true **Celandine** <term>Chelidonia: A plant traditionally associated with the sun and used to treat eye and liver ailments.</term>. These flowers are like gold and heavy as **Mercury** <term>Mercurius: Quicksilver, often used here to describe the weight and density of the liquid.</term>. If the water is used daily, it maintains health. It should be administered in wine or Malmsey <note>A sweet, fortified Greek wine.</note>, and it is said that all the virtues of **potable gold** are within it. It is for the **falling sickness** <note>Epilepsy.</note>, making the sufferer healthy in a short time simply by washing with it. Through practice and use, you will find many virtues in it; mixed with rosewater, it becomes a confection that one may eat with meat instead of salt.

### The Oil, Very Good for Medicine.

<margin>still-head</margin>
Take the old oil and pour it over the **residues** <term>Feces</term> after the water has been drawn off by the **still-head** <term>alembicum: The cap of a distilling apparatus that collects and cools vapors.</term>. The oil that is made afterward is very good for the **falling sickness** <term>Caducum: Another term for epilepsy.</term>, fistulas, and other foul holes and sores. It has a sharp and powerful effect. However, if it were poured over the black **residues** from which the **strong water** <term>Aquafort: A corrosive acid, usually nitric acid.</term> or **secret water** was drawn, it would not be as powerful or as healing. It is still good, to be sure, but only for cases where a great effect is not required. The reason is this: the "best" residues still retain their **spirits** <term>Spiritus: Volatile essences believed to hold the medicinal power of a substance.</term> within them, which are afterward mixed with the oil, whereas the other residues have been robbed of these **spirits** and **souls** <term>Animæ: The vital or fixed essence of a substance in alchemy.</term>.

<margin>7th Addition.</margin>
Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, take the rectified secret water, as shown above; put it in a strong glass and place it in the furnace, well-surrounded by ash so that you do not need to move it until the end of the work. And note: however much of the secret water you took, add the same weight of the aforementioned <margin>5th Addition.</margin> rectified water. <margin>tested. v.</margin>

It is called the **Vegetable Stone** <margin>Vegetable Stone <note>original: lap: veg:</note></margin>, which is without end and requires no other body than its own birth and composition.

Take the black earth that you kept from before and calcine it <term>calciniers: To heat a substance to high temperatures in order to oxidize it or reduce it to powder.</term> in the reverberatory furnace until it becomes as red as possible. Put it in a glass with its alembic and receiver; distill until the dregs <term>Feces: The solid matter or residue remaining in the vessel.</term> lie dry at the bottom in a white color like salt, etc.

<margin>Water of Metals <note>The symbol 🜔 represents Water; here referring to the metallic water.</note></margin>
Take this salt, which is called the **Salt of Metals**, and add as much of the secret water that was rectified above, pouring it on gently. Leave it in tempered warmth until finally the salt is purified with the mentioned water, becoming hard and dry. # OIL OF VITRIOL
<margin>This is in Roger Bacon's treatise.</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' with floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
Vitriol <note>a naturally occurring sulfate mineral, often appearing as green or blue crystals</note> is a noble mineral, held in great dignity and esteem by the true philosophers—and indeed not without reason: for the Almighty and Greatest GOD has exalted it far above His other mineral creations and creatures.

And although many of the observers have noticed something from the true philosophers, they have ultimately not been able to reach the correct understanding of the philosophical cause of such secrets. It has also been the custom and habit among the ancients, as Isaac <note>likely referring to the alchemist Isaac Hollandus</note> says, that they recorded and made their secrets understood either in obscured riddles, stories, fables, or images, or else composed them in hidden philosophical sayings, sentences, and rhymes, as they have also done and said regarding Vitriol, etc.

> ->Visit the interior of the Earth; by rectifying, you will find the hidden Stone, the true medicine.<-
<note>original Latin: "Visitetis interiora Terrae, rectificando, invenietis occultum Lapidem veram medicinam." This famous sentence forms the acronym V.I.T.R.I.O.L.</note>

To understand this thus, the words themselves indeed indicate correctly, which we thus explain or interpret: Since the ancients say that one should visit the Earth by **rectifying** <term>rectification</term> <note>the process of purifying a liquid by repeated distillation</note>, "rectifying" is not to be understood as the poor, common earth of any of the mountains of vitriol.

<margin>Vitriol is green on the outside. <br/> Vitriol is red on the inside.</margin>
Furthermore, they say that the inner parts of the Earth should be visited and not the outer. Thus, vitriol is green in color on the outside, as can be seen with the eyes, but the philosophers find it red on the inside. The tongues find it or taste it from the outside as sharp and harsh, yet it is sweet and lovely on the inside. The hands touch it from the outside as hard and coarse, yet it is delicate and lovely on the inside, and is truly a subtle, noble juice, balsam, and pure oil. The noses perceive its smell as quite wild and misshapen, like sulfur, yet in its interior it is nobler and more lovely than **ambergris** <note>a rare, sweet-smelling substance used in perfumes</note> or a balsam, and is tasted as such.

Although many philosophers have perhaps dreamed, or from other indications—

### Of Philosophical Vitriol.

However, they did not wish to understand that neither through **distillation** nor **calcination** <note>the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to powder</note>, as they were accustomed to doing, could anything useful be brought forth—though some achieved more than others. <margin>green Oil.</margin>
as soon as it loses its green color, its oil, spirit, and the secret of all philosophers is already lost. For you should know that in all creatures—whether **vegetables** <note>original: "Vegetabilia"</note> or other minerals as they are, and also the metals—they are red in their true **essence** <term>Arcanitet</term> <note>from "Arcanum," meaning the most secret, concentrated medicinal or spiritual core of a substance</note> and in their primary state. Such **secrets** <note>original: "Arcana"</note> and praised oils should be taken from them while raw and red as blood. Therefore, there is a great error in the distillations of common apothecaries and physicians, for they have not allowed nature enough room, nor have they helped her so that she could bring her essences in the plants to such a blood-red oil.

Indeed, nature herself gives us to understand that she is capable and ready—if only she is helped—to transform herself in a short time into her own red juice and secret oil. This can be seen in the common distillation of plants, such as in **Pennyroyal** <note>original: "Pulegi"</note> and **Rue** <note>original: "Rhute"</note> and others; how from year to year they become what they are through their own **rectification** <term>rectification</term> <note>the process of refining and purifying a substance through repeated distillation or aging</note>. Thus, eventually, if they were to be preserved for several seasons, they would transform and **transmute** themselves into a blood-red oil and juice. But the reason this happens and proceeds so slowly is that the unlearned preparers, during distillation, take away the greenness too harshly and quickly, not allowing nature enough room or protecting her until the noble color transforms itself.

One sees the same thing in ripe, well-timed wines: when they age, are drawn off, and kept for a year, how they **rectify** and clarify themselves, and from day to day work and strive toward their natural colors. Nature does this in her own time and according to her own properties.

However, a **destruction, corruption, and putrefaction** <term>Putrefactio</term> <note>the alchemical stage of "blackness" where a substance breaks down or rots before it can be reborn in a higher form</note> must first occur in certain natures; and if these are successfully completed by nature, she proceeds to her rightful goal, which was given to her by GOD.

Take this as an example: if you place rain or other simple water into a beautiful glass or a well-sealed jar, set it in the air, and let it stand for a time, you will see how the elements in nature begin to **rectify** the plain, simple water. For in a few days, it will become cloudy and stinking, and will cast its **dregs** <note>original: "Feces," referring to the solid impurities or sediment</note> and coarse, earthly, and corruptible uncleanness to the

I tell you truly, when this **rectification** <term>Rectification</term> <note>the alchemical process of refining a substance through repeated purification, often involving distillation or settling</note> of nature has occurred in this way, you will find the water clearer and purer than any **essential spirit** <note>original: "Essentialischen spiritum"</note>, and it will be as sweet as sugar. Look also at the bones of poor sinners who have been condemned and executed; how quickly the nature of the elements, or the elements within nature, begin a **rectification** of the bones. First comes a **destruction** or **corruption**, or as others call it, a **putrefaction** <note>original: "Putrifaction"; the stage of decomposition where the matter turns black and "dies" before being reborn</note>; for the bones become black and stinking. But through the passage of time and years, they are purified by the elements until they appear chalk-white, as if they had been **calcined** <note>reduced to a white powder through high heat</note> snow-white by a burning fire—and nature does this herself.

Look at the old roofs covered with metallic plates, such as **lead** or **copper**; see how dear nature works and rectifies within the metallic bodies through the properties of the elements. For they stand under the open sky of the elements and the sun, which, through its lovely warmth along with the **essential** and **spiritual rays** <note>original: "Radijs"</note> and other stars, works upon such a metallic **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note>; and how the clouds bring water and the winds labor, always persisting and never ceasing. For I have seen how nature, with great power through her lovely operation, drove a great dross <note>original: "Schaum," literally "foam" or "scum"</note> out of the lead and calcined the lead until it was completely brittle, and transformed half of it into silver. Keep this in mind and do not forget it, for there are great mysteries within them revealed to us by nature.

Thus, after all this, let us proceed to the work and follow the order of nature.
