...if they are rough and impure, it brings the master-worker <note>original: "Werckmeister"; the practicing alchemist</note> great harm, for the reason that the Medicine <term>Medicine</term> <note>original: "Medicin"; another name for the Philosopher's Stone or the Tincture in its final, active state</note> remains partially stuck in the impure slag and does not touch the pure part of the metal.

Therefore, I think it right to provide a small instruction at this point, so that one does not bring the noble Medicine to nothing and uselessly pour it away with the slag. For you should know that all bodies of the imperfect metals are so impure that some hardly retain a third part, such as Antimony <term>♁</term>, some a half part, such as Copper <term>♀</term>, and some a third part, such as Lead <term>♄</term> and Tin <term>♃</term>; the rest is nothing but a foam and slag, which the Medicine casts out from the metals and separates from them.

Some have indeed claimed—though falsely and from a fictional basis—that one could tinge <term>Tinge</term> <note>original: "tingieren"; the act of changing the color and nature of a metal, usually from base to noble</note> the metals through the oils and waters of the metals, or the tinctures, so that they remain entirely whole. Some then add more and say they also remain malleable; just as I was once approached by a liar who said he had a silver Groschen <note>A common silver coin of the era</note> that was entirely transmuted into pure and malleable gold without any injury to its body. But when I told him that it could not possibly be true, as it was against Nature and her essence, he scoffed at me. However, when it came to the proof, it all amounted to nothing.

Therefore, you faithful seekers of this mystery should know that when the Medicine of the oils is spread upon an imperfect corpse <note>original: "unvollkommen Leichnam"; refers to a base metal like lead or tin</note>, the metal breaks and falls apart entirely like clay; for the Medicine penetrates all the members, and none remains unbroken. Then one must let that same earth melt together into a solid body in a crucible, and that which is under the slag will be its gold, malleable and noble.

# Experiments of Raymond Lully.

...happened to us / because of the mighty great fire / so that we had to take a new vessel. Therefore, know / that the fire with which one reverberates <note>Refers to a "reverberatory" furnace where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof onto the material</note> must be tempered in a proper way / so that it must be equal to the glass-maker's fire. When now the body <term>corpus</term> <note>The solid substance being worked upon, in this case, the Tartar</note> is calcined <term>calciniert</term> <note>Reduced to a dry powder or ash through intense heat</note> and ground in the moisture / then set it upon a marble stone / cover it up / so that the dust does not fall upon it / and other things / by which it would become filthy. Now dissolve it / or break it / and take the broken or dissolved matter into a strong vessel or glass / which you should distill <term>distillieren</term> through a felt <note>A piece of felt used as a primitive filter</note> / and thereafter place it in the urinal-flask <term>Urinal</term> <note>A bulbous, long-necked glass vessel used for distillation</note> with the alembic <term>Alembick</term> <note>The cap or "head" of the still that directs vapors into a condenser</note> and receivers <term>Recipienten</term> / and distill <term>distillieren</term> it in hot ashes with a gentle fire / so that the glass does not break / and thus coagulate <term>coagulieren</term> <note>To turn a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state</note> it / which when it has happened / and you have cooled the vessel / then pour the water which you have distilled down / back over the matter <term>Matery</term> / and soon thereafter this noble salt <term>Saltz</term> shall be dissolved in its water / and distill the water again through the felt. Since, however, this thing, according to our thought and understanding / has less annoyance and danger about it / so that no filth or other thing falls into the vessel / it is my advice / that you take a subtle linen cloth / and let that which you have distilled pass through it / and do not dry it out / thus there will remain in the cloth a perishable or destructible earth / which you should throw away / and once again through a new subtle and delicate linen cloth / let the previous liquid <term>Liquorem</term> <note>original Latin: "Liquorem"</note> run through as before / and continue this until no more filth remains in the cloth. When you now see the sign / you shall put that same liquid <term>Liquor</term> or juice back into the urinal-flask / securing it with its helm [the alembic head] and receivers <term>Recipienten</term> / so that it coagulates <term>coagulier</term> / as mentioned above / and after it has coagulated <term>coaguliert</term> / dissolve <term>soluieren</term> it again / and let it run through the cloth again / as before. Then you will see a new earth in the cloth / put it away / and this work shall be often repeated / until by God's help no more earth remains behind / or is left behind / but stays white and glittering / clean and well-polished and shining / as it was from the beginning. But you can also have another sign / which is more certain / of the purification of this matter <term>Matery</term> / or visibility / for after you have completed the distillation <term>Distillation</term> / and the entire moisture or wateriness is gone / the precious salt <term>Saltz</term> will remain in the vessel / over the fire / in the form of an oil / which / when it is taken away from the fire / is instantly coagulated <term>coaguliert</term>. You, most beloved son, do not let yourself be made weary / by the long time spent in dissolving <term>soluieren</term> / because this matter <term>Matery</term> often coagulates <term>coaguliert</term> / and every time the impurity that remains in the cloth / should be removed from it / which / if they remain behind / it will never be able to come together / with its spirit <term>Spiritu</term> <note>original Latin: "Spiritu"; the volatile essence or vaporous part of the substance</note>, which [has been drawn] out—

Take good tartar <term>Weinstein</term> <note>Potassium bitartrate, the hard crust found in wine barrels</note> / grind it and place it in a glazed vessel / then place it in a glass furnace / and calcine <term>calcinier</term> <note>To heat a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash</note> it in the reverberatory furnace / for three days / or as long as it takes until it becomes white / after that, dissolve it in water of life <term>aqua vita</term> <note>Distilled alcohol or spirit of wine</note> of the first distillation / in this manner: place this "Individual of Tartar" <term>Indiuiduum Tartari</term> after it has been calcined and become white / into a urinal-flask / that is / into the cucurbit / and pour the water of life <term>aqua vita</term> over it / so that it rises seven fingers' breadth above it / and seal it / with its lid / and place it in the ashes so that it boils / for about two hours / thereafter pour that which remains behind / back out into another vessel. Praise GOD at all times and help the oppressed.

Now, dear son, it remains and is necessary that we describe the wondrous **Projection** <term>Projection: The final step of the Great Work where the alchemist "projects" or throws a small amount of the finished "Medicine" onto a larger mass of molten base metal to transmute it into gold.</term> <note>original: "auffwerffung"</note> of this Medicine. Its virtue, power, and effect are so great that it is a marvel to behold. Should you ever see it, I do not want you to believe it occurs through sorcery or incantations, for it is the very power of **Nature**. One can see an example of this in bread: for a single pound of sourdough or **leaven** <note>original: "Saurteigs oder Höffels"</note> can ferment and increase 100 times 1,000 pounds of bread dough.

This can happen much more powerfully through our Medicine. When we tested its strength, it seemed almost impossible to us that it could be converted further into a metal, because in every projection it created a metal or a powder out of every body <note>In alchemy, "body" refers to any base metal like lead, tin, or copper.</note>, and it always seemed to us that there was no loss or diminution of its power. Furthermore, one of our associates grumbled and said that we had attributed too subtle or violent an effect to this Medicine.

Finally, with God's help, we threw the aforementioned Medicine over such a large mass of material, or upon such a multitude of bodies, that the fire was ultimately hardly large enough; yet the **body** <note>the base metal</note> upon which the projection was made finally turned into **gold** that was better and purer than any found in a mine. # Of the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

[...most] carefully considered / therefore I have wished to withhold or hide nothing / of what good and true things I have ever been able to find and bring about through true thoughts from the best and most proven *authors* after much suffered and vain labor in *sophistic recipes* <note>original: "Sophisticis Receptis"; refers to fraudulent or deceptive alchemical formulas that look plausible but fail in practice</note> / such as *Geber* in *his Summa* <note>original: "Geber in sua Summa"; refers to the "Summa Perfectionis Magisterii," a foundational 13th-century alchemical text attributed to Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan)</note> / and others. In this first part, I indicate many means and ways / through which I came to a true knowledge of this Art.

In the second part / I will explain from which books I have learned / with their *technical terms* <note>original: "Terminis"</note> / and other circumstances.

That I call it such a divine and glorious thing / happens solely because / no one can come to such an Art or understand it through their own knowledge or intellect / however learned and experienced a **philosopher** <note>In alchemical texts, "Philosopher" specifically refers to a master of the Hermetic Art (alchemy)</note> he may be. # Of the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

# The first part, in which is treated by what means and way he came to the true knowledge of this Art.

**Hermes Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus: the "Thrice-Great," a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy</note> is rightly called the first prophet and father, indeed the first founder of this Stone; after he truly knew and experienced this Art, he left it behind in writing. He held it so high and dear that only the fear of the Last Day compelled him to describe it. This was the opinion held by all those who followed him in this regard. Hence it happens that their books, as many as there are, appear so contradictory to the readers. As King **Geber** <note>Geber: the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "father of chemistry"</note> speaks in his **Summa** <note>Summa: referring to the *Summa perfectionis magisterii*, a highly influential alchemical text</note>, [they were written] for the edification of the ignorant and the Children of Wisdom, who nonetheless initially cannot refrain from erring, so that after diligent effort and much applied labor of both mind and body, they might know all the better how to value and conceal it.

It is also mostly hidden for this reason (not to mention the labor involved here) unless great expense were involved, among those alone who hope for such things from books or through Divine inspiration. When I was about twenty years old and had been instructed at home in the basics of grammar through my father's providence, and had now been promoted to the higher arts—in which I progressed so much over about three years through the diligence of my special **tutor** <note>original: "Præceptoris"</note>—that my guardian (since both my parents had now passed away) thought it good to send me to study **jurisprudence** <note>original: "Iurisprudentiam"; the study of law</note> with the aforementioned tutor. But during these things, and before I departed from the College of Arts, I had made friends and associations with many of my schoolmates, some of whom had various **chemical books** <note>original: "Chimische Bücher"</note>, which I received from them and transcribed with the greatest diligence. Yet this was done through the means of my aforementioned tutor, who had already begun to experiment and work in this art long before, so that before I moved away, I had acquired a considerable number of these books and **recipes** <note>original: "Recepta"</note>.

As soon as I had come with my tutor to where I was to apply myself to jurisprudence, I began to read through the aforementioned recipes. Among them were several **projections** <note>term: projections; the act of casting an alchemical substance onto a base metal to transform it into gold or silver</note> that taught [transforming] one part onto ten parts, another onto 20, 30, etc. For the "red" <note>the *Rubedo*, or final stage of the alchemical work to produce gold</note>, [they taught] onto eighteen or twenty parts into the best Crown or Ducat gold, indeed as high as it is and can be possible. One was supposed to be able to be made fluid, another to withstand the test of the [touch]stone, another all tests. For the "white" <note>the *Albedo*, or the stage of the work that produces silver</note>, one should yield ten **denarii** <note>original: "Denarios"; a unit of silver weight or currency</note>, another 11; one should be stable in the fire, another withstand the mark of the stone. But before the first year was even out, I had already spent everything I was meant to use for two years and sent it away in smoke.

During this time my *tutor* was severely ill with a hot fever, which in my opinion he caught from the coal fire that we kept burning intensely, just like those in the *Arsenal* at *Venice* get from casting cannons. But when he took a cold drink in such heat, he thereafter passed away; I felt heartfelt sorrow over this, partly because my parents would no longer send me any money—only as much as I needed for my own person. However, so that I might now bring my intended work to an end, I was forced to move home so that I could settle with my guardians and be of my own mind, and also apply my paternal inheritance just as it well pleased me. After I had gathered it all in *Amsterdam* <note>original: "Arendam"</note>, it was worth about 400 crowns. Afterward, I tried a recipe that had been granted to me by an Italian; I kept this man with me until I saw the outcome of this work, for he swore highly that he had experienced it in practice. For this, we bought 2 ounces of gold and 1 ounce of silver; these we first dissolved in a water, then we calcined it for three months before we prepared this powder to perform the projection <note>original: "tingieren," meaning to "tinge" or tint, a common term for the final step of transmutation</note>, which we did according to the contents of the recipe. But it was in vain, and thus our increase became a decrease, and out of 8 ounces only three ounces remained for us—I will say nothing here of other expenses—so that my 400 crowns became 230 crowns. But when the joyful summer arrived—though accompanied by a plague <note>original: "Peſtilenz"; the narrator is likely referring to one of the periodic outbreaks of bubonic plague in 16th-century France</note>—I was forced to depart with my other companions for half a year. During that time, I came across an old man who was commonly called "the Philosopher." I joined him and shared my recipes with him, asking him to point out the most prominent ones among them. He showed me ten or twelve that seemed the best to him. After the plague came to an end, I returned to my old place and immediately began to test those same recipes. I worked through the entire winter until **St. John’s Day** <note>June 24th, a common quarterly marker in the legal and liturgical calendar</note>, but I gained just as much from them as I had from the previous ones. My 400 crowns had diminished until I had only 70 left; however, I was not yet despondent. At that time, there was an Abbot who had a recipe that had been written to him from **Rome**, from the court of **Cardinal Armagnac** <note>Georges d'Armagnac (1501–1585), a powerful French cardinal and diplomat known for his interest in the arts and sciences</note>. I joined him, and we each put in 100 crowns, intending to work from a common fund.

After we had built new furnaces of a strange shape, we also had to have an *aqua vitae* <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; literally "water of life," a highly rectified alcohol used as a solvent</note> with which to dissolve an ounce or an ounce and a half of gold. We therefore bought a barrel of good strong wine, from which we produced a great quantity of that same rectified water using a **Pelican** <note>an alchemical vessel used for circulatory distillation, named for its shape which resembles a pelican pecking its own breast</note>; we put it into many glass vessels that we bought for that purpose. After that, we took better gold and calcined it <note>reduced it to powder through heat</note> beforehand for one month. We took one ounce of gold and four ounces of the water and put them into two thick, strong, glazed **retorts** <note>glass bulbs with long, downward-pointing necks used for distillation</note> where one fitted into the other, well-sealed. We placed them in two large round furnaces, for which we bought thirty guilders' worth of coal at once to maintain the fire. This lasted for a whole year, although we also tested other recipes on the side, from which we drew no more profit than from the "Great Work" itself. Namely, we had nothing from either except that we had to keep our fire burning for an eternal time until we might see—as this recipe claimed—the **Coagulation** <note>the process of a liquid becoming solid</note> without a preceding **Solution** <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</note>.

However, we were not working with the right material, nor was this the true water that was supposed to dissolve our gold. Thus, we found the gold or powder still whole, only a little more subtle. We threw this onto living **mercury** <note>original symbol: ☿</note> according to the instructions of the recipe, but in vain. This vexed us greatly, especially the Abbot, who had boasted loudly before his monks. He was waiting only for the end, at which point he intended to turn the "Lead Well" <note>likely a reference to a specific fountain or a metaphorical source of base metal</note> into gold; but for now, he had to save that for another time. He did this to provide support to the German artist who was traveling past at the time I was in **Paris**. But the Abbot took heart again and advised me that I, for my part, should scrape together three or four hundred crowns...

# Of the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...whatever I put in, the Abbot also wanted to contribute an equal amount. I was then to travel with him to **Paris**, where there is a great number of <term>laborants</term> <note>original: "Laboranten"; people who work in a laboratory, specifically alchemical practitioners</note>. I was to stay among them for as long as it took until I finally obtained a perfect and true result, which we would then divide as brothers.

Once the pact was made, I again drew funds from my paternal inheritance. When I arrived in **Paris**, I brought 800 crowns with me, intending not to leave until the money was spent or I had found something. I departed from my relatives with no small amount of resentment on their part; they had wanted to make a councilman out of me, believing I was an excellent legal scholar. But I resisted their plans and acted as if I intended to buy a government office with this money. After taking my leave, I set out and reached **Paris** on the third day after **Epiphany** <note>original: "Heiligen drey König tag"; January 6th</note>. I stayed there for a whole month without anyone knowing me. Soon after, I began to visit the craftsmen, goldsmiths, furnace-makers, and others, making such friends that within a month, a hundred <term>artists</term> <note>original: "Artiſten"; in this period, the term referred to practitioners of the "Hermetic Art" or alchemy</note> knew me. 

Some worked on <term>tinctures</term> <note>original: "Tincturen"; substances capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</note> of metals through <term>projections</term> <note>original: "Proiectiones"; the act of casting an alchemical powder onto molten metal to trigger transformation</note>, some through <term>cementations</term> <note>original: "Cementationes"; a process of heating metals with powdered chemicals to purify them</note>, others through dissolution, and the majority through the union of the essence of the stone <term>Simrilli</term> <note>a cryptic name for a specific alchemical substance or "stone"</note>. Some engaged in long-lasting boilings, some in the extraction of <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurij"</note> from metals, and some in the stabilization <note>original: "beſtendigmachung"; also known as "fixation," turning a volatile substance like mercury into a solid that can withstand fire</note> of the same. We were constantly together, now in houses, then in the Cathedral <note>likely referring to Notre Dame de Paris, a common meeting place for alchemists due to its symbolic carvings</note>, for we paid no heed to Sundays or workdays. 

Some said: "Oh, would to **GOD** that we could start our work again, then we would do it right!" Others said: "If only our vessel had remained whole, it would have turned out well." Another said: "If we had had a copper vessel that was perfectly round, we could have stabilized <term>mercury</term> with <term>silver</term> <note>original: "Mercurium mit Luna"; Luna is the alchemical name for silver, associated with the Moon</note>." There was not one of them who did not have an excuse. I turned a deaf ear to them for a long time, for I regretted my expenses, into which I had so carelessly allowed myself to be talked. 

Then there was a powerful and learned **Greek** who came to someone well known to me and promised him great things from the stabilization of <term>mercury from cinnabar</term> <note>original: "Mercurij Cinabris"; cinnabar is the bright red ore from which mercury is extracted</note>. This gave me cause—together with my good friends and for my own part—to prepare the money to accomplish this. For this purpose, we had to have three ounces of fine, thinly beaten silver, from which he formed nails with specially made pliers. These he mixed in and cooked in a furnace for a time. Finally, having dried them well, there were no more than three ounces of silver left—and a little more, which he said was his own. The silver we had previously added had vanished into smoke. But **GOD** knows what benefit we had from this work, since I personally contributed 30 crowns and more to it.

# Of the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

This rumor of the nails spread through the entire city of **Paris**, so that almost everyone was talking about it, especially those who busied themselves with <term>sophistry</term> <note>original: "Sophiſterey"; in alchemy, this referred to the use of deceptive methods to produce alloys that looked like gold or silver but were not genuine</note>. Just as before, there had been a rumor about copper stoves used for <term>fixing mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium... figieren"; the process of turning liquid mercury into a solid, stable metal</note> into silver. Eventually, a nobleman came to us who was well-learned in all manner of sophistry—indeed, so highly skilled that he could actually earn something from it. He offered his products to the goldsmiths for sale. I struck up a friendship with him, though not without great expense, so that he would not think me poor. I associated with him for an entire year before he explained even the smallest thing to me. At last, he shared his secret with me; however, though he held it in high regard, it was actually worth nothing. Nevertheless, I wrote everything that had happened to my Abbot and sent him the second part of the Work, along with the <term>practical instructions</term> <note>original: "Practica"</note> of the aforementioned nobleman. Upon this, the Abbot wrote back to me that I should remain in **Paris** and spare no expense, especially since I had obtained such a magnificent <term>secret</term> <note>original: "arcanum"; a hidden alchemical recipe or elixir</note>. However, I had resolved in my own mind not to use any material that did not remain stable in the state in which it first appeared. I determined to work on nothing that served roguery or intended to make one rich through the harm of other people. Thus, according to his letter, I stayed there for another year—making three years in total—and went now to this person, then to that one, and especially to those who were rumored to possess something. By now, I had spent almost all my money. Then my Abbot wrote to me that as soon as I had looked over and read his letter, I should come to him. This I did, for I did not want to break the brotherhood we had formed. When I arrived, he gave me a letter that had been sent to him by the **King of Navarre**, requesting that if he wished to do the King a service, he should send me to him to teach him the art of the aforementioned nobleman. He also promised a gift of 3,000 or 4,000 crowns. This made the Abbot so fervent that he could never be happy unless he had that money in his pocket. He had no peace until I set off to the King. When I arrived there, I could not begin work for six weeks because the <term>materials</term> <note>original: "materialia"</note> had to be sought elsewhere. When the work finally came to an end, I received no reward for it. For although the King had intended not to leave my labor unrewarded (to say nothing of the inclined and good will shown to me by the inhabitants), his own people—especially the most prominent of the nobility—persuaded him otherwise. They mostly brought it to the point that he let me depart empty-handed, though he did promise me, along with his thanks, that if there were anything in his land over which he had power, he would give it to me if I desired it. I thus became quite dejected and would no longer trust the promise of the false King; I returned to my Abbot in a state of great dissatisfaction. # On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...came to me and recounted [what had happened]; after that, we traveled to **Lausanne** located in **Savoy**, so that from there we might move to a well-known town in Germany, yet with only a few companions so that no one would recognize us—specifically those who had read my little book during my lifetime, which I wrote for the purpose of leading those wandering in **sophistry** <term>In alchemy, "sophistry" refers to false, deceptive, or purely chemical practices that mimic true transmutation but fail to produce the Philosopher's Stone.</term> back onto the right path.

To conclude this first part of mine, I wish to remind everyone of what the **poet** <note>likely referring to a classical author or the common Latin proverb "Felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum."</note> sang: *blessed is he who becomes wise through another’s misfortune.* <note>original: "ſeelig iſt der/ der an eines anderen ſchaden witzig wirdt"</note> Let every man take me as an example, learn from my errors, and guard himself against unnecessary expense and avoid the detours that occur in sophistry. Instead, read good authors patiently—those who were, as if with their own hands, engaged in the **Work** <term>The "Magnum Opus" or Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term>—and then labor accordingly. Always pray to God for wisdom and understanding, for no one comes to this art by chance, but rather through God’s calling more than through study alone. To whomsoever it is granted, it is given; it is hidden from the godless, but revealed to the pious. Let everyone understand this: let it be used only for God’s honor and praise. Amen.

Socrates, Zeno, Hali, Senior, Rasis, Geber, Morienes, Arnoldus de Villa Nova, Raymond Lully, and many others, to list all of whom would be tedious; from these we have compiled this little book of ours with no small labor, as their own books testify. For they have written in such a manner and in this way (indeed, had they not had the fear of God before their eyes) that it is impossible to arrive at the secret through reading the books alone. As Geber says in his *Summa* <note>original: "sua Summa"; likely referring to the *Summa perfectionis magisterii*, a foundational alchemical text attributed to the 8th-century chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note>: "Thou son of wisdom, thou shalt not despair herein, for through manifold contemplation thou shalt finally reach that which thy heart desires." For the Philosophers wrote in such a way that they alone might understand; the true practitioner simultaneously mixed in the method of research and divided the principal works into many different chapters. They did this so that not everyone would understand this divine science in a single day—nay, in a single hour. Therefore, because it is noble, it is hidden.

Alphidius speaks: "It is to be believed that our ancestors, the Philosophers, communicated their principal meaning and hidden speeches in many figures and riddles <note>original: "Rähtrischen," referring to rhetorical tropes or enigmatic language.</note>, so that the whole world would not perish through knowledge of it; for no one would want to work if they found themselves overwhelmed with such wealth." Hermes also excuses himself for this when he says at the beginning of his book: "You should not think that the wise did this out of envy toward the pious and good-hearted, but only for the sake of the ungodly." For Rosinus <note>A Latinized name for the Arabic alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> says: "In this case, the fool would be equal to the wise, and the ungodly would also make use of it." Geber makes the same excuse in his *Summa* in the chapter on the "Administration of the Solar Medicine" <note>original: "de Administratione Medicine solaris," referring to the preparation of the alchemical Elixir or "Gold-medicine."</note>, speaking thus: "It should not surprise the children of wisdom; to the ungodly it has become a darkening, but for the pious, a path is prepared to reach it."

# On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...exactly to the end as Gold is brought; for it lacks nothing but stability, which is also brought to it over time. And they are now spoiled on account of immaturity <note>The author uses the concept that metals "grow" in the earth; base metals are simply "unripe" or "immature" gold.</note>; therefore, what follows we shall hear in the fourth part of our division. Thus, what Nature does in the earth, we fulfill upon the earth through our Art and **Projection** <term>projection: the final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" or powder is cast upon base metal to transmute it</term>, as you will read further concerning this in the last part but one of our division <note>original: "Discision," a Latinate term for a section or cutting</note>. Furthermore, we see also that the elements, which are contrary to each other in their properties (as the Philosopher <note>Commonly refers to Aristotle.</note> speaks in the second book of *On Generation* <note>original: "Geberung," referring to Aristotle's *De Generatione et Corruptione*</note>), transform into one another. How much more so the metals, which are of one nature and are the materials which are not contrary to you in quality, are easily transformed into that. For this reason, *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says their generation is circular; yet not exactly so, as he himself admits, for by Nature they are not ordered toward one end—that from the *perfect*, *imperfect* things are made—but rather the opposite. Therefore, their generation is not entirely circular, but only in part. Now, although these and similar reasons were enough in themselves to confirm this Art, yet because the sophists <note>Here used to mean critics or those who use false logic to deny alchemy.</note> constantly attempt to prove the contrary, we wish (though we cannot do everything, for this booklet would become too long) to show here the most prominent and sharpest arguments with which a good young person might perhaps be led astray, and bring them to the floor, in order to teach how to overturn others by them.

Our adversaries argue based on the opinion of *Avicenna*, *Albertus Magnus*, and also *Aristotle* in the 4th book of *Meteorology* in this way: the artists labor in vain and exert themselves for nothing to perfect the metals, unless it be that they bring them into the *first matter* <term>first matter: or *prima materia*, the primordial, formless substance from which all things originate</term>.

Since they do not do this, it follows that all **Alchemists'** work is sophistry, as *Albertus* himself speaks of it: All and every one who colors metals with various *simples* <term>simples: basic, uncompounded medicinal or chemical substances</term> and materials into many kinds of colors are deceivers, unless it be that they first reduce it again into the first matter. Many of the wisest have also attempted to overturn this argument, for it is nearly one of the most prominent. Some say that although in **Projection** the imperfect metal is not brought into the first matter, yet a uniform reaction <note>original: "Rection," referring to the alchemical process or governing of the substance</note> occurs in the preparation of the Stone into *Sulphur* and *Mercury* <note>original: "Sulphur und Mercurium," the two fundamental principles of all metals in alchemical theory</note>, which are the true *matter of metals*, as will be better mentioned below in the fourth part. It is therefore enough that the active agent is brought into the first matter, even if no restoration occurs in the passive part.

And this was the opinion of *Arnaldus de Villa Nova* in the great *Rosary* <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova's *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a seminal alchemical text.</note>, who was followed by *Raymond Lully* in his *Testament*, though with the favor of the excellent...

# On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...learned scribes and authors, this opinion now seems entirely contrary to the opinion of all the philosophers. For they unanimously desired that metals should be brought into the **first matter** <note>original: "erste Matery," or *prima materia*, the formless base substance from which all things were thought to be created</note>, which then happens through corruption <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the breaking down or "death" of a substance so it can be reborn in a higher form.</note>. According to *Aristotle*, they also hold this **reduction** <term>reduction: the process of returning a substance to its simplest or original state</term> to be only in the flow <note>likely referring to the molten state</note> and in the **projection** of this Divine Stone upon the metals. But this would be against all the philosophers and is something they do not grant and is impossible. For in this way, the metals are not robbed of their first form—at least according to the majority of those who do not have the various **solutions** <term>solutions: methods of dissolving solids into liquids</term> as one ought to see in their books. I, however, will also bring forth and explain my solution to this argument.

If we undertook to make new metals, such as **Mercury**, **Venus** <note>original: "Mercurium, Venerem"; Venus is the traditional alchemical name for copper.</note>, or something else from metals, they would necessarily have to be brought into their first matter, and this by the means mentioned above. But because our intention is solely to **perfect** the imperfect into Gold or Silver, without any change into new forms, we instead clean and wash it through our Divine Work of **projection**. Only a cleansing is necessary by means of our Stone, so that they may be abundantly perfected. There is a great difference between **ripening the unripe** <note>The author views base metals not as different species, but as "unripe" versions of gold.</note> and thereafter birthing something new out of a thing. Otherwise, one would have to conclude that all unripe things must be brought back to their first form if they were to be ripened at all, which is contrary to all philosophers.

But the other objections that are commonly brought up against this Art, I will let pass in this place, for anyone can easily learn from this how to parry the other arguments as well.

However, *Avicenna* <note>A famous Persian polymath (Ibn Sina) whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy and medicine.</note> also says that *Aristotle* in his youth argued thus against **Alchemy** <note>original: "Chimiam"</note>. I have recognized, he says, the intentions of those who deny our Art, as well as those who confess it to be true. The former, such as *Aristotle* and his like, use rather careless arguments. The others say this Art cannot be sufficiently proven with true reasons like other arts, because it uses a different path, opposed and contrary to all other arts; for it completes and conceals the properties of its **terms** <note>original: "Terminen," referring to the starting and ending points or boundaries of a chemical process</note>, whereas all other arts undertake to show such things clearly.

So that we may proceed in an orderly fashion, I will take in hand the third part of this our little book, and I will recount all the necessary operations for the completion of our Divine Work.

This is caused partly by means of the mineral heat, and partly through the warmth of the Sun, which by itself does not cause full ripening—as Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist who spent decades seeking the Stone.</note> explains and as daily experience also indicates and teaches us. For we see clearly in the mines the differences between metals: some are coarser, others more subtle and pure.

> The falcon on the peak of the mountain cries out: I am black, white, yellow, citron-red. <note>These colors represent the essential stages of the alchemical transformation: nigredo (blackness), albedo (whiteness), citrinitas (yellowness), and rubedo (redness).</note>

The reason our science is nothing without this union is this: at the time of the "birth" of our Divine Work, the volatile part carries the fixed part away with it. It can be made to remain in the fire and become stable through no other way than through this wondrous and more-than-supernatural <term>Conjunction</term> <note>The sacred marriage or union of opposites in alchemy</note>. According to the inquiries of all philosophers, they say primarily that the stable must become volatile, and the volatile must become stable. This <term>Conjunction</term> must happen precisely at the hour of its birth, as Hali <note>likely Haly Abenragel, an Arab astrologer</note> says in the *Book of Secrets*: "He who does not find our Stone at the time of its birth need not wait for another in its place." For whoever begins our Divine Work without knowledge of the specific hour of its birth will receive nothing from it but useless and vain labor—indeed, the punishment for his error. Rhazes, in the *Book of Commandments*, specifically calls this <term>Conjunction</term> the "Weight of the Sages," and their Rule <note>original: "Regiment"</note> advises everyone to abstain from this Divine Work if they do not know the "Weights" most precisely; the philosophers have hidden this above all things, as can be seen well enough from their many writings.

Therefore, where there is one who confesses that this union occurs on the 7th day, you will soon find another who says it is completed in 40 days; another says in 9 months or in 7 (such as Rhazes); and another at the end of the year, such as Rosinus <note>a common Latin corruption of the name Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note>.

I wish to show by this that nothing is easier than our Work after the union has taken place, because nothing more is needed then than the steady cooking of the two united materials. In this cooking, the much-desired rest will be granted, as the philosopher says in the *Book of Ethics* <note>referring to Aristotle's "Nicomachean Ethics"</note>, that rest is much more pleasant than labor. Thus also speaks *Barseus* in the very same book: "All your cooking, *tinting* <term>tincturing</term>, and *calcination* must be fulfilled in this Divine Work through cooking alone."

However, so that the fraudulent artists <note>a common term for "false" alchemists or charlatans</note> do not also claim their work is nothing else but cooking, we wish to present here, alongside these, many other opinions of the philosophers, from which their error may be recognized. *Alphidius* says: "In the generation of our Stone, we have no more than one single material (which they properly call a water), and also one cooking, as it occurs in one fire without removal from the same." This is also testified by King *Solomon*: "In the preparation of our Divine Stone (which he calls our *sulfur*), we need no more than one means." *Lilius* also says: "Our Divine Work occurs in one vessel, and through one means and cooking." *Muhammad* <note>Machomet</note> says: "We have no more than one means with one cooking alone, one vessel, in which we complete our Divine Work, both for whitening and reddening."

### On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

All philosophers hold the opinion that everything that congeals or hardens due to cold mostly contains moisture in its <term>first matter</term> <note>The "materia prima" or fundamental substance from which all things are thought to originate.</note>, as **Aristotle** says in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*. Since liquid metals are hardened by cold, their first matter must necessarily be rich in moisture. But **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher famous for his work on natural science and alchemy.</note>, who described minerals more magnificently than anyone else, says that this moisture of metals is not like other watery moistures, because the latter are turned into smoke <note>evaporated</note>, whereas softened metals do not evaporate away. From this, we must conclude that their moisture is mixed with a substance through which it is preserved in the fire. Now, there is nothing that resists fire except <term>viscous humidity</term> <note>original: "viscosa humiditas"; a sticky, oily moisture that was thought to give metals their flexibility and resistance to heat.</note>, which is mixed with earthly subtlety, as **Bonus of Ferrara** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemical writer.</note> says and daily experience teaches. Therefore, it is well believed that the moisture of metals is as described; but experience also teaches us that some parts of the metals vanish into smoke, yet they are not entirely consumed in the fire. Thus, we must admit with all writers of this Art that two kinds of moisture are required for the birth of metals: an external one and an internal one.

The first is a coarse moisture, not sufficiently mixed with its earthiness; therefore, it is easily consumed like smoke by the fire. The latter, however, is entirely subtle and mixed with its earth in the best possible way, so that the two become a single, closely united matter. This moisture cannot be divided or consumed by the fire; rather, both remain together in the fire or leave it at the same time. From this moisture **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, Mercury often refers to the philosophical principle of fluidity and volatility, not just the liquid metal.</note> is born, as we see and learn from daily experience. **Arnold of Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> testifies to this, saying: "This makes us certain that both materials, as said before, are perfectly united in it; for either the earthiness keeps the moisture with it, or the moisture carries the earthiness away." This was also well recognized by **Albertus**, who investigated the cause of metals most precisely: namely, that Mercury is always mobile and fluid because one part dominates the other. In the other, the moisture (which is the cause of flowing) persists, but the dry earthiness prevents it from sticking to the first. **Albertus’s** opinion is further strengthened by the *Book of Simple Minerals*, where it is written: "The first matter of metals is a viscous humidity <note>original: "viscosa humiditas"</note>, unburnable, and very strongly united in the ores of the earth." This agrees beautifully with **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early alchemy.</note>, who says in his *Summa* <note>Referring to the "Summa Perfectionis Magisterii," a core text of medieval alchemy.</note> that the right, true matter of metals is a living mercury; for immeasurable nature creates Mercury out of the aforementioned mixed matter. **Bonus of Ferrara** says: "Mercury is the closest matter to the metals, but primarily the viscous humidity with its subtle..."

# On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...earths mixed together. **Geber** <note>original: "Geber"; refers to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century polymath and legendary father of Islamic alchemy whose works were fundamental to European science.</note> says in the description of Mercury, which he places in his *Sum of Perfection* <note>original: "Summa"; specifically Geber’s *Summa perfectionis magisterii*, one of the most influential alchemical textbooks.</note>, that the moisture of Mercury is ordered through the help of its subtle earths in its inward composition.

Therefore, it is necessary for us to diligently consider the work of Nature in the birthing of all things, through which the properties of matter are mixed—which the philosophers have called the **acting principle** <note>original: "das wirckend"; the active force or agent that triggers change in a substance.</note>, because matter cannot make or bring itself forth on its own—that is, it cannot demonstrate its own action. As **Aristotle** speaks, it does not prove its own effect. Therefore, when Nature created Mercury as the "Matter of Salt" <note>This likely refers to the "body" or salt-like stability required for the birth of metals.</note> for the birth of metals, she very wisely added to it its own acting principle: namely, a **fatty mineral earth** of its own kind, entering into the minerals through long-lasting decoction <note>A process of heating or "cooking" within the earth over long periods.</note>, which we commonly call a **Sulfur**. This Sulfur is to be regarded in relation to Mercury <note>original: "☿"</note> as the curdling agent <note>original: "die gegen der Milch"; literally "that which is against milk," referring to rennet used in cheesemaking.</note> is to milk, and as the man is to the woman, and as the active principle is to matter. The philosophers have named two kinds of **Sulfur**: one that is quite easily fluid, and the other quite hard and non-fluid.

In order for Nature to demonstrate such acting power, it might be shown that the salt of the Sulfur within the matter to which it is added causes them, in the composition of some metals, to be hardened in a wondrous way, or on the other hand, to become entirely fluid. But other minerals of inferior composition do not become fluid by the **action of sulfur** <note>original: "actione ſulphuris"</note>, such as the **Marcasites** <note>A common mineral, iron pyrite, often mistaken for gold or silver ore.</note> or **Magnesia**, so that they are not volatile, and others of the same kind. Since the active principle cannot be a **part of the composite** <note>original: "theil des Compoſiti"</note>, as **Aristotle** says, after Nature has mixed the aforementioned Sulfur with Mercury in the mines in a wondrous way, she makes from it the precious metal, namely **Gold**, solely through **perfect decoction**—that is, to separate the Sulfur from it. This is its action, and this is the reason why it is more perfect than all other metals. Since we further see in Nature that it cannot be transformed into anything better, for that reason it also unites and mixes easily with Mercury, because it is nothing other than Mercury cooked with its own Sulfur and finally entirely separated from this decoction. This separation of the Sulfur is the perfection of Gold, whereas in other metals it remains; this is the cause of their imperfection. Hence, **Silver** is more imperfect than Gold, and **Copper** more imperfect than Silver, solely due to a lack of complete maturation, through which alone the active principle—namely, the Sulfur—is separated from it. In this lies the foremost secret of our entire Art.

Since, then, Art must follow Nature, it is necessary that it completes our **Divine Work**, so that the acting principle may be separated from it, which...

This is nothing other than to purify the metals and separate them from all [excess] Sulfur. I have also heard from his miners that such things often occur. Therefore, it follows from this how Nature operates in the stability of metals.

...mixed with earth. *Geber* <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of alchemy.</note> says in the description of *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurii"</note> which he sets down in his *Summa* <note>The *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii*, a highly influential medieval alchemical handbook.</note> that the moisture of *Mercury* is ordered by the help of its subtle earth within its internal composition.

As *Aristotle* says, it does not demonstrate its effect. The Philosophers have called it two kinds of **Sulfur**: one entirely volatile and fluid, the other very hard and unyielding. But so that Nature may show such active power, it might demonstrate the Salt of the **Sulfur** in the matter to which it is added; it causes, in a wondrous way, the composition of some metals so that they become hardened, and others so that they become entirely fluid. But other minerals of poor composition are not made fluid by the **action of sulfur** <note>original: "actione sulphuris"</note>, such as **Marcasites** <note>A term formerly used for various iron sulfide minerals often mistaken for gold or silver ores.</note> and **Magnesia**, so that they are not volatile and other such things. Now, since the acting principle cannot be a part of the **Composite** <note>original: "Compositi"</note>, as *Aristotle* says, after Nature has wondrously mixed the mentioned **Sulfur** with the **Mercury** in the mines, she makes from it the precious metal, namely **Gold**, solely through perfect **decoction** <term>decoction|The process of ripening or "cooking" minerals within the earth's heat over long periods of time.</term>—that is, to separate the **Sulfur** from it; that is its effect, and this is the reason why it is more perfect than all other metals. Since we further see this in Nature, it cannot be transformed into something better; for this reason, it also unites and aligns with **Mercury**, since it is nothing other than **Mercury** cooked with its own **Sulfur**, and finally entirely separated from this cooking. And the separation of the **Sulfur** is the perfection of Gold; however, when it remains in other metals, this is the cause of their imperfection. Hence Silver is also more imperfect than Gold, and Copper more imperfect than Silver, solely due to the lack of full ripening, through which alone the acting principle—namely, the **Sulfur**—is separated from it. In this consists the primary secret of our entire Art.

...all Philosophers have hidden, and in this case, have pointed toward Nature, whose properties they have also sufficiently indicated.

We have also sufficiently mentioned the first path which Nature is accustomed to using in the beginning—namely, in the birth of metals, and especially Gold.

This is nothing other than to purify the metal and separate it from all Sulfur. For what the Art achieves in the first path through **perfect cooking**, Nature accomplishes through long-lasting and steady **cooking** <term>cooking|Also called 'coction,' this refers to the natural heat of the earth that slowly matures base metals into gold over decades or centuries.</term>—namely, by purifying the imperfect metals for so long until they finally become the best gold.

The great *Albertus* <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar whose writings on minerals were foundational to later alchemists.</note> also says that this once happened in the Kingdom of **Liburnia or Slavonia** <note>original: *Liburniæ vel Sclauoniæ*; historical regions in the modern-day Balkans known for their mineral wealth.</note>. I have heard the same from his miners, that such things often occur. Therefore, it follows here how Nature behaves in the stability of metals. In this way, the Art must follow Nature—namely, to perfect the imperfect through the separation of Sulfur. Specifically, when the mentioned Stone is cast upon them while they are fluid, they are quickly purified into the best gold by means of the **excessive cooking** <note>The Philosopher's Stone was believed to possess a concentrated, "over-cooked" heat that could perform in an instant what Nature takes forty years to achieve.</note> which they receive through the addition of our Art. It is no different than the many paths Nature uses in the purification of metals; there are also many paths in that place (I mean in their Perfection). They named it "enlivened Mercury" to distinguish between common mercury and this special Mercury, because common mercury remains as it is since Nature has not mixed its own active agent into it. Therefore, most people falsely believe that common mercury and common sulfur are the true matter of metals; however, it never happens that both are mixed together at the same time in the mines. For this reason, they cannot be the true matter of metals in the mines of the Earth or in our Art on Earth, as **Geber** says in his *Summa* when speaking of the beginning of the Art. And in another place, he says: "Our Mercury is nothing other than a viscous water, perfected with its metallic Sulfur." This is the true matter that Nature prepares for our Art and has established in a certain and true form known to the Philosophers, without any change in itself. Likewise, **Avicenna** <note>The Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina.</note> also says: "Nature has prepared for us one single matter, which our Art cannot create for itself in the slightest degree." ### On the Natural Philosophy of Metals.

...that which was cold, subtle, and windy, they called **Air**. These two are enclosed and hidden within the other two, as **Rhazes** <note>Abū Bakr al-Rāzī (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and one of the most influential figures in early alchemy.</note> says in the *Book of Precepts* <note>original: *Praeceptorum*</note>: every **composite** <term>Composite|A substance formed by the combination of different elements or principles, often referring to the "Philosophical Stone" in its developing stages.</term> consists of the four elements—two hidden and two manifest. Specifically, **Air** is hidden in **Water**, and **Fire** is hidden internally within the **Earth**, as we have stated before. For this reason, they called two of these "weak" and the others "strong." Because of this, they say that **composites** are **perfect** when **Water** and **Earth** are mixed by the equal aid of Nature with the moist and the dry—which are **Air** and **Fire**—which come through the transformation of one into the other. Therefore, **Alexander** <note>Likely referring to the pseudo-epigraphical works attributed to Alexander the Great, such as the *Secretum Secretorum*.</note> says in the *Book of Secrets*: "If you transform one element into the other, you shall have what you desire." This opinion perfectly demonstrates to us the true matter and the complete science of our Art. So that you may understand it even better, I will speak specifically of the four elements and their nature, as this is necessary for the **composition** of our **Divine Work** <note>The *Opus Magnum* or Great Work: the process of transmuting base metals into gold or creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> says: "In our created Earth are all the elements you could wish for." Conversely, **Alphidius** <note>An Arabic alchemist known to the West through medieval Latin translations.</note> says that the primary element is **Water**, from which all other elements belonging to the composition of our **Divine Work** are created. Within these, no adversity or contradiction arises, for from the beginning of the creation of our Divine Work, nothing appears but **Water** alone, which the **Philosophers** call a ***Mercurial Water***. From this, the **Earth** was created when it was hardened through union and supernatural **cooking** <note>In alchemy, "cooking" or decoction refers to the application of steady, external heat to mature the substance.</note>; without this union, we have no use for it. Therefore, **Hermes** was not wrong when he said that the other elements were born from the **Earth**, since it alone is proven in the second cooking. From the beginning of the Work, **Alphidius** wrote to **Valerandus** and others that it [Earth] is the most noble element in the assembly of our **Divine Work**.

These are the two elements of which the **Philosophers** write that one must recognize them before starting this Work, as **Rhazes** says in the *Book of Lights* <note>original: *Luminum*</note>: "Before one begins this Work, one must recognize the nature and property of the two elements, namely **Water** and **Earth**." Since the four elements are contained within these two, otherwise the **volatile** <note>Substances that easily evaporate or escape the vessel when heated.</note> part would carry away the stable part, and our Work would come to nothing. For this reason, we are commanded to transform the four elements so that our **Divine Work**, properly qualified, becomes stable in the end and can withstand the **cruelty of Sulfur**, the **destruction of Sulfur**, rust, and the rotting of the **Earth** and **Sulfur**—not unlike mineral gold, of which...

I have also sufficiently indicated above why it can perfect the imperfect ones.

But because it is entirely powerful and perfect, it can separate the aforementioned **Sulphur** from the metals and turn the remaining **Mercury** into **Gold**. As we then see, when one performs a **Projection** <note>The final stage of the Great Work: casting the finished Elixir or Stone upon base metal to transform it.</note> upon common **Mercury**, we find that it is entirely turned to gold. But the opposite is seen when it is cast upon [base] metals: out of one pound, barely 6 ounces remain. Yet the more they are cooked, the less they are purified in that manner.

Now I will bring the second part to an end and turn toward the third part, in which I will explain the true **Practice** <note>original: *Practicam*.</note> amidst many riddles, which God reveals to all His believers and lovers who diligently read through these my writings. May He give them true understanding through His **Holy Spirit** and to the honor and praise of His name, who is blessed in eternity.

# The Third Part of the Booklet by Denis Zachaire the Frenchman,
## Concerning the Practice of the Divine Work.

<note>Denis Zachaire (1510–1556) was a French alchemist whose "Opuscule" (The Little Work) became a classic. The name "Galli" is Latin for "the Frenchman."</note>

The entire world has been written of by the **Philosophers** and through the **Cosmographers**, divided into three primary parts: namely, into **Asia, Africa, and Europe**, under the four directions: Rising, Setting, Midday, and Midnight <note>East, West, South, and North.</note>. Therein rule many Emperors, Kings, Princes, Regents, and Lords, each of whom possesses many and varied things for his pleasure—both for their rarity and for the powers within these things. However, the latter <note>The inner powers</note> are not as readily accepted as the former <note>External luxury</note>, which I have learned through experience. I have traveled through many and various lands, and precisely where there are the most learned people, it is there (though to my own detriment) that the learned are quite poor and despised; indeed, they are held in no honor. Conversely, the unwise and the rich are held in great value. Where there is a lack of experienced and learned men, in those same places the wise are held in high esteem, and especially by those of the highest rank. 

It is exactly the same with **Metallic Ores** (from which **Gold** and other **Metals** come). In those places where they are not found, they are held in high and dear regard. Likewise, they are despised by the rich who have much of them. But for the despised and lowly, who have no perfection, their eyes are blinded so that they do not recognize the precious and the perfect. 

For this reason, the **Wise** are angered; when they see that fools are preferred over them, they depart elsewhere to demonstrate the power of their wisdom in other places. This was done in ancient times by a **Prince** who set himself to have no rest until he had made the other part of the world—beyond that which he already possessed—subject to him. He sought to do this through the help of his soldiers and especially his faithful **Steward** <note>In alchemical allegory, the Prince often represents the "King" or the primary substance, while the "Steward" represents the chemical agent or "mercury" that facilitates the work.</note>. As he then deliberated with him, he made many and various friendships with foreigners. However, because these foreigners were not very faithful to him, but instead thought they would be better received by other Emperors, they became estranged from him (as is the way of spies) and revealed all his intentions to them. These others, however, made little of it, for they knew that no earthly power could withstand their own—and how much less the undertaking of this Prince. 

Meanwhile, we see that at court and in the houses of Princes, nothing is practiced but gambling, dancing, singing, and the like; precious time is consumed with useless play. Indeed, the ears are offered up to flatterers, whisperers, and fools, but the **Wise** are despised and the **Philosophers** mocked—whom the great potentates and princes of old were once not ashamed of. But in the meantime, the aforementioned Prince, with the help of his soldiers, has captured a prominent city of the Empire; there the Emperor recruited many people, and...

Yet they all escaped unharmed from the hands of the enemies.

On the next day, as his enemies pursued them manfully, the aforementioned Prince was compelled by the advice of his people, together with all his folk, into an invincible fortress, surrounded with bulwarks and trenches. Inside, in the depths, the aforementioned Prince sat within a rock, well-guarded with walls. 

This castle was round and invincible; near it stood a very high tower, through which the Householder, by means of secret underground passages, could bring in everything necessary for food and war without the enemies knowing—just as happened in former times at Naples <note>original: "Neapolis." They could not wrestle with him, for the door of his dwelling was so tightly closed that no one could open it except his faithful Householder, who had provided everything so diligently that during a whole year—as long as the siege lasted—nothing was lacking. 

But the mentioned Prince was compelled by the manifold and cruel assault of the Imperial troops to divide his people into five groups <note>Likely representing the five stages or elements required for this phase of the alchemical "Work."</note>, so that each should keep watch in turn. ## Dispute and Conversation
### of Gold and Mercury against the Philosopher's Stone.

<margin><unclear>Point in the middle of the war</unclear></margin>
A true philosopher <term>philosopher: in this context, a practicing alchemist or "lover of wisdom"</term> writes / and swears by God and his soul / declares and says: You lovers of the Art <term>the Art: "The Great Art" of alchemy, or the Hermetic Art</term> / out of true favor and compassion for those who have sought for a long time / that our entire Work springs from only one thing / and is completed within itself / and requires nothing more than dissolution / and its own hardening <note>original: "wider hertung," referring to the alchemical principle of *solve et coagula*—the repeated process of dissolving a solid into liquid and solidifying it again to achieve purity.</note> / and this must happen of its own accord without any foreign things / just as ice in a dry vessel / placed over the fire / is turned to water by the warmth / so it is also with our Stone / and it requires no more help than the artist's manual labor / and the natural fire / for of its own power it could not accomplish this even if it lay in the earth for an eternity / therefore one must help it / but not in such a way / that one adds foreign and contrary things to it / but rather / just as God gives us the grain in the field / and we must thresh, grind, and bake it / so that it becomes bread / so it is here as well.

<margin>Ez</margin>
God has created this ore for us / so that we might take it and, by destroying the coarse body / take out the good that is within / cast away the superfluous / and make a medicine <term>medicine: the alchemical elixir or "Tincture," believed to heal "sick" (base) metals into gold and cure human ailments</term> out of the poison / and so that you may understand this all the better / I will write for you a fine conversation and disputation that occurred between the Philosopher's Stone, Gold, and Mercury / so that those who have sought for a long time / and who know how to work with metals and minerals / may easily arrive at the true foundation / and it will be necessary / that one learns to recognize every thing in the earth well, both inside and out / and what it is capable of in the foundation of nature.

Now, Gold and Mercury once came to our Stone / with armed hand / intending to overcome it / and Gold began in a defiant manner and spoke: O you poisonous worm and dragon <note>The "dragon" or "worm" is a common alchemical symbol for the raw, volatile, or "mercurial" matter that must be "slain" or fixed during the Work.</note> / why do you exalt yourself above me and my brother Mercury / seeing as I am the very best and most constant metal / and all princes and lords / as well as the common man, seek their wealth in me / and in my brother Mercury / whereas you, of all metals...

# A Conversation between Gold and Mercury
## (and the Philosopher's Stone)

[...that you are an] enemy, and you know that all physicians <term>physicians: originally "Medici," referring to doctors of medicine who used gold in tinctures</term> highly praise and laud me for the health of mankind.

->Answer of our Stone.<-

Dear Gold, why do you not rage against God, and ask Him why He did not create that which is in me within you as well?

->Gold.<-

God has given me honor, beauty, and glory, which is why the whole world desires me; because I am also the most stable metal both within and without the fire, I am loved by everyone. But you are volatile <term>volatile: "flüchtig," meaning a substance that evaporates or escapes when heated</term> and unfaithful, and you deceive people; for one sees that whoever works with you, you flee from their hands.

->The Stone.<-

Dear Gold, it is true: God has bestowed upon you honor, beauty, and stability, and for such things you should rightly be grateful to God, and not despise others alongside you. But that you thus diminish me, you do so with untruth. I say that you are not the Gold of which the philosophers <term>philosophers: here meaning alchemical masters like Hermes or Geber</term> write; rather, that very thing is hidden within me. For although it is true that I am volatile in the fire, you know well that I am ordained to this by God and Nature, and my moisture <term>moisture: the "mercurial" or liquid principle necessary for transformation</term> serves the worker's benefit. 

If he can rightly extract it, the permanent soul <note>original: "bestendige Seel," referring to the fixed, non-volatile essence that remains after the "moisture" is removed.</note> remains within me, which is far more stable than you and all your brothers and companions—which no fire nor water may consume nor destroy while the world stands. Thus, I am also not to blame if the seekers cannot work or prepare me correctly, often adding foreign and contrary things like water and powder and the like, thereby ruining my innate nature and properties. 

Furthermore, among a hundred thousand one finds hardly one who works with me; instead, they all seek with you and your brother and companions <note>Referring to common Gold and Mercury (Quicksilver) found in shops.</note>, in which they all fail and work falsely, as one sees in all of them—that they achieve nothing and spend their money uselessly, thereby falling into ruin and poverty. For this, you, Gold, bear the most blame, because you know particularly well that outside of me no true Gold or Silver can be made; rather, I am capable of all things. Why then do you allow the whole world to work only with you and your brother Mercury? If you were sincere and desired to act honestly, you would warn people against harm; therefore, I can rightly say with the truth that you yourself are that very deceiver.

### Gold.

I will prove it through the philosophers <note>original: "Philosophis," referring to the ancient masters of alchemy</note> that the art can be accomplished through me and my brother Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>; for read Hermes <note>original: "Hermetem," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, who writes thus: "The Sun is its Father, and the Moon is its Mother." <note>This is a famous quote from the Emerald Tablet, a foundational alchemical text.</note> For I am compared to the Sun, as the philosophers—many of whom could be cited here—write quite clearly and plainly about it: that the tinctures <term>tinctures: medicinal or transformative substances intended to "dye" or change the nature of a base metal into gold</term> as well as the metals must be composed and put together from Sulfur <note>original: "Sulphur"</note> and Mercury. And the Sulfur should be red and incombustible <note>original: "unuerbrennlich"</note>, and stable in the fire; and the Mercury should be clear, pure, and purged. And they write without any digression, calling me openly by name and saying that in me, Gold, is the well-cooked, stable, incombustible red Sulfur, which is then true and obvious to everyone: that I am the better metal and possess the best Sulfur, which cannot be burned in the fire and is entirely fixed <term>fixed: "fix," referring to a substance that remains solid and does not evaporate or change when exposed to high heat</term>.

At this, Mercury also sided with Gold and spoke: It is true what his Lord Brother Gold has recounted, and it can be proven through the aforementioned masters. Furthermore, everyone knows generally what love and unity these two have for each other above all other metals. This alone is plainly visible here: when one wishes to perform gilding <note>The process of applying a thin layer of gold to another surface</note>, one can join and unite Gold and Mercury together; what then might not happen with great effort and labor, more diligence, and a long time of work?

### The Stone.

The Stone spoke with a laughing mouth: Truly, you are both well-deserving of being laughed at for your "proofs." And I wonder, especially at you, Gold—since you boast so highly of yourself in many things and yet have no more understanding. Do you think that the ancient philosophers wrote in their writings so plainly according to common understanding, wanting to be understood exactly according to those very words?

### Gold.

These cited masters have written no untruth, and they agree with one another regarding my virtue. However, there have indeed been others who searched for my cousins and powers in other unbecoming things, such as in various herbs, animals, blood, urine, seeds, sperm <note>original: "Spermaten"</note>, and the like; and those people surely failed and perhaps also wrote falsely. But the aforementioned masters have good testimony that they truly possessed the Art; therefore, their writing is truly to be believed.

# A Dialogue of Gold and Mercury

->The Stone.<-

Do not doubt me in this, for it is all true, that they <note>The "philosophers" or ancient alchemical masters.</note> certainly possessed the Art; yet I except some whom you have cited, for there are a few among them who did not possess it for certain, but rather wrote about it only by hearsay. But where they simply use the names of Sol <note>original: "Solis"; the Sun or Gold</note> and Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"</note>, they do so for the sake of the ignorant and the unworthy, to hide the Art from them; for they well know that such people only focus on the bare letters and names, and on the written recipes and processes, and do not reflect upon the foundation of the matter. 

But the wise and industrious read with understanding and consider well how one thing agrees with another; they draw a foundation from this and thus devise, from the speculation and sayings of the philosophers, the right Matter <note>original: "Matery"</note>, which no philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus"</note> has described or indicated by its right name. They prove this themselves when they say: "Where we write most clearly according to common understanding, there we have most hidden the Art. But where we speak in figures, parables, and proverbs, there we have truly brought it to light." 

And where they withhold something regarding gold and mercury, they soon after explain themselves and say that their Gold is not common gold and their Mercury is not common mercury. For gold, by reason of its perfection, can never be further advanced <note>original: "verhindert," here meaning changed or pushed beyond its already perfect state</note>, because it has already become a metal of perfection. Even if one were to extract its colors a thousand times and work with it in a most skillful manner, it can do or color no more than the color it already possesses within itself. Therefore, the philosophers write that one should seek in imperfect things, and thus one will find perfection—just as you may read in the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosario," referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical text</note>. Likewise, Lully <note>original: "Lulius," referring to Raymond Lully, a major figure in alchemical literature</note> writes: "That which is to be improved must not be perfect; a perfect thing does not change, it sooner perishes."

->Gold.<-

I know well that they write this, but that may be understood as referring to my brother Mercury; he is still imperfect, and if we both mix with one another, then he is made perfect by me. For there is a Female and Male gender; therefore, the philosophers say the Art is entirely a homogeneous thing <term>homogeneous: original "Homogenium," meaning a substance of a single, uniform nature or kind</term>. You see this clearly in humans: no child can be born without man and woman, but only through the mixing of both. The same is also to be seen in all animals that have life.

## The Stone.

Your brother Mercury is indeed imperfect, but he is not the Mercury of the Sages. Even if you were to mix yourselves together and stand in the fire for many years, it would be impossible for you to be truly united. As soon as Mercury feels the fire, he escapes from you into the heights and sublimates <note>original: "supplimiert"; the process of a substance turning directly from a solid or liquid into a vapor</note> at the top, leaving you lying at the bottom. And if you are joined together with sharp water <note>original: "scharpffem Wasser"; typically referring to nitric acid or other strong mineral acids used to dissolve metals</note>, and are thus dissolved and coagulated, you yield nothing more than a dead powder and precipitate. If one then throws this upon imperfect metals, it does not tincture <note>original: "tingiert"; in alchemy, the power of the Stone to "stain" or transform a base metal into gold</note> them; instead, one finds only your original gold again—exactly as much gold as was added at the beginning—and your brother Mercury escapes from you entirely.

The seekers of the art of Alchemy have experienced this sufficiently for many years now and have learned it to their own detriment. But when you cite the saying of the ancients—that the Art is entirely a homogeneous substance <term>original: "Homogenium"; a substance of the same nature or kind throughout</term>, and that no child is born without a man and a woman—and you think the philosophers intend to examine you and your brother Mercury, that is worth nothing. It is poorly and incorrectly understood by you, even if they wrote it correctly and well. I tell you in truth that this is the very cornerstone that the ancients laid, upon which many thousands have stumbled and gone astray.

Do you think that metals must behave exactly like other things that have life? This is what happens with all false workers of the Art: when you read such things in the books of the philosophers, you do not fundamentally reflect on whether it agrees with what comes before or after. For what the ancient and true philosophers described regarding the Art with such figurative words is understood by me alone, and by no other thing in the world. That alone is the truth, and without it, no righteous and true gold or silver can be made.

## Gold.

God forbid! Do you not fear sin, and are you not ashamed of lies, that you are so immeasurable? How dare you claim for yourself alone everything that so many wise and learned people have written about this Art for many hundreds of years? After all, you are but an unripened, coarse poison and an unclean thing. You yourself confess that the Art is a homogeneous substance of one nature, yet you further claim that outside of yourself no true gold or silver can be made, even though it is well known that many have sought it so diligently and industriously through other ways, such as Particulars <term>original: "Particularien"; chemical processes intended to produce small amounts of gold or transform only a portion of a metal, rather than a total transformation</term>...
